events.event_narrative: A strong winter storm brought combination of moderate-to-heavy snow and strong winds across the northern Idaho Panhandle. Snow began around 1600PST bringing 6 to 12 inches of snow overnight across Bonners and Boundary Counties in locations such as Bonners Ferry, Moyie Springs, and Sandpoint.
Idaho State Highway 64 was closed, between Kamiah and New Perce, due to blowing and drifting snow. Gusty winds reached up to 40 to 60 mph across the southern Idaho Panhandle.

Snow began to accumulate at 2100PST and taper off around 1200PST the following day. A total of 6 to 8 inches of snow fell overnight across the Wenatchee area including Cashmere, Wenatchee, and Entiat.

Light snow began in the early evening hours and began to accumulate around 2000PST. Snowfall rates picked up overnight and tapered off around 1100PST the following day. Heavy snow fell overnight with an accumulation of 5 to 9 inches across the Okanogan Valley.

Light snow began in the early evening hours and began to accumulate around 1900PST. Snowfall rates picked up overnight and tapered off around 1600PST the following day. Heavy snow fell overnight with an accumulation of 7 to 11 inches across the Okanogan Highlands, including 6.5 inches at Sherman Pass.

Light snow began in the early evening hours and continued off and on over the next 24 hours. Snowfall rates picked up overnight with an accumulation of 6 to 12 inches across the northeast mountains. 49 North Ski Resort recorded 10 inches at the base in the morning of January 3rd.

US Highway 2 was closed at Stevens Pass for avalanche control at 0500PST. There was additional closure due to spin outs, blowing and drifting snow, and strong winds. Stevens Pass recorded 12 inches of snow accumulation in the morning of January 3rd.
Numerous state routes across the Washington Palouse were closed due to blowing and drifting snow. Fresh snow and strong winds led to white conditions throughout the morning.
Snow began to accumulate at 2100PST and taper off around 1200PST the following day. A total of 6 to 10 inches of snow fell overnight across the eastern Cascade slopes, from Leavenworth to Plain.

Light snow began in the late afternoon hours and began to accumulate around 1700PST. Snowfall rates picked up overnight and tapered off around 1000PST the following day. Heavy snow fell overnight with an accumulation of 6 to 12 inches down the Methow Valley.

Light snow began in the early evening hours on January 5th and heavy snow began to accumulate around midnight. Snowfall rates picked up overnight with an accumulation of 15 to 23 inches across the Methow Valley, including Twisp, Winthrop, and Carlton, by the morning. Snow began to taper off that evening with Twisp receiving a 36 hour snow accumulation of 30 inches ending 0700PST January 7th.

Across the Columbia Basin, in Moses Lake, Quincy, and Ephrata, heavy snow began falling overnight that accumulated to 5 to 10 inches by mid-morning. Quincy School District cancelled school due to the poor weather conditions.

Moderate to heavy snow fell in Republic, and surrounding areas, with an overnight 12 hour accumulation of 4 to 6 inches. Light snow continued off and on throughout the day with an additional 1 to 2 inches over the following 24 hours and ending around 0700PST on January 7th.

Moderate to heavy snow fell across northeastern Washington with an overnight, 12 hour accumulation of 4 to 5 inches in Newport, Kettle Falls, and Elk. Light snow continued off and on throughout the day with an additional 2 to 5 inches over the following 24 hours and ending around 0700PST on the 7th. Elk and Newport received a 48 hour total 7 to 10 inches of snow. There were several power outages due to the weather conditions on the 6th.

A strong winter storm brought moderate to heavy snow across the upper Columbia Basin. Snow began around 2200PST bringing 4 to 6 inches of snow overnight in locations such as Ritzville, Odessa, and Davenport. Due to the heavy snow and slick road conditions, there was a slide off on Interstate 90 near Sprague. No injuries were reported.

A strong winter storm brought moderate to heavy snow across the Spokane County. From midnight to 1600PST, there were 4 to 8 inches snow accumulation, with 5 inches measured at the Spokane International Airport. With rising daytime temperatures, the snow turned to sleet and freezing rain around 1600PST. There were 0.19 inches of ice measured at the airport from 1600 to 2000PST. Gusty winds, with a peak gust of 46 mph at the airport, led to tents collapsing at the county fair grounds and testing site.
Gusty winds peaked at 1200PST with a gust of 64 mph measured in Pomeroy. There were reports of downed trees and roofs damaged due to the strong winds.
Sustained strong winds and fresh snow created drifting snow and near zero visibility across the Waterville Plateau. There were numerous road closures and cars stranded on U.S. Highway 2.

There was a major winter storm that led to a state of emergency in the city of Leavenworth. Light snow early January 5th intensified overnight and continued into the early evening hours of the following day. Locations, such as Leavenworth, Coles Corner, and Plain, received 20 to 30 inches of snow in less than 24 hours. A two-day total snow accumulation of 27 inches was measured at Blewett Pass. The heavy snowfall led to numerous roof slides with widespread road closures and power outages. With the fresh snow, strong winds created blowing snow and snow drifts.

A major winter storm dumped 30 to 40 inches of snow across Stehekin and Stevens Pass over 48 hours. Large avalanches, with blowing and drifting snow, led to a seven day closure of US Highway 2 at Stevens Pass. There were more than 200 snow slides in Tumwater Canyon, east of the pass. Some slides measured 30 to 35 feet in height.

A major winter storm brought heavy, fresh snow, and freezing rain followed by strong winds to the Washington Palouse. There were 24 hour snow accumulations of 5 to 10 inches in Pullman, Colfax, and Oaksdale on January 6th. Blowing and drifting snow closed roads and led to accidents due to poor visibility and strong winds. A semi-truck rolled over on US Highway 195 shortly after the Pullman Airport and ASOS site reported a peak gust of 58 mph on the 7th. There was one minor injury.

Moderate to heavy snow fell in the Okanogan Valley, with an overnight, 12 hour accumulation of 5 to 11 inches in Okanogan, Malott, and Tonasket. Light snow continued off and on throughout the day with an additional 1 to 2 inches in parts of the valley.

A strong winter storm brought moderate to heavy snow, with some freezing rain, across the Wenatchee area along the Columbia River. Snow accumulations were significant - 24 hour totals from 15 to 25 inches and 48 hour totals reaching 20 to 30 inches. There were reports of 2 inches of snow per hour for the first 12 hours of the storm. Near Chelan and Ardenvoir, there were numerous large snow slides leading to the closure of State Route 97. Blowing snow, due to strong winds, create poor visibility and difficult driving conditions.

A strong winter storm brought heavy snow with strong winds to the northern Idaho Panhandle. Locations across the Coeur d'Alene area received overnight snow accumulations of 4 to 6 inches and reached 7 to 12 inches by the morning of January 7th. On the morning of January 6th, a vehicle slid off the road due to slick road conditions along the Lake Coeur d'Alene roads. No known injuries.

A strong winter storm brought heavy snow with strong winds to the northern Idaho Panhandle. Locations across Bonner and Boundary County received overnight snow accumulations of 3 to 6 inches and reached 12 to 19 inches by the morning of January 7th. For many, the snow melted throughout the day and re-froze overnight the leading to icy roads. No known collisions, but multiple power outages reported.

Moderate to heavy snow fell across central Idaho Panhandle with an overnight, 12 hour accumulation of 5 to 10 inches in Viola and Moscow on January 6th. Light snow continued off and on throughout the day with an additional 3 inches in Moscow over the following 24 hours and ending around 0700PST on the 7th. There were reports of blowing and drifting snow on US Highway 95 on the 6th. The Latah County government closed buildings in Moscow due to the poor weather and driving conditions.
A period of moderate snow in the central Panhandle and Lookout Pass led to numerous car accidents, disabled cars, and road blockages. There were several power outages across the area.
Gusty winds reached peak speed of 61 mph at Corral Creek. The gusty winds throughout the afternoon led to drifting, fresh snow with an accompanying road closure.
A cold core funnel was spotted near Lewiston Hill by several public sources. The location was estimated based on reports and pictures. It did not impact people or property.

There were locations across the central Idaho Panhandle that the Coeur d'Alene River reached action or minor flood stage: Cataldo and Enaville. Low laying areas, fields, and campgrounds saw minor flooding. The Coeur d'Alene River View Road, from Cataldo to Kingston, was closed due to water seeping over the road. Enaville had minor road flooding and closures as well. The flooding was initiated by heavy rainfall and snow melt. There were no injuries or fatalities.

There were locations across the central Idaho Panhandle that the Coeur d'Alene River reached action or minor flood stage: Dudley, Medimont, and Cataldo. Low laying areas, fields, and campgrounds saw minor flooding. The Coeur d'Alene River View Road, from Cataldo to Kingston, was closed due to water seeping over the road. The flooding was initiated by heavy rainfall and snow melt. There were no injuries or fatalities.

The Moscow-Pullman Daily News reported that the rising Palouse River, near Potlatch, led to several parks and a softball field flooded. The Palouse River reached action stage from mid-day March 3rd until March 4th. The flooding was initiated by heavy rainfall and snow melt. There were no injuries or fatalities.

US Highway 2 was closed at Stevens Pass for avalanche control at 0115 PST on February 28th due to heavy, wet snow. The pass remained closed until 1045 PST. Snow began mid-day in the Cascade Crest on February 27th. Stevens Pass recorded 22 inches of snow accumulation in the 24 hour period from 0700 PST February 27th to 0700 PST February 28th. In the same time period, the Lucerne and Stehekin COOP stations recorded between 20 and 24 inches.

Snow began mid-day in the eastern Cascade valleys on February 27th. Numerous observation sites in Leavenworth and Plain recorded 14 to 16 inches of snow accumulation in the 24 hour time period from 0800 PST February 27th to 0800 PST February 28th.

Snow began to accumulate at 0000 PST on February 28th and taper off in the late evening around 2100 PST. A total of 8 to 10 inches of snow fell overnight, February 27th to 28th, across the northern Idaho Panhandle in locations such as Sandpoint, Elmira, and Coolin.

US Highway 2 was closed at Stevens Pass for avalanche control at 0430PST. Stevens Pass recorded 23 inches of snow accumulation in the morning of January 20th. A majority of the snowfall accumulated overnight.

With numerous reports from broadcast media and the Washington Department of Transportation, early morning snowfall had a major impact on the commute due to the accumulations and icy roadways. Many accidents, rollovers, and slide offs occurred in the Spokane Metropolitan area. With icy roadways, numerous roads across hilly areas were closed, or unable to navigate, due to lack of traction. County and state officials were out plowing and deicing following the intense morning snowfall.

US Highway 2 at Stevens Pass recorded 23.5 inches of snow accumulation over almost 36 hour time period. There were high winds, with gusts up to 58 mph, that led to blowing snow and poor visibilities. The Stevens Pass Ski Resort was closed on April 4th due to power outages from the weather conditions and avalanche mitigation work.

Site near Athol Idaho reported a Southwest 59MPH gust at 1430LST. Winds were strong from 1330-1530LST with gusts in the range of 30 to 50 MPH across the zone. The winds caused downed power lines and outages affecting around 2400 customers.

Coeur D'Alene Airport(KCOE) recorded a gust of 55MPH at 1329LST. Winds across the rest of the zone ranged in the upper 20s to low 50s MPH for the hours of 07-23LST. There were reports of downed power lines affecting at least 100 customers.
Mt Margaret Sensor reported gust of 53 MPH at 1445. The zone had power outages impacting around 50 customers.
Shirrod Hill recorded gust of 63 MPH at 1500. The Lewiston airport also recorded a gust of 59MPH at 1330.
Corral Creek Raws recorded gust of 56 MPH at 1349. Craigmont and Lewiston Cwops recorded gusts of 45 and 41 MPH.

Site near Pullman WA recorded a gust of 60 MPH at 1200LST. Other stations across the zone recorded gusts of 40s to low 50s MPH.

Mesonet Beverly recorded a gust of 81 MPH at 1230LST. Several other sites in the zone recorded gusts into the upper 40s and low 50s. The winds caused blowing dust to reduce visibility to near 2 miles.

Mesonet in the Washtucna area recorded a gust of 54 at 1630LST. Several other sites recorded gusts into the upper 40s to low 50s. Power outage in Wilbur affected 52 customers. Winds also broke 1 inch thick tree limbs and blew shingles off roofs in the Spring Canyon area East of Grand Coulee.

Spokane International Airport recorded wind gust of 60 MPH at 1453LST. Other wind gusts across the zone ranged from 35 to 50 MPH. There were numerous power outages of around 7000 customers. Trees fell over the roadways of Hwy-195, I-90, and Cedar Road. A tree fell on house in South Hill area with minimal damage.
Deer Park Airport recorded a gust of 54 MPH at 1407LST. There multiple reports of trees down in the zone along SR-25, US-395, and SR-211. Around 4200 customers had power outages.

Tornado followed a due west-to-east path along W. Greenwood Road. The damage indicators along the road mainly consisted of trees that were uprooted or snapped. Several powerline poles were brought down by fallen trees toward the middle of the damage path. No substantial damage was noted to structures along the path. A video that was shared by a resident near N. Kynan Rd. showed a very weak circulation moving due east along W. Greenwood Rd. This video footage confirms the timing and width of the tornado. Residents in the vicinity of Russell Rd. confirmed no further damage beyond this point.

Tornado generated a discontinuous line of damage first observed near the intersection of E. 9th Avenue and S. Cuba St. Video footage confirms a funnel cloud lowered at times and was disorganized as it moved from west to east. A second area of more significant damage was observed along 6th Avenue that included roof damage and many trees uprooted or snapped at the base. The third and longest track of damage began near E. 5th Ave and S. McKinnon Rd and included significant damage to trees and unsecured items along E 4th Avenue. The most noteworthy damage along E. 4th Ave was to a line of travel trailers, vehicles, and boats, several of which were tossed or displaced. Numerous large ponderosa pine trees were uprooted or snapped along E. 4th Avenue before the tornado again lifted. The final isolated area of damage was located along E. 5th Avenue between S. Coleman Rd and S Grand Rd. Security camera footage confirmed brief circulation at the surface along with two downed trees along the southern edge of the track before the tornado lifted for the final time.

A small funnel cloud dissipated shortly after formation. There is no indication that the circulation ever made contact with the ground. The location is estimated from social media shared by the media.

A strong thunderstorm dropped hail ranging from half an inch to 2.75. Most hail reports ranged from 0.75 to 1.5. A 2.75 size was reported around Newman Lake at 1700PST. It traveled from Albion WA to Newman Lake WA around 1525PST to 1715PST. It damaged at least 15000 acres of crops, broke windows and damaged siding of homes in Liberty Lake, and dented numerous vehicles.

Thunderstorm winds moved North from Oakesdale WA to Rockford WA. A weather station clocked gusts to 60 mph. It damaged or knocked down power lines and over 100 trees. It caused power outages around 3200 customers.

Most hail reports ranged from 0.75 inch to 1.5 inch. An estimated 2.75 inch size was reported around Hauser. Wind  also knocked down power lines near Carlin Bay airport.

The fire started in the Williams Lake area around 1330PST by suspected human cause. It spread in timber and reached 1868 acres. The estimated cost of the fire is around three million dollars.

Farm equipment working a field sparked a wildfire that was quickly spread through grass fields by winds. It burned from August 4-6. It burned 2500 acres. Six homes and eight outbuildings were destroyed.

A combine caught fire South of Hay. The fire spread into nearby grass and grew to 5680 acres. It burned from the afternoon of August 4 until August 7. The driver of the combine was injured. No structures lost.
The Mohr fire started Aug 8 by undetermined cause. It was controlled by Aug 21. It burned in grassland and nor structures were lost. It burned 6944 acres.
Lightning started the White River Fire. It started burning August 11 and lasted through the end of the month. It is burning timber in rugged wilderness. No structures lost. It has burned 5640 acres.

Lightning started the Irving Fire. It started burning August 11 and lasted through the end of the month. It is burning timber in rugged wilderness. No structures lost. It has burned 5639 acres. The fire has been combined with the White River Fire.
The Thor Fire is burning approximately 5 miles east of Sullivan Lake in heavy timber and steep terrain. The fire was caused by lightning and discovered on August 13, 2022. It has burned 1300 acres.
The Wagner Road Fire is located 12 miles west of St. John, WA. This fire started on Thursday, August 18th and has burned approximately 7,381 acres of rangeland, stubble and standing wheat.
Lightning started the Alligator Wildfire on August 25. It was contained on September 29. It burned through timber in rugged terrain. It was 800 acres in size.

The Bear Gulch Fire was lightning caused and detected on August 18th, 2022. It is located approximately 6 miles east of Murray, ID, and is within a mile of the Idaho/Montana state line. It has burned 100 acres of timber and brush.

The Columbus Fire was detected on August 22nd, 2022. It is located approximately 6 miles northeast of Murray, ID, and is within a mile of the Idaho/Montana state line. This fire was likely a holdover lightning start from the same storm that started the Bear Gulch Fire. It has burned 2298 acres.

The Russell Mountain Fire was reported early afternoon on August 24, 2022. It is located within the Selkirk Mountain Range on the Bonners Ferry Ranger District of the Idaho Panhandle National Forests. It is approximately 10 miles southwest of Copeland Idaho. It has burned 4811 acres of timber and brush. The Kootenai River Complex consists of the Eneas Peak, Katka, Russell Mountain, Scotch Creek, and Trout Fires. They have combined to burn 25401 acres. Cost of the Complex is around 15 million dollars.

The Blackburn Fire is located just north of the Heller Creek Campground near the headwaters of the St. Joe River. It was discovered on August 14. Several other fires were detected the same weekend, all from a single lightning storm days before. It has burned 360 acres of timber.

The Columbus Fire was detected on August 22 and active through September. It is located approximately 6 miles northeast of Murray, ID, and is within a mile of the Idaho/Montana state line. This fire was likely a holdover lightning start from the same storm that started the Bear Gulch Fire. It has burned 2298 acres.

The Russell Mountain Fire was reported early afternoon on August 24, 2022 and remained active through September. It is located within the Selkirk Mountain Range on the Bonners Ferry Ranger District of the Idaho Panhandle National Forests. It is approximately 10 miles southwest of Copeland Idaho. It has burned 4811 acres of timber and brush. The Kootenai River Complex consists of the Eneas Peak, Katka, Russell Mountain, Scotch Creek, and Trout Fires. They have combined to burn 25401 acres. Cost of the Complex is around 15 million dollars.

At approximately 0625 PST, SPD responded to a commercial vehicle versus tree collision at Highway 2 near Sunset Frontage Road.  Initial callers reported that a tree had fallen onto the highway and struck an eastbound truck, causing the truck to leave the roadway.  Spokane Police and Washington State Patrol responded and found that the two occupants of the truck were deceased at the scene.  Collision investigators with the SPD Major Crimes Unit (MCU) also responded to assist with the investigation.  Highway 2 (eastbound) was briefly shutdown during the investigation. At this time, investigators believe that heavy winds this morning caused the tree to dislodge from the ground and fall across the roadway. Spokane Airport ASOS recorded a gusts of 30 MPH at the time of incident.

Blizzard conditions were experienced at Stevens Pass. The area saw wind gusts up to 81 mph causing downed trees. Heavy snow reduced visibility to near zero miles.
Observer reported 14.5 inches of snow 9 miles west of Lucerne.
High winds sustained in the 40 to 50 mph range with gusts up to 73 mph caused power outages for 2096 customers.
High winds with sustained in the upper 30 to 45 mph and gusts up to 58 mph. It downed a few trees and branches around the Milan area.

High winds of sustained 35 to 45 mph and gusts up to 68 mph impacted the Spokane area. Damage included numerous trees and power lines down through the Spokane, South Hill, and Dishman areas. One tree fell on an unoccupied vehicle. Another fell on a mobile home. No injuries reported. Cost is estimated.

Mission Creek flooded a residence due to debris from 2025 Labor Mountain fire burn scar causing a backup on the river. Other than this spot, creek was within its banks. Time estimated from river crest.
Social media shared a video showing water Company Creek Road. Exact location and time estimated.
EM reported Wenatchee River rerouted in a spot following December 2025 flood. Current river levels are resulting in flooding near Sleepy Hollow Road. Time and exact location estimated.
Large road washout on Green Hollow Road at MP5, with large boulders in road and mud flowing across road.
Heavy rain led to mud and water over Banner Road and Palouse Albion Road.
Heavy rain led to road washout, mud and rocks on Upper Union Flat Road.
Mesonet station Lakeview Triple SWTZ1 reported a max gust of 57 mph.

An EF0 tornado was observed two miles south of Highway 2 between Creston and Wilbur.  This was one of four tornadoes that occurred within a 25 minute period.  This tornado tracked west-northwest and stayed just south of Ramsey Road.

An EF0 tornado formed two miles south of Highway 2 between Creston and Wilbur, then tracked northwest before dissipating less than a mile from Highway 2.  This tornado was one of four tornadoes observed in a 25 minute period in the area.

An EF0 tornado formed two miles south of Highway 2 between Wilbur and Creston.  This tornado tracked west before dissipating.  This was one of four tornadoes that occurred within a 25 minute period in the area.

An EF0 tornado formed two miles south of Highway 2 between Creston and Wilbur.  This tornado tracked to the west-southwest before dissipating.  This was one of four tornadoes that occurred within a 25 minute period.
A short-lived tornado from a thunderstorm touched down and caused damage to two structures.  It also uprooted and snapped numerous coniferous trees,  many with trunk diameters greater than 15 inches.

Strong downburst winds from a thunderstorm knocked out power to 2,000 customers in Clarkston when a tree blew down on a power line. An addition, a portable carport was blown into another power line. Another tree was uprooted knocking down another power line and landing on a shop.
Mud and debris was observed flowing over Highway 23.  In addition, water was observed over the road at Rock Lake Road and Glorfield Road.
Water and mud was observed over North Palouse Road near the Golf Course.
A funnel cloud was observed for five minutes along Highway 28.
Three inch diameter tree limbs and heavy metal lawn furniture were blown over by strong thunderstorm winds.
A trained spotter reported wind gusts of 66 mph from a severe thunderstorm.
In addition to the nickel size hail, 0.48 inches of rain also fell in 27 minutes.
Several trees were blown down after a severe thunderstorm passed through Priest River.  Roof damage was also observed from the storm.
Priest Lake Ranger Station reported numerous trees down along Idaho Highway 57.  There was also a loss of power in the area.
Four to five 100 foot trees were blown down.

Numerous powerlines were blown down and tree tops were snapped off.  Trees were estimated to be 25-30 feet high and 2-2.5 inches in diameter.  The top of one tree was thrown through the rooftop of an RV.  The metal roof of a home was also lifted in the air.
Multiple uprooted trees damaged at least three homes on Kalispell Bay of Priest Lake.
Several trees were blown down on structures in Newport after a severe thunderstorm tracked through the area.
Sheriff reported downed trees across Cedonia and Addy roads.
The Sheriff reported the public utility company had to clear the road and repair powerlines at Lesig Road and Locke Road and clear downed trees.
A strong thunderstorm knocked down a pine tree that fell on a home on Pete's Retreat Road by Curlew Lake. Another large tree was blown down in the area as well.
The roof at an Athletic Club in Omak was damaged from strong outflow winds from a thunderstorm. In addition, the winds toppled a large weeping willow tree onto a vending truck.
Mature pines were blown over on highway between Rice and Gifford.
Neighbors reported roof damage from strong winds associated with a thunderstorm.
Several trees were uprooted in the area.
Two one and a half foot diameter trees were uprooted and four ten inch diameter trees were snapped 15 feet up.
Mature Pines were uprooted along Highway 31 north and south of Metaline.
Mature Pines were snapped off and landed along Highway 57 and Reeder Bay Road.

Four to five pine trees downed by downburst winds from a thunderstorm.  Yard furniture was tossed about and two small empty trailers were overturned.  Two campers had minor damage and numerous small tree limbs were downed.

An EF0 tornado touched down five miles northeast of Moses Lake on Northeast Road P.  Non-continuous track from south to northwest for one-half to one-third of a mile.  The tornado had an estimated width of 100 yards with winds of 65 to 85 miles per hour.  The tornado lifted a section of roof that was unattached and sitting on the ground or leaning against something on the ground. The wind lifted this unattached roof about 20 feet off the ground and dropped it 30 feet from its original location onto the old barn, destroying it.  A grain silo was damaged by the tornado.  Numerous large tree branches were downed, including one tossed 300 feet from the tree.  Numerous shingles were spread 120 yards.  The time of the tornado is estimated from 5:15 PST to 5:20 PST.
Very heavy rain led water running down the road and ditches along Highway Two.
Large hail from a thunderstorm accumulated to a depth of six inches.
Several farmers in the area reported wind gusting to approximately 60 miles per hour.

Strong winds from a gust front damaged Simplot's Moses Lake Plant, forcing it to close down for 24 hours for repairs.  The damage partially ripped the siding from the wall in the raw potato receiving area.
Strong wind from a thunderstorm in Kamiah blew down several trees.
A severe thunderstorm brought high wind gusts that blew over several trees.  Pea size hail and heavy rain was also observed with the thunderstorm.
High wind gusts from a thunderstorm blew down several trees.
Estimated wind gusts of 60 miles per hour were observed from a thunderstorm.
Road damage from heavy rain was observed on Dunlap, Airport, Powerline, Fisher, and Laufer roads.
Road damage from heavy rain was observed on Roberts, Sandhill, Wilsey, Tiede, Woodlawn, and Mission Creek roads.
Road damage from heavy rain was observed on Johnson and Synder roads.
Road damage from heavy rain was observed on Drake, Gibler, Hull, Ida, Lawyer, McLead, Miller, and Z West roads.

A tornado was spotted for a brief period by the public just south of New Hope Road near Lawyer Canyon approximately six miles southeast of Craigmont. The tornado then moved into Idaho County (see Storm Data for Idaho).
Large trees were uprooted in a park, as well as a tent structure blown over and wrapped around a tree.  Part of a roof was also blown off a structure.

Thousands of people went without power near the Viola area on the Idaho Palouse as 11 transmission structures went down in a domino effect on Highway 95 between Moscow and Potlach.  The highway was shut down for a four mile stretch.
Several CocoRahs reports of seven to twelve inches with as much as eighteen inches reported near the Cascade crest.
Widespread three to six inches of snow fell overnight with an isolated report of nine inches.

Flooding was reported on the Coeur D'Alene River along Coeur D'Alene River Road into Enaville and downstream to the border of Kootenai County near Cataldo.  Coeur D'Alene River Road was closed between mile post 2 and 19 due to flooding of three to four feet of water over portions of the roadway.  Other reports of flooding occurred at the north end of Montgomery Gulch and Moon Gulch.  Moon Gulch road was washed out crossing Beaver Creek trapping an individual on his property, multiple motor vehicles and homes flooded, and landslides were also reported.  The Coeur D'Alene River at Cataldo went above its flood stage of 43 feet at 2330PST on the 16th; crested at 45.94 feet at 2345PST on the 17th; and then went back below flood stage at 415PST on the 19th.

Moderate flooding occurred along the Coeur D'Alene River in Cataldo resulting in road closers of CCC Road and Latour Road.  The flooding in Cataldo was the western most extent of moderate flooding along the Coeur D'Alene River.  More extensive damage was felt upstream in Shoshone County.  Minor flooding continued further downstream from Cataldo to Harrison along the Coeur D'Alene River.  High water levels and strong currents on the Coeur D'Alene River caused a float home and two boat houses to break free from the Harrison Dock Builders (HDB) Marine in Harrison and drift down river into Coeur D'Alene Lake.  The Coeur D'Alene River at Cataldo went above its flood stage of 43 feet at 2330PST on the 16th; crested at 45.94 feet at 2345PST on the 17th; and then went back below flood stage at 415PST on the 19th.

Flooding was reported along the St. Joe River from Avery to Calder.  Avery Creek rose above its banks and flooded parts of the old Forest Service building and nearby residences in the town of Avery.  The old highway from Marble Creek to Avery was washed out as well.  Mudslides and high water wiped out sections of Calder Road and Trout Creek Road near Calder.  More flooding was reported along the St. Joe River downstream of Calder into Benewah County.  On the 17th, the St. Joe River at Calder went above its flood stage of 13 feet at 1045PST; crested at 13.18 feet at 1445PST; and then went back below flood stage at 2000PST.

Significant flooding reported along the St. Joe River Road from St. Maries to Avery in Shoshone County as the St. Joe River spilled over its banks.  The road to St. Joe City was completely under water and flooding reported five miles up St. Maries River Road at Kittle Loop.  The St. Joe River at St. Maries went above its flood stage of 32.5 feet at 1023PST on the 17th; crested at 35.97 feet at 905PST on the 18th; and then went back below flood stage at 500PST on the 20th.

Described as a moderate flood event with multiple roads inundated with water where roads crossed streams and creeks in the area.  Flooding reported on roadways with road closures in Potlatch along the Palouse River and in Paradise Creek, and on Highway 95 near Flannigan Creek; in Moscow along Paradise Creek; and on Highway 8 at milepost 21 between Troy and Deary.  The Palouse River at Potlach went above its flood stage of 15 feet at 1630PST on the 16th; crested at 16.5 feet at 530PST on the 17th; and then went back below flood stage at 615PST on the 18th.  No damage was reported.

The Palouse River at Palouse overflowed its banks inundating portions of downtown.  The hardest hit were low lying areas, where water surrounded homes and covered nearly all of Hayton Green Park on the west end of town.  A basement of a local resident and a former school gymnasium were flooded on Main Street.  Additional flooding was reported along the Palouse River upstream in Latah County.  The Palouse River at Potlach went above its flood stage of 15 feet at 1630PST on the 16th; crested at 16.5 feet at 530PST on the 17th; and then went back below flood stage at 615PST on the 18th.  No damage was reported.

Nearly 150 traffic accidents were attributed to light ice accumulation on area roadways due to freezing rain.  Numerous damaged or disabled vehicles were reported on I-90 through Spokane and Spokane Valley with traffic brought to a standstill in spots along the freeway.  At least six accidents were reported in Lincoln County.  One collision at the intersection of State Route 2 near Oehlwein Road east of Davenport resulted in 3 injuries of two teenage girls and one adult male.

Strong winds reported in Desert Aire near Mattawa resulted in two buildings receiving roof damage.  This was an isolated report of wind damage as the strongest wind gusts seemed to stay primarily to the southwestern portion of Grant County.  Land-line telephone service was out for a portion of Grant County as well.
The exact time of the landslide is unknown; however, the accident was reported to have occurred Sunday night.
Snowfall amounts ranged from three to four inches in Omak to six inches in Brewster.  Malott and Okanogan reported five inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four inches in Mansfield to six inches in Waterville.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four inches in Chewelah and Newport to just over five inches in Colville.
Snowfall amounts ranged from two to four inches in southern portions of the zone to five inches in the north including Republic and Christina Lake.

Widespread snowfall amounts of three to four inches with Mead and northwestern areas of Spokane reporting four to five inches.  Precipitation ended with a brief period of freezing rain producing a light glaze of ice on top of the snow.  A newspaper article reported several accidents along interstate 90 during the morning commute in the Spokane area.
Widespread snowfall amounts of four to eight inches with several reports of seven to fifteen inches northeast of Sandpoint.  SNOTELS indicated ten to twenty inches of snow in the mountains.
Widespread snowfall amounts of five to six inches.
Widespread snowfall amounts of four to five inches valleys with an isolated report of seven inches in Mullan.  Ski resorts and SNOTEL data in the zone reported eight to fourteen inches.

Extremely icy roads helped to cause multiple vehicle collisions and closure of several Grant County schools includng Ephrata, Moses Lake, Royal City, and Warden.  Around forty vehicle collisions were reported to the sheriff's office.  Many of those collisions caused only minor damage to vehicles and no serious injuries.  There was one serious injury which resulted when debris from the collision of a truck and parked vehicles (from an ealier accident) struck a pedestrian.  A propane semi-truck rolled over and shut down Dodson Road for nearly ten hours.
Extremely icy roads helped to cause multiple vehicle collisions and closure of several Grant and Lincoln County schools includng Almira-Coulee-Hartline Districts.
Icy roads lead to twenty-five or more collisions in Grant County.  Schools were delayed two hours.
Icy roads lead to several vehicle collisions in Grant County.  Schools were delayed two hours in Grant, western Adams, and western Lincoln counties.

Four to nine inches of snow was reported with the first round of snow which fell between the 21st and 22nd.  A second wave of moisture resulted in two to five inches of snow between the 22nd and 23rd.  A third wave of moisture interacted with an arctic boundary the evening of the 23rd into the morning of the 24th resulting in an additional three to eight inches of snow.  Four day snowfall totals in the valleys ranged from eight to fifteen inches.  In the mountains, three to five feet of snow fell over the four day period with the most impressive total coming from Lookout Ski Resort which received 52 inches of new snow throughout the period.

Two rounds of heavy snow moved through the area resulting in two-day snow totals ranging from eight to sixteen inches.  During the early morning hours of the 22nd, a semi-truck lost control coming down the north grade into Bonners Ferry, crashed through the jersey barrier, and nearly went over an embankment.  No injuries were reported however, the truck's fuel tank was punctured spilling one hundred gallons of diesel fuel along the highway.

A third round of heavy snow in three days brought an additional three to six inches of new snow.  Arctic air began spilling into the region resulting in sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts up to 38 mph at the Sandpoint Airport.  A combination of heavy snow from the previous two days, single digit temperatures causing the snow to become light and fluffy, and strong northeast winds resulted in widespread areas of snow and blowing snow.

Sustained winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts to 47 mph were recorded at the Sandpoint Airport with frequent visibilities of a quarter mile.  A trained spotter in Naples, Idaho reported six birch trees, approximately six inches in diameter, were blown down due to the strong winds.  Additional reports from trained spotters and law enforcement confirmed blowing snow and large drifts along highway 95 from Bonners Ferry to Athol, Idaho.
Snowfall amounts varied from four to eight inches with isolated locations receiving around a foot.

The Coeur D'Alene airport reported sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts to 40 mph along with visibilities at or below half a mile due to snow and blowing snow.  Travel was severely disrupted along highway 95, highway 41, and Interstate 90 due to blowing snow.  All school districts were closed on the 24th.
Snowfall amounts over a two and a half day period ranged from eight to fifteen inches.
Snowfall totals ranged from four to eight inches through midnight on the 24th of February.

The Spokane International ASOS reported sustained winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts in excess of 30 mph.  This combined with snow and blowing snow created visibilities near a quarter of a mile.  State Route 195 from Spangle to Rosalia and Highway 27 from Fairfield to Tekoa were both closed due to blowing snow.  Three foot snowdrifts were reported in Airway Heights.  An additional three to six inches of snow fell the morning of the 24th increasing storm total snowfall amounts between seven and fourteen inches.  Spokane and other Lincoln county school districts closed school on February 24th.
A spotter four miles west of Anatone received twenty-two inches of snow over the three day period.
Several rounds of highly convective snowfall over a three day period resulted in three day snowfall totals ranging from eight to twenty inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four to seven inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four to six inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches.

Strong winds in the range of 45 to 55 mph were reported from 2000PST through just after midnight.  By 2000PST, 369 customers were reportedly out of power.  A tall ponderosa pine estimated to be three feet in diameter snapped during the event on Trevino Drive in Coeur d'Alene.

Numerous reports of traffic accidents were reported in the Silver Valley due to this storm, which carried over into March 1st.  The Idaho State Police reported seven crashes and fourteen slide-offs.  One fatality was reported near Mullan, ID, but the gender and age of the deceased person is unknown.

A landslide blocked Tunk Valley Road for about three hours at the hairpin turn northeast of Riverside.  Another small mudslide impacted Riverside-Eastside Road.  All roads were cleared by the afternoon of the 14th.

Minor flooding was observed along Bridge Street in Moscow as water overflowed its banks along Paradise Creek.   The City of Moscow utilized sandbags and temporary gravel walls to contain the flood waters.
Heavy snowfall resulted in school closures for the Garfield-Palouse and Colton school districts.

Two large debris flows occurred around noon along Forest Road 208. The first slide was near the intersection of Lost Creek.  The second slide was near the intersection of Clee Circle Road.  No injuries were reported however 14 residents were trapped due to impassible roads and two of these residents had to be evacuated by the sheriff for medical appointments.  The road blocked access to six permanent residences.  There was an estimated 25,000 cubic yards of rock and mud over the road with the larger slide and 8000 cubic yards associated with the smaller slide.  The debris slide was still sliding the first week of April.  The estimated cost to remove the earth and fix any damage to the road was 330 thousand dollars.
Excessive runoff into Hauser Lake caused the lake to expand out of its banks flooding portions of Hauser Lake Road between Matheson and Ragged Ridge roads.
North Latah County Road Department reported water over portions of Hatter Creek Road.
North Latah County Road Department reported water over roadways along portions of Randle Flat Creek Road and Driscoll Ridge Road near Troy, Idaho.
A trained spotter reported minor flooding of First Creek which resulted in some damage along First Creek Road.

Multiple debris slides occurred along Highway 2 between mile markers 99 and 84.  |The largest slide, which occurred in the Tumwater Canyon, was six to eight feet deep.  Three-day rainfall amounts near the debris slides ranged from two to five inches.  Highway 2 was closed from March 31st through April 3rd.

A culvert measuring 24 inches in diameter and 50 feet in length became plugged allowing water to run over Old Coeur D Alene River Road.  The water washed out some of the shoulder and road surface.  The culvert was severely damaged and will need to be replaced.

A 28 year old male skier triggered an avalanche at the top of Hooky Bowl located near Mt. Cashmere.  The slab depth, at the point where the avalanche was triggered, was just over a half a foot in depth and increased in depth up to three and one quarter foot.  The horizontal dimension of the slab was approximately 3 feet by 200 feet.  The skier was carried through several groups of trees and funneled down a steep gully.  After the avalanche ended, the skier was found alive with one leg dismembered and the other leg suffering significant fractures.  Other skiers arrived within two minutes of the event and performed lifesaving measures immediately, however, patient eventually died as a result of his injuries.

The emergency manager of Bonner County relayed numerous road damage reports from across the county due to flooding from March 31st.  The roads included in this report were Fish Creek, Sandborn Creek, West Shingle Mill, Bottle Bay, Dufort, Peninsula, Eastriver, Blacktail, Beare, Eureka, Helen Thompson, Moore Loop, South First Street, Spring Haven Drive, Wells, North Riley Creek, Mountain Creek, Snow Valley, Forest Siding, Comeback Lane, Cocolalla Loop, and LeClerc Road.  Several other private roads were also damaged from flooding.

Residence of Crescent Bar, approximately 2.5 miles west-southwest of Quincy, reported strong winds around 1945PST Thursday evening.  Multiple large, shallow rooted trees were toppled over and numerous heavy red clay tiles were blown off on the south side of the Crescent Bar Condos.  Two windows were shattered by the roof tiles as they were blown off.  Funneling effects down into the canyon off the east slopes of the northern Cascades or developing mountain waves may have been a contributing factor to the localized nature of the wind damage from this event.
Ski resorts in the area reported around a foot and a half of storm total snowfall with Mount Spokane reporting 20 inches and 49 Degrees North reporting 15 inches.

Storm total snowfall across the mountains was estimated at around a foot and a half to over two feet from the morning hours on March 9th through the early morning hours on March 11th.  Silver Mountain ski resort picked up 28 inches of total snowfall from these systems and Lookout Pass ski resort picked up 15 inches.

A pickup truck heading west on Government Way lost control near the intersection of Aubrey L. White Parkway and flipped off the road.  The 47 year old male driver was pronounced dead on the scene shortly after law enforcement arrived.

A large debris slide destroyed outbuildings, vehicles, and portions of an orchard in the 6100 block of Campbell Road in Peshastin, WA on the afternoon of March 27th.  Damage from the mudlside mainly impacted one resident who reported that his barn, shop, pump house, and three large vehicles were completely destroyed.  The resident at this property reported that the slide ripped a hole through his land that he described as a 600-foot long channel 100 feet wide and 10 to 50 feet deep.

A large debris flow which began around noon on March 30th along Forest Road 208 continued to slide as of April 20th. The slide blocked access to six permanent residences.  There was an estimated 25,000 cubic yards of rock and mud over the road.  The estimated cost to remove the earth and fix any damage to the road was 330 thousand dollars.

Flooding of several creeks and streams resulted in damage, closures, and evacuations along numerous roads along with minor flooding of six homes.  Roads that were damaged include Webb Road, McCormack Ridge Road, Garden Gulch Road near Highway 95, Cottonwood Creek Road, Flatiron Road, and Mission Creek Road near Highway 95.  Reservation Line Road and Webb Canal Road were also closed for a short time due to flooding.  The worst of the flooding occurred along Webb Creek which flooded several low-lying areas, including the junction with Highway 95 and the junction with McCormick Ridge Road where reports stated water covered the bridge at the junction of McCormick Ridge Road.  The Web Store Smoke Shop was inundated with approximately one foot of water.  Around six homes along Webb Road experienced flooding up to the homes foundations.  Mission Creek also spilled out of its banks with water reported to be flowing down Mission Creek Road, over the Mission Creek Bridge, and into nearby pastures and front yards. Sweetwater Creek, Lapwai Creek and Cottonwood Creek also had minor flooding with the Spalding church suffering the greatest damage.  A culvert was plugged along Lapwai Creek near the intersection of Highway 95 and Garden Gulch Road causing road damage and a two day road closure.  A plugged culvert along Sweetwater Creek led to approximately 30 feet of pavement erosion along Flatiron Road and 1500 feet of ditch and shoulder erosion.  The Emergency Manager of Nez Perce County estimated flood damage to the roads was around $74,000 with most of the damage along Flatiron Road and Garden Gulch Road near Highway 95.  On the Nez Perce Indian Reservation, at least one septic tank was compromised due to flooding.  The flooding caused basement flooding in at least four homes throughout the reservation.  Two private bridges were destroyed or compromised and classified as unsafe for use.
A landslide was observed along Flatiron Road at the south end of Sweetwater Creek near Waha.
A house in the Waha area (40486 Hawkview Lane) and its hillside had minor sliding.  Residents at the location were evacuated by the Sheriff's Office.  Exact time of the slide was unknown.
A landslide was observed on the Old Winchester Grade above a pond which is adjacent to a private residence.  Exact time of the slide was unknown.

The Lewiston Tribune reported a couple of small mudslides along highway 12 late Monday, April 4th that resulted in one road closure and some lane blockages.  The exact time and location of each slide was unknown.

Flooding of Lawyer's Creek resulted in closures of Lawyer's Creek Road between highway 162 and Flying B Ranch.  The main creek split with one flow going toward Flying B Ranch where one resident reported at least one foot of water around his house.  The rest of the creek flowed eastward to Robinson's Pond where it ate away at the levy between the pond and highway spilling about three feet of water over the road.

A 24 inch culvert separated under a two lane paved road (Dobson Pass, FR 456) on a steep hill causing the slope to slide down the hill taking one half of the paved lane with it.  The fill slope failure was 160 feet long and the paved roadway failure is 80 feet long.  At the Dobson Pass Narrows, the outside fill slope was sliding down the hill reducing the road to one lane.  The road shoulder was gone and pavement was undermined.  The site was 300 feet long.  The slide may have begun with heavy rainfall from March 31st and April 1st but was not discovered until April 2nd.  The estimated cost of damage to the roadway was $75,000.

Deep Creek flooded portions of Deep Creek Loop, also listed as Old Highway 95 causing sloughing of the roadway and embankment.  Pavement damage was 500 feet by nine feet wide.  The route is a major county through route from Naples to Bonners Ferry.

Cut slope failure 200 feet wide and 200 feet above Lions Den Road.  Ten foot rotational shear slid onto roadway.  Some areas of the slope had sheared but not slipped completely.  Estimated cost to remove slide and repair road is 500 thousand dollars.  Exact time of slide was unknown.

Cut slope above Fleming Creek Road sheared and slid bringing trees and clay onto and across roadway.  Outside shoulder over fill is settled and roadway cracked along the mid-lane.  Damage occurred along a 2500 foot long section of the roadway.  Estimated cost to remove slide and repair roadway is $800 thousand.  Exact time of the slide was unknown.

The Coeur D Alene Press reported that the St Maries River flooded it banks at Fernwood covering a manhole in town, leaking wastewater into the river.   There were no direct impacts to health or wildlife.
A brief funnel cloud was observed on the base of a strengthening thunderstorm west of the Spokane WFO.  The funnel cloud coincided with the timing of two merging cells.

Waves produce by these winds were large enough to dislodge one launch dock and damage two boat docks, with one boat dock able to hold 20 boats and the other 24 boats. A couple of boats parked at the docks were damaged as well.  This damage was reported to have occurred sometime between the nighttime hours on May 13th through the early morning hours on May 14th.  Mesonet sites in the area reported winds picking up just before 0800PST on May 14th.  Winds from these Mesonet sites ranged from 8 to 18 mph sustained with gusts between 18 and 30 mph.
SNOTELS in the area received approximately a half to one foot of total snowfall between Monday morning and early Tuesday morning.
SNOTELS in the area recorded about a half an inch of total snowfall during the morning hours.

At elevations generally above 2500 feet, approximately forty mature trees fell down along Highway 206 from northeastern Mead to Bear Creek Lodge with an additional 15 to 20 trees uprooted from Bear Creek Lodge to the Mount Spokane Ski Lodge.  The Quartz Peak SNOTEL recorded 28 inches of snow; Ragged Mountain SNOTEL 22 inches; and the park ranger from Mount Spokane State Park reported 30 to 36 inches.

A trampoline was blown into a power substation resulting in power outages to approximately 11,000 customers.  Avista Utilities estimated damage cost to the power station to range from 10 to 15 thousand dollars.

A landslide moved down Tumwater Canyon and covered highway 2 about a mile west of Leavenworth.  The slide closed Highway 2 in both directions.  The road was covered with six to eight feet of mud and debris for approximately one-eighth of a mile.  The highway remained closed until Saturday afternoon 300PST April 2nd.

A hillside gave way in the Icicle Canyon resulting in a landslide the hit at Eight Mile Campground.  The slide started as high as 1,000 feet above the valley floor and stretched across Icicle Creek Road at the bottom of the hill.  The slide cut off access to four homes and Eight Mile Campground.

A blocked railroad culvert resulted in water flooding out onto Chumstick Highway near Freund Canyon about 1.3 miles north of Leavenworth.  The water was about a foot deep across the road for a brief period resulting in its closure.  Parts of the road were damaged by the flowing water.

A landslide along East Hayden Lake Road at mile post 5.5 resulted in half of the road breaking off and sliding down the embankment.  Time of the slide is approximated.  Lakes Highway District reported that the slide occurred sometime between their morning and afternoon inspections.  Exact cost of road repairs is unknown, but it is thought that the total cost will be between 50 and 100 thousand dollars.

Chewelah Creek rose to bank level on May 12th resulting in portions of Chewelah Park being inundated with water next to the creek.  By May 16th, the creek had risen considerably out of its banks with flooding observed over Lincoln Avenue south of the park forcing its closure.  The creek continued to rise through May 17th at which time water began flowing over state route 395 between mile post 206.69 and 207.81 forcing its closure as well.  Flood waters approached businesses next to the park, but did not appear to make it inside any buildings.

Heavy rain and snow melt resulted in flooding along Colockum Road.  Kingsbury Bridge was undercut by Colockum Creek resulting in its closer.  Further down the creek flooding was reported on Tarpiscan Road, which blocked vehicle access to the Washington State University agricultural research station.  Colockum Creek flowed in the basement of a rental home, forcing the renters to evacuate.  Property damage was estimated.

State Route 206 was undercut by Deadman Creek at mile post 14.5, which forced a temporary closure of the road.  Only damage that occurred was along the shoulder of the roadway.  Damage costs were estimated.

A man became stranded as the North Fork of the Coeur d'Alene River flooded Sunday morning.  The camper and his trailer had to be pulled out 1,000 feet through 3 1/2 feet of water by a tow truck.  Property damage was estimated.
Eastbound lanes of Highway 4 were flooded between Gem Hill and Frisco Roads at mile post 5.  Roadway was reduced to one lane.

A resident located southwest of Clayton, WA sustained minor damage to her trailer when a strong dust devil moved across her property.  The dust devil ripped siding off of both sides of her trailer.  The siding landed in her neighbor���s horse pasture. It also picked up her trampoline and threw it several feet.  There were no injuries.  Damage costs were estimated.

Approximately three-hundred trees were toppled at the Indian Creek Campground located within Priest Lake State Park. Trees began to fall around 1530PST and were still falling at midnight. Some trees were snapped halfway down and others were toppled completely. The park ranger stated you could hear the trees snapping along the ridge-tops and the wind and damage would work its way down the valleys in waves with some damage swaths as long as a football field. This was the worst tree damage he had seen since he started working at the park in 1984. Campers had to be evacuated around 1700PST. Within the campground, twelve picnic tables were destroyed; one electrical pedestal, and a camper's truck and camper sustained some damage. The campground was forced to close for two weeks for cleanup operations.  Downed trees were also reported along Cape Horn Road, Pinto Point, Huckleberry Bay, and in the town of Coolin, ID.

Flooding of the Coeur D Alene River resulted in several roads being inundated with water between Rose Lake and Cataldo.  Approximately three-quarters of a mile of Rose Creek Road from Highway 3 had nearly a foot and a half of water over it and was closed for several days.  A mile of Dudley Road, just west of Cataldo, was under a foot of water.  The community of Rose Lake itself at Highway 3 experienced some backflow from the Coeur D Alene River, causing a slight build-up of water up to some houses foundations.  The west end of King Street in Rose Lake was completely covered in water.  One resident living at the end of King Street reported having as much as three to four feet of water against his foundation.  The only damage to his property was to sheetrock in his garage.

Precipitation amounts from SNOTEL sites across the Central Panhandle Mountains reported anywhere from 0.50 to 1.20 inches of liquid.  Those sites with snow pillows recorded 4 to 10 inches of snowfall.

Precipitation amounts from SNOTEL sites across the Central Panhandle Mountains reported anywhere from 0.80 to 1.80 inches of liquid.  Those sites with snow pillows recorded 4 to 10 inches of snowfall.  Schweitzer Ski Resort received eight inches of snow.
Liquid precipitation amounts from SNOTEL sites within the Northeast Mountains received anywhere from 0.60 to 1.50 inches of liquid. Those sites with snow pillows recorded 4 to 10 inches of snowfall.
Liquid precipitation amounts from SNOTEL sites within the Okanogan Highlands received anywhere from 0.60 to 1.20 inches of liquid. Those sites with snow pillows recorded 4 to 8 inches of snowfall.
Several trained spotters viewed a large rope-like funnel cloud attached to a storm that moved from approximately five miles north of Colton toward the town of Pullman.

A major landslide occurred in the USFS land above Conconully.  Three parties of campers were trapped at the Salmon Meadows Campground after mud and debris flowed across Salmon Creek Road.  One camper was almost swept off a USFS road by the slide but was able to navigate his truck and 35 foot camper in reverse quick enough to reach safe ground.  The slide was caused when a tributary above the road dammed during this spring's high runoff and broke loose Wednesday evening.  The slide was estimated to be 70-foot wide and anywhere from five to ten feet deep.  There were no injuries.  County officials were able to clear a path through the mud and debris on Thursday allowing the campers to evacuate.
On May 22nd, Sinlahekin Road was closed between Fish Lake and Blue Lake due to water and debris flowing over the roadway. The road was later reopened but closed on and off for the next few weeks.

On May 22nd, Salmon Creek Road was closed between Spring Coulee Road and Danker Cut-Off Road due to water and debris flowing over the roadway from Salmon Creek. A combination of high spring runoff and log jams in the creek was responsible for the flooding. The road was later reopened but closed on and off for the next few weeks.

Several roads sustained water damage from flooding creeks and streams within the Okanogan National Forest.  These roads include West Chewuch Road, Volstead Road, Cub Creek Road, Boulder Creek, and Harts Pass.  The extent of the damage is not known at this time and damage costs were estimated.

Several landslides occurred in the Okanogan National Forest within the War, Scaffold, and Eagle creeks area of the Twisp River. The largest slide was along the War Creek Ridge which inundated about 100 yards of the Forest Service Road leading to the War Creek Trailhead. A survey done from a helicopter shortly after the slide indicated two long channels, which was estimated to be some 30 feet deep. The time of the slide is estimated based on reports.

A massive landslide occurred in the Pearrygin Lake area just outside Winthrop, WA|on the afternoon of May 31st.  The Okanogan Sheriff's Office reported that the landslide was about 40 acres long and covered 200 yards of Walter Road and majority of a property located at the end of Walter's Road.  The mudslide damaged and spun the homeowner's travel trailer around, damaged a hot tub, pushed a pickup truck 75 feet, but missed his home by 50 feet.  The property owner stated that he had roughly 13 thousand in property damage; 40-60 thousand in cleanup cost; and additional loss due to the range and alfalfa fields being covered in mud and large logs.  The property owner estimated it would be three years before the fields could be planted again.  Agriculture losses were estimated to be near 17 thousand dollars over the three year period.  The slide may have also compromised the aquafer in the area.  Springs which fed the aquifer were torn apart and are currently running down the top of the slide much like a stream.  Residents in the area are digging new holding ponds to mitigate the loss of spring water.  Additionally, a U.S. Forest Service vehicle and four employees were trapped behind the slide but were able to walk through the slide that afternoon and return to town.  The slide was believed to be caused when Pearrygin Creek got dammed upstream and changed course toward Walter Road.   There were no injuries.

The north end of Deep Lake overflowed its banks flooding portions of Deep Lake Boundary Road with six inches of water.  Since May 26th, small creeks flowing into the lake have spilled out of their banks and flooded several fields and driveways leading to homes in the area.  No property damage has been reported.

Chewelah Creek flowed out of its banks on May 26th flooding portions of Highway 395, Lincoln Street, and Chewelah City Park.  Water had dropped significantly by the |evening of May 28th with only some residual standing water on Lincoln Street.  Damage estimates were only for the park and playground equipment.

Mud and debris flowed into Lake Chelan down the Meadow Creek drainage.  A section of the Lakeshore Trail was damaged during the landslide.  Estimated the timing of the slide as it was reported to have occurred sometime either the 14th or the 15th.

Lost River Road flooded approximately three miles east of Mazama as debris clogged the flow of water underneath a bridge.  Two feet of water was observed to be flowing over the roadway resulting in its closure.  No damage was reported to the road.

The combination of saturated soils and strong winds resulted in two trees toppling over onto highway 14 east of Republic.  The first tree fell just after 2350PST on May 13th fourteen miles east of town and the second fell around 0430PST nine miles east of town.

Heavy rain Sunday resulted in water pooling on eastbound Interstate 90 at mile post 294.  Traffic was reduced to one lane starting Sunday night May 15th through Monday morning due to the flooding on the interstate.
Heavy rain resulted in water pooling on Flora Road in Spokane Valley resulting in its closure Sunday night May 15th.

Heavy snowfall was mainly confined to those elevations above 5,000 feet.  Moses Mountain SNOTEL recorded about four inches of total snowfall based off snow depth measurements.  Sherman Pass webcam showed the roadway to be snow covered with low visibilities down to one mile or less at times during the early afternoon hours.

A swollen Columbia River flooded portions of the Apple Capital Recreation Loop Trail just north of Confluence State Park the evening of the 28th through the 29th.  The flow on the Columbia River hit 335,500 CFS at Rocky Reach Dam.  The high river levels also submerged parts of the sandy spit and pedestrian bridge at Walla Walla Point Park.  Restrooms were closed at Kirby Billingsley Hydro Park for public safety concerns due to high water levels threatening electrical wiring which supplied the restrooms pumping system.

A strong thunderstorm produced in the neighborhood of one inch of rain and large amounts of pea size hail over portions of Northwest Spokane between 1900PDT and 2000PDT.  The bulk of the precipitation fell within 30 to 45 minutes causing drainage systems to become overwhelmed.  This resulted in several low crossings of highway 291 between Division Street and Nine Mile Road to quickly flood with anywhere from six inches to a foot and a half of water.  Roughly forty basements in the area also became flooded with several inches of water.  In the Indian Trails area where the terrain is steep, as much as three inches of water was observed flowing down the streets and carved out two to four foot trenches on a steep embankment going through the neighborhood park.  According to city officials, the city's sewer infrastructure did not sustain any damage however several public properties submitted claims due to water damage in their basements.  Twenty-five residents submitted claims with the city with an additional ten to twenty properties assumed to have gone through private insurance companies.
A severe thunderstorm moved across eastern Nez Peerce County during the late afternoon hours.  This storm dropped several one inch hail stones mixed in with marble and pea-sized hail.

A severe thunderstorm moved into Asotin County from northeast Oregon during the late afternoon or early evening hours.  The public reported hail stones up to the size of golf balls as the storm moved over Montgomery Ridge.
Silver Falls Creek (near the upper end of the Entiat drainage) went out of its banks and flooded two camp sites at the Silver Falls Campground.

A mudslide was reported over upper Icicle Road about ten miles west of Leavenworth.  The slide was about 200 yards wide and 10 to 12 feet deep.  About 30 people were stranded at a campground above the slide.  Some damage was reported to the road.  Damage reported was estimated.

A rockslide occurred across a busy railroad line approximately 15 miles east of Bonners Ferry.  The slide was about 30 feet high and reportedly occurred during the afternoon on Sunday June 12th.  Crews worked through the night to clear the slide and the section of railroad was opened at 2210PST on Monday June 13th.
A thunderstorm produced heavy rain that resulted in water gushing down a sloped gravel driveway.  Minor sections of the driveway were damaged.  Pea sized hail was also reported with the thunderstorm.
Rainfall accumulation of 1.10 inches was reported within a span of 45 minutes to one hour.
It was estimated that 0.75 inches to 1.00 inches of rain fell within ten minutes.

Widespread flooding was observed along the Pend Oreille River throughout the month of June 2011 impacting the communities of Newport, Dalkena, Usk, Cusick, Ruby, Blueslide, Lost Creek, Ione, and Metaline Falls.  Some of the worst flooding was noted along the following roads: Alaska Way, Davis Road, McCloud Creek, Deeter Road, Riverbend Loop, Sandy Shores, Yergens, Le Clerc Road, Pow Wow Park Road, Dike Road, Needles Road, and Main Street in Metaline Falls; four private roads including Beehive Lane, Bear Paw Drive, Echo Lane, and Hawk Lane were also flooded.  Numerous homes along these roads suffered flooding with as much as two to three feet of water in their basements and significant damage to docks, sheds, and other outbuildings.  The town of Metaline was forced to bypass sewage treatment and allow its storm drains to flow directly into Pend Oreille River.  The flooding had enormous impacts on recreation with many boaters avoiding the river due to a no-wake restriction in place.  Additionally, the Kalispels' 37th Powwow and 4th of July celebration were cancelled due to the flooding.

Minor spring flooding occurred along the Pend Oreille River, Clark Fork River, and Lake Pend Oreille.  Johnson Creek Road on the south side of the Clark Fork River had some sloughing.  In central and western areas of the county, Priest River inundated portions of LeClerc Road just east of Oldtown as well as Dufort Road, just east of Priest Lake.  Numerous docks and lakeside yards were flooded by high water levels along the shores of Lake Pend Oreille.  In Sandpoint, ID the basement of the Old Power House was flooded.

Lake Pend Oreille spilled out of its banks flooding portions of Lakeview Avenue in Bayview, ID.  The lake enveloped recreational sites, docks, and ramps. There was also minor flooding of yards and the parking lot of the Scenic Bay Marina.

A landslide occurred on the morning of June 10th and covered South Shore Drive between Lake Chelan Yacht Club and Cove Marina.  The slide covered the equivalent of one city block.  It took four workers roughly three days to clear the road.  The exact time of the slide was unknown.
Salmon Creek Road was closed June 1st between Spring Coulee and Danker Cutoff roads due to flooding of the Salmon Creek.
Cape LaBelle Road was closed at milepost 7.8 due to a mudslide. The exact time and size of the slide is unknown.
Bead Lake flooded its banks and water inundating a few basements of lakeside homes.  The exact number of homes impacted was unknown at the time and damage costs were estimated.
Diamond Lake flooded its banks and water inundating a few basements of lakeside homes and private roads. The exact number of homes impacted was unknown at the time and damage costs were estimated.

A combination of a log jam on the Oak Street bridge and washout of a dike at Pine Street in the city of Okanogan resulted in seepage of the Okanogan River into a few basements of homes along Second Avenue.  Damage costs were estimated.

A combination of landslides and flooding along creeks and rivers resulted in the closure of numerous campsites within Perygian State Park through the first two weeks of June.  Damage costs were estimated based on an average loss of revenue from closed campgrounds.

Significant rainfall resulted in cherry damage to several orchards from the Wenatchee area, northward toward Pateros.  It was reported that up to approximately fifteen percent or more of the cherry orchards were damaged.  The Skeena variety of cherries was most damaged as the rainfall resulted in severe cracking of fruit.  The ASOS at the Wenatchee Airport reported 0.30 inches of rainfall between 0600PST and 1200PST.  Damage estimations were based on a loss of 150 tons of cherries combined with the additional costs of renting roughly a dozen helicopters used to dry the orchards.  One helicopter pilot died when the low-flying aircraft clipped a power-line and crashed.
Hail size, location, and crop damage are estimated.
Hail size, location, and crop damage are estimated.
Hail, location, and crop damage are estimated.
Hail size, location, and crop damage were estimated.
Bead Lake flooded its banks and water inundating a few basements of lakeside homes. The exact number of homes impacted was unknown at the time and damage costs were estimated.
Diamond Lake flooded its banks and water inundating a few basements of lakeside homes and private roads. The exact number of homes impacted was unknown at the time and damage costs were estimated.

Widespread flooding was observed along the Pend Oreille River through the first week of July 2011 impacting the communities of Newport, Dalkena, Usk, Cusick, Ruby, Blueslide, Lost Creek, Ione, and Metaline Falls. Some of the worst flooding was noted along the following roads: Alaska Way, Davis Road, McCloud Creek, Deeter Road, Riverbend Loop, Sandy Shores, Yergens, Le Clerc Road, Pow Wow Park Road, Dike Road, Needles Road, and Main Street in Metaline Falls; four private roads including Beehive Lane, Bear Paw Drive, Echo Lane, and Hawk Lane were also flooded. Numerous homes along these roads suffered flooding with as much as two to three feet of water in their basements and significant damage to docks, sheds, and other outbuildings. The town of Metaline was forced to bypass sewage treatment and allow its storm drains to flow directly into Pend Oreille River. The flooding had enormous impacts on recreation with many boaters avoiding the river due to a no-wake restriction in place. Additionally, the Kalispels' 37th Powwow and 4th of July celebration were cancelled due to the flooding.

Minor spring flooding occurred along the Pend Oreille River, Clark Fork River, and Lake Pend Oreille. Johnson Creek Road on the south side of the Clark Fork River had some sloughing. In central and western areas of the county, Priest River inundated portions of LeClerc Road just east of Oldtown as well as Dufort Road, just east of Priest Lake. Numerous docks and lakeside yards were flooded by high water levels along the shores of Lake Pend Oreille. In Sandpoint, ID the basement of the Old Power House was flooded.

A highly localized microburst or possible gustnado resulted in minor damage of the Eagle Point subdivision approximately four miles east of downtown Lewiston. A section of a sheet metal roof was lifted off a two-story shop, a boat trailer was pushed into the outbuilding denting the sheet metal, three two-inch diameter trees were snapped, a travel trailer was knocked down, and lawn objects became airborne breaking one window of a house.

A microburst was thought to be responsible for snapping twenty consecutive power poles between the Setters substation and Highway 95 along Setters Road.   It is inconclusive whether the initial wind gust snapped only a few poles or was the direct cause for damaging all the poles.  It is speculated that a few poles broke in response to the microburst resulting in a domino effect to the remaining poles due to the absence of additional damage in the area.
The Marlys Road wildfire initiated near Hanging Rocks off Highway 20, roughly 20 miles east of Tonasket, and burned to Big Boulder Lane.  The fire burned 408 acres along with one outbuilding.

Heavy rain fell at rate of approximately one and one quarter of an inch per hour resulted in fast flowing water down a sloped front yard of a residence.  Loose soil was easily carried by the runoff, which created a flow of mud that covered the driveway of the residence.  No damage was reported.

A relatively small wildfire of around 75 acres completely destroyed a historic railroad trestle.  The estimated cost to rebuild the trestles and railroad track to its original state was between three and four million dollars.

Heavy rain washed out a section of a dirt road approximately three-quarters of a mile north of Newport on the west side of the Pend Oreille River.  Recent road work by the planned utility development installing a fiber-optic cable along this section of the roadway likely made the hillside more susceptible to the washout.  Property damage was estimated.

A farmer in northern Whitman County spotted two funnel clouds the afternoon of October 5th approximately thirteen miles northwest of Saint John.  One funnel cloud briefly touched down over open wheat fields.

Wind gusts ranging from 45 to 55 mph were common in the Spokane area between 1530 and 1730 PST.  The Spokane International Airport ASOS measured a peak gust of 52 mph.  Several trees were downed mainly on the western slopes of the South Hill.  Some trees toppled on power-lines causing an estimated 1200 power outages.  A 60 foot Ponderosa Pine tree top fell on a South Hill home causing significant damage to a third of the home.  The exact location was unknown.  Local media reported downed trees at the intersections of 43rd and Scott, Hatch and Tomaker, and Hatch and Westchester Drive.

SNOTEL sites from the Northern Idaho Panhandle measured 0.60 to 1.30 inches of liquid precipitation during the event.  Temperatures were in the upper teens to lower twenties |Fahrenheit suggesting precipitation fell as snow.  Using a rough 10 to 1 snow to liquid ratio, most locations received eight to eleven inches.  This was confirmed by the Northern Rockies Avalanche Center.
Valley snowfall amounts ranged from 2 to 7 inches.  A snow plow driver located on Mogul Hill, roughly 5000 feet elevation, reported twelve inches of snow through 1130 AM PST on the 22nd.
Valley snow accumulations ranged from 2 to 5 with locally up to 6 inches near the Canadian Border.  49 degrees North Ski Resort reported 23 inches of snow over the two-day period.
The St Maries COOP reported a tree had fallen onto power-lines in the Benewah Valley due to strong wind gusts associated with thunderstorms between 1230 AM PST and 100AM PST.

Strong wind gusts knocked down at least four large trees in the town of Osburn, Idaho.  The toppled trees caused extensive damage to a motor home, car, storage shed, car port, and patio cover.  One tree clipped a house resulting in minor damage.  Two roofs were completely blown off from primary residences and several other roofs were damaged.  Several power poles and power-lines were damaged.  The Nuckols RAWS, located at 4000 feet just outside the town of Osburn, measured sustained winds of 31 mph with gusts to 60 mph.

Eight inches of snow was reported in Chelan and five inches in Ardenvoir.  Most accumulations were at or above elevations of 1300 feet with a mix of sleet, snow, and freezing rain observed in the lowest elevations.
Four to six inches of snow was reported in the communities of Republic and Boyds.

Steady light freezing rain started on the evening of the 20th and continued through the morning hours of the 21st.  Roadways throughout the Spokane area became treacherous as surfaces accumulated between a glaze to 1/16 inch of ice.  Numerous slide-offs and collisions were reported along Interstate 90 between Cheney and Spokane Valley between 1930 and 2230 PST.  A semi-truck jack-knifed on the eastbound lane near the Broadway Exit rupturing its fuel tank and leaking 100 gallons of fuel.

Freezing rain resulted in ice accumulation of approximately 1/8th of an inch on trees and road surfaces within the Newport and Sacheen Lake areas.  Hilly, untreated roads in the area were said to be impassable at the time of the report, approximately 0600 PST on the 21st of January.

A combination of light snow and freezing rain created slick driving conditions across the Northern Idaho Panhandle during the morning hours of the 21st.  The slick road conditions were thought to have played a large role in a six car accident along Highway 95 near Sagle, ID.  It is still unclear if weather or aggressive driving was directly responsible.  The accident resulted in one fatality and one serious injury.  Two semi-tractors and four cars were involved in the incident.
A combination of light snow and freezing rain fell across the Coeur d'Alene area creating treacherous driving conditions throughout the Coeur d'Alene area.

A combination of trained spotters and the public reported between 0.25 to 0.30 inches of ice in the Winthrop area.  Five hundredths to eight hundredths of an inch of ice was reported eight miles west of Chelan and five miles west of Peshastin respectively.  All reports stated roadways were extremely icy and treacherous.

CocoRahs observers reported widespread 1 to 2.5 inches of rainfall on the morning of the 30th.  The media relayed that Highway 200 from U.S. Highway 95 to the Montana had several spots with water over the roadway.
