Several roads throughout Kootenai County experienced minor flooding.  These roads included Highway 41 between Rathdrum and Spirit Lake, Old Highway 95 and Prairie View Road, along with several other secondary and private roadways.  Widespread CocoRahs reports of two inches were received from the area.

CocoRahs reports from across eastern Whitman County between Tekoa and Pullman reported between 0.50 and 1.00 of rainfall on the morning of the 30th. The heavy rain combined with snowmelt and poor drainage lead to localized flooding along several county roads including: State Route 27 near Oaksdale, Seeberry Road, Warner Road, Fanning Road, and Endicott - Diamond Road.

Southern portions of Whitman County were hit particularly hard with heavy snowfall, which included towns of La Crosse, Endicott, Colfax and Pullman.  Several schools over these areas were closed the morning of the eighteenth due to snow covered roadways.

Forty-one traffic collisions were reported in the city of Spokane between 0600PST and 2200PST due to snow covered roadways resulting in hazardous driving conditions.  A semitruck jackknifed on Interstate 90 near Sullivan Road.  A three car accident on the T.J. Meenach Bridge forced a temporary closure of Meenach Drive; one person had to be extracted from a vehicle and two other people suffered minor injuries.  A vehicle landed on its top in the westbound shoulder of Interstate 90 and wedged itself against a utility pole near Evergreen Road.
A semitruck wrecked and lost a load of logs on Highway 95 north of Tensed.  No injuries were reported.
Police reported 25 accidents during the event.  No injuries were reported.

One hundred vehicle slide-offs were reported in Spokane County.  School districts in Spokane, Mead, Coeur d'Alene and Post Falls closed public schools on Friday the morning after the heavy snowfall event.
Washington State University cancelled classes due to the heavy snowfall.
Gusty southwest winds were believed to be responsible for blowing over a scissor lift in Cheney at around 1430PST. Two construction workers were inflicted with nonlife-threatening injuries.

Spotters reported around four to five inches of heavy snowfall south of Naples.  One spotter reported nine inches of snowfall just to the south-southeast of Clark Fork.  Schweitzer Ski Resort received fourteen inches of new snowfall.

A three day stretch of accumulating snowfall in Bayview weighed down three float homes on Lake Pend Oreille.  One boat home tipped over significantly and was being supported by a neighboring boat home.  The Bayview COOP site recorded five inches of new snowfall on the nineteenth with thirteen inches of snow on the ground.  The thirteen inches of snow all fell within the three day period of January seventeenth through the nineteenth.  Residence living in the boat homes stated that they were caught off guard due to the lack of winter storms up through the seventeenth.

Gusty winds along Interstate 90 resulted in blizzard like conditions, especially over Lookout Pass.  Several spinoffs were reported along the interstate during the day on the seventeenth.  An accident was reported between Osburn and Silverton on the interstate as well as a one vehicle accident occurring at 1335PST just past westbound milepost 39.  Nuckols and Magee Peak RAWS sites reported sustained winds of over 20 mph with gusts up to near 50 mph during the evening hours on the seventeenth.  There were numerous reports of heavy snowfall, which varied from five inches to fifteen inches. Silver Mountain Ski area reported ten inches of new snowfall.

Heavy convective snow bands along with gusty winds created near blizzard conditions across the Spokane Area during the morning and early afternoon of the 25th.  Snowfall amounts ranged between four and eight inches.  The Spokane County Sheriff's office reported 125 collisions between 0900-1600 on the 25th with no serious injuries.  Highway 195 and 395 were temporary closed due to multiple traffic accidents.  Highway 206 leading up to Mount Spokane was also closed as the weight of the heavy snow led to numerous downed trees.
Storm total snowfall amounts ranged from five to nine inches.
Cocorahs reports throughout the zone reported four to six inches of snow.
Storm total snowfall amounts over the two-day period ranged from five to ten inches.

Storm total snowfall amounts ranged from four to eight inches.  The heaviest snow fell within convective bands during the morning and afternoon hours of the 25th causing numerous accidents and resulted in a temporary closure of Interstate 90 at 4th of July Pass.
Snowfall totals across the Wenatchee Area ranged from four to six inches.
Snowfall totals ranged from four to six inches.
Storm total snowfall amounts ranged from three to six inches.
Storm total snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches.
Storm total snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four to six inches in the valleys with close to a foot in the mountains.
Snowfall amounts ranged between four and six inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between four to eight inches in the valleys with close a foot in the mountains.
Strong winds blew over a tree onto a power line.  Damage was estimated.
Two young evergreens blew over and were approximately ten to twelve inches around.  One of these trees fell onto a house.  Damage was estimated.
One tree blew over onto a power line and another tree blew over onto a parked car in the Hillyard area.  Damage was estimated.
Wind gusts of 71 mph and 90 mph were reported by the Shirrod Hill sensor between 1200PST and 1230PST.

The Red Cross North Central Disaster Response Team helped a family evacuate their Harvard home early March 26th due to flooding along the Palouse River and Gold Creek. The family had been fighting minor flooding for days but finally decided to evacuate their home when standing water began to fill the house.  The water was four inches deep in some spots.

Moderate to major flooding occurred along Paradise Creek on the morning of March 26th flooding numerous streets, bridges, and homes within the city of Moscow, Idaho.  The creek crested at ten feet, making it the fourth highest crest on record.  Among the list of flooded streets, bridges, parks, and homes which were impacted from the flooding along Paradise Creek include: the intersection of Bridge and Hillcrest Streets, intersection at 5th and Roosevelt, D Street bridge, Main Street, Mountainview Park, the University of Idaho bike path, Blaine Street Bridge, South Lynn Street, and Sand Road.
Water was reported over Moyie River Road.  There were also some reports of a few culverts being blocked and minor damage to the shoulder of roadways.  Damage was estimated.

There were numerous reports of water over roadways and washouts.  Road closures included the south end of Sagle Road, Talache Road at Camp Stidwell, Blacktail Road near Little Blacktail Mountain Road, Cocolalla Loop Road near address 3900 and Sportsmans Access Road.  Partial road washouts included Jewel Lake Road at mile marker 2.5, Schneider Road between mile marker 3 and 4, Nettleingham Road, Snow Valley Road, Petterson Road and Boyer Road near Vedelwood Road.

Numerous mud slides reported in Bonner and Boundary County as heavy rainfall saturated soils across the area.  A mud slide impacted East Spring Creek Road below Hatchery, Sunnyside Road at Osprey Roost Road and multiple slides along Moyie River Road from Moyie Springs to the Canadian border.  Timing of each slide is unknown and was estimated toward the conclusion of heaviest rainfall in the area.

About a dozen basements flooded in and around Republic and in the Curlew Lake area.  Several roads had some washout damage, including Fishermans Cove Road, which was impassable.  Large rocks were also reported on Highway 21 south of Republic.

A portion of the hillside slid and blocked Cheweka Creek along Pleasant Valley Road.  Minor damage was reported to the road and to a shop.  Damage amounts are unknown, but it was reported that dollar amounts were very minor.

Heavy rainfall resulted in urban flooding north of downtown Spokane.  Street water pooled into the parking garage of the Northtown Mall and street flooding was reported at Monroe and Euclid and at Wellesley and Lincoln.  Large puddles were also reported in downtown Spokane, which added to the congestion of afternoon rush hour traffic.

Heavy rain and excess snow melt from the 25th through the 26th caused the Potlatch River to flow out of hits banks causing some damage to an Earthern Berm in the city of Kendrick.  The costs of equipment and material to repair the berm was 13 thousand dollars.

Heavy rain on the 26th combined with excess snow melt caused a small landslide along Cedar Ridge Road in Latah County.  There was no damage to the roadway or any structures however the Highway District estimated 30 thousand dollars to remove the slide material.

The combination of heavy rain and snow melt caused several creeks and streams to flood causing minor damage to multiple roads between Genesee and Moscow.  The most significant damage occurred along Blaine, Eid, Danielson, Swenson, and Troy-Genesee Roads.  The South Latah Highway district estimated repair cost to these roads at 50 thousand dollars, primarily to procure, haul, and replace material to restore the roadways for safe travel.

East bound lane on Interstate 90 over Mullan Pass was closed between 2140PST Wednesday night through 0200PST Thursday morning due to a jackknifed semi-truck.  Lookout Pass received a total of 31 inches of snowfall and Silver Mountain received 27 inches of snowfall for the event.
School closures were reported in the Boundary County, west Bonner County and Lake Pend Oreille school districts.
Storm total valley snowfall accumulations varied between two to four inches in the north to four to seven inches further south.

A semi-truck jackknifed on Salnave Road and struck a car passing in the opposite lane head on.  The women driving the car was injured and transported to a nearby hospital; the driver of the semi-truck was not injured.  Snow covered roadways caused numerous other accidents, including at Third Avenue and Maple Street, eastbound on Bigelow Gulch Road near Weile Avenue, westbound I-90 at Sprague Avenue and at Medical Lake, and eastbound I-90 at Broadway Avenue and at Barker Road.

Several days of moderate rain and excessive snow melt lead to numerous road washouts, plugged culverts, minor rock slides, flooded basements, and impassible roads from flooding across Shoshone County.  These roads included: Bear Creek, Ross Ranch, Riverview, French Gulch, Old CDA River, Golf Course, Kelly Gulch, Wier Gulch, Trapper Creek, Upper Pine Creek Bridge, Lynch Gulch, Galena Gulch, Daly Gulch, Nine Mile, Placer Creek, Revenue, Gulch, Mullan, Bingville, Willow Acres, Sunny Slopes, Nuchols Gulch, Tank Creek, North Side, Markwell (between 6th and 7th), and numerous sections of the Saint Joe River Road (Forest Road 50).  In addition, the flooding resulted in waste water overflow in the communities of Mullan, Osburn, and Smelterville with no known health risks at the time of the report.

A section of road and supporting earth along Dobson Pass Road broke loose and slid down the hillside rendering the road impassable.  This compromised emergency access to the communities of Prichard and Murray.
A landslide occurred along Forest Road 50 (St Joe River Road) at mile post 34.  The slide filled a ditch and blocked the eastbound lane.

Excess runoff from heavy rain and snow melt resulted in sharp rises of Lake Coeur D Alene and minor flooding of its tributaries.  Kid Island Bay Road which parallels the eastern shores of Kid Island Bay, a small outlet on the northwestern sections of Lake Coeur D Alene, had several inches of water over the roadway.

Flooding was reported along several low spots along Highway 97 between Cataldo and Harrison.  While the exact location was unknown, some residents were forced to sandbag to avoid flooded creeks from seeping into their homes.
Two homes in Fernan Village were flooded by Fernan Lake.  Three other homes along the shores of the lake had their seawalls heightened with sandbags to prevent the lake from entering their homes.
Blue Creek Road washed out near Yellowstone Trail.

The Coeur D Alene River at Cataldo went above flood stage of 43 feet at 1800 PDT on March 31st, crested at 45 feet 1100 PDT, and receded below 43 feet around noon on April 1st.  CCC Road at Cataldo flooded and was impassible.  Latour Creek Road at Cataldo also flooded but was passable.  Portions of Dudley Road, west of Latour Creek Road were underwater and impassible.  Wolf Creek and Kahnderosa RV Campgrounds flooded.  A few homes near the river experienced minor flooding of basements. Minor flooding was also observed in farmlands between Cataldo to Harrison.
The Ridgeview Apartments located in Saint Maries had to be evacuated when Mutch Creek flooded its banks and began to seep into the building.

High runoff and saturated grounds from a month of record rainfall combined with excessive snow melt resulted in a major road washout under a section of Cocolalla Loop Road.  It was estimated that 25 feet of earth below the road, roughly 100 feet in length, was washed down the hillside as the underground culverts became overwhelmed or clogged.  The road washed out on March 31st.  Additional flooding was observed along the northeastern shores of Lake Cocolalla, specifically Melody Lane, where several secondary, recreational houses were inundated with water from the swollen lake.  Minor damage was also observed at a small wooden bridge where Cocolalla Creek crosses under Cocolalla Creek.
Kootenai Trail Road was inundated with water from Cow Creek.
Portions of Old Highway 95, north of Naples, were flooded when heavy spring runoff flooded caused Deep Creek to flow out of its banks.

Fourteen cars of an Union Pacific Train derailed when 350 feet of track was washed out near the intersection of Colburn and Selkirk Roads.  Six of the rail cars were carrying soybeans with the other eight cars empty.

A landslide occurred 20 miles east of Bonners Ferry along a section of Burlington Northern Track which connects Troy, Montana to Bonners Ferry, Idaho.  Large boulders slid onto the track causing twenty trains to be delayed but no damage.  A report suggested that the boulders fell from a hillside 150 feet above.

The Saint Joe River at Saint Maries rose above the flood stage of 32.5 feet at 0300 PDT on March 31st, crested at 33.9 feet at 0600 PDT on April 1st, and receded below flood stage 2100 PDT on April 3rd.  Saint Joe City Road flooded.  Minor flooding was observed throughout low lying areas of the Saint Joe Valley and of the Aqua Park in Saint Maries.

Several roads were washed out, flooded, or experienced some damage across Bonner County due to high spring runoff caused by record March rainfall and excess snow melt.  These roads including Gold Creek (8 NE Sandpoint), Talache, East Shores Drive (4 NE Coolin), Geenan, Schneiders, Rapid Lightning Creek, Bowen Arrow (4 NE Colburn), and Merril Martin.  Six homes and some businesses were isolated due to road closures.  Five homes and some businesses had limited one lane access.

Numerous roads across Pend Oreille County experienced washouts, floods, or minor damage due to flooding from March 29th-31st.  These roads included Deeter (8 NW Newport), Westside Calispell (3 SW Cusick), Rocky Gorge (9 SW Cusick), Rockwood (1 N Diamond Lake), West Telephone (2 SW Diamond Lake), and McCloud (5 SW Bead Lake).
A landslide along Highway 20 near Riverside Bible Camp, temporarily closed the road until road crews were able to remove a foot of mud that slid onto the highway.
Swamp Creek flooded it banks and washed out the bridge on Reservation Road near Highway 231.
A mudslide partially blocked Highway 12 between mile marker 49 and 50.
West Oregon Road was washed out between North Spotted Road and North Grove Road due to a plugged culvert.
A trained spotter observed a funnel cloud to the northwest of Wenatchee toward Cashmere.  The funnel cloud lasted a few minutes before dissipating.
The media relayed a report and pictures of a funnel cloud that was sighted on the Lewiston Grade, roughly five miles northwest of Genesee between 1605 and 1610 PDT.
Calls made to businesses three to four miles southeast of Clark Fork, Idaho reported hail to size of quarters.

Three kayakers capsized on Rock Lake when strong southwest winds created high waves.  This particular lake is oriented southwest to northeast with steep rock walls.  Consequently, if a boater capsizes on Rock Lake, it can be difficult to get out of the water due to the very steep shoreline.  Each of the three capsized kayakers were rescued and treated for hypothermia; sadly one died at the hospital.

Multiple roads flooded, including East Dudley Road, Latour Creek Road and Riverview Drive in Cataldo.  Kahnderosa Campground along Latour Creek Road was flooded and water across Dudley Road left some residents stranded.  One resident on East Dudley Road estimated about three feet of water was over the road at one point.  No damage was reported.

Portions of Riverview Drive along the Coeur d'Alene River were flooded.  Stretches of Old Coeur d'Alene River Road along the north fork of the Coeur d'Alene River was flooded and impassable upstream of Bumble Bee Bridge.  Fifty people on Old Coeur d'Alene River Road were issued voluntary evacuation notices stating to leave or be stranded for the weekend.  No damage was reported.
Calder Road was closed due to flooding on the St. Joe River.  Residents of Calder had to detour eleven miles to get onto the main St. Joe River Road.  No Damage was reported.

Flood waters from the St. Joe River at St. Maries covered Lagoon Road and inundated some residential properties in this area.  Some damage was observed to the levees.  There was a rotational failure on the riverward side and slippage in a part of the one of the levees.  Damage reported was estimated.

Two to four inches of snow, graupel, and small hail fell within an hour across portions of North Spokane between Francis Street and Newport Highway.  Southbound lanes of Highway 395 near Magnesium Street were closed for an hour due to treacherous road conditions and steep terrain.

Hayton Green Park in Palouse was flooded as well as the residence at 415 West Main Street near the park.  Flooding was also observed up to the base of the house in the neighboring property.  Damage was estimated.
Two homes in Fernan Village were flooded by Fernan Lake.  Three other homes along the shores of the lake had their seawalls heightened with sandbags to prevent the lake from entering the homes.

The Saint Joe River at Saint Maries rose above the flood stage of 32.5 feet at 0300 PDT on March 31st, crested at 33.9 feet at 0600 PDT on April 1st, and receded below flood stage 2100 PDT on April 3rd. Saint Joe City Road flooded. Minor flooding was observed throughout low lying areas of the Saint Joe Valley and of the Aqua Park in Saint Maries.

The Coeur D Alene River at Cataldo went above flood stage of 43 feet at 1800 PDT on March 31st, crested at 45 feet 1100 PDT, and receded below 43 feet around noon on April 1st.  CCC Road at Cataldo flooded and was impassible.  Latour Creek Road at Cataldo also flooded but was passable.  Portions of Dudley Road, west of Latour Creek Road were underwater and impassible.  Wolf Creek and Kahnderosa RV Campgrounds flooded.  A few homes near the river experienced minor flooding of basements.  Minor flooding was also observed in farmlands between Cataldo to Harrison.
There was extensive flooding of the low lying areas west of Potlatch.  South River Road was flooded where it crosses the Palouse River at Wellesley Road.

A large landslide along the steep terrain adjacent to Myrtle Creek washed out a section of the Forest Road 633 and covered other sections of the road with boulders, mud, and logs making the road impassible.  The slide was discovered on May 1st, but the exact time was unknown.

A trained spotter from the Sacheen Lake area relayed information and images of collapsed roof from a RV located just off Tennant Road.  A second report from Moose Jaw Lane (about a mile from the scene of the collapsed roof) reported hearing several tree���s falling in the surrounding forest.  The winds, according to the spotter were estimated to be between 45 and 55 m.p.h. and were gusting from varying directions.

A severe thunderstorm developed in the northeast Blue Mountains and drifted north-northeastward.  The thunderstorm produced hail up to the size of quarters before it weakened as it moved off the northern foothills of the Blue Mountains.

A severe thunderstorm developed northwest of the St. Joe National Forest.  The thunderstorm intensified as it moved northeast between Heyburn State Park and St. Maries.  The thunderstorm proceeded to head northward as a new updraft developed across Benewah County into Kootenai County.

A thunderstorm with a history of producing hail to the size of Ping-Pong balls in Benewah County drifted north of Benewah Lake into Kootenai County.  By this time, the thunderstorm was reportedly producing hail to the size of nickels.
A United States Navy buoy on Lake Pend Oreille measured an outflow wind gusts of 61 mph from a severe thunderstorm moving north across the Coeur d'Alene National Forest.

Denton Road was partially washed out by Riser Creek.  The cost to repair the washout was estimated at $15,000.  Other minor flooding was reported along Riser Creek, Strong Creek, and Lightning Creek in the area.  Portions of East Spring Creek Road were underwater due to flooding from Lightning Creek.
Grouse Creek came out of its banks and flooded a portion of Samuels Road as well as a residence near Colburn Culver Road.  No damages were reported.

A wildfire broke out near the Grant, Adams County line along State Route 26.  The fire consumed approximately 1500 acres of sage brush and cheat grass.  The fire was believed to be contained sometime Friday morning on the fifteenth.  No injuries or damage was reported.
Spotter reported a quarter inch of rainfall in thirty minutes.
Spotter reported nickel to quarter size hail.
Hail cracked a windshield at the Boggans Oasis Bar and Grill.

Strong winds associated with outflow from a cluster of thunderstorms was thought to be responsible for damaging a roof on a resident house.  The roof was picked up on the east side of the house and completely flipped over to the west side of the property, damaging two cars parked next to the home.  The roof was actually a second roof on top of an old one.  Showers the following week resulted in damage to the ceiling, drywall, and the carpet.
Hail sizes were generally between pea to dime but a few nickel to quarter size hailstones were observed.

Interstate 90 at exit 283B, below the Freya Street overpass filled with one to three feet of water bringing traffic along Interstate 90 to a brief standstill.  Lacey and 5th Street were also submerged in several inches of water.  Residents of five houses in that neighborhood sustained some flood damage, mainly to their basements.
Dime to quarter size hail.

Highway 97 north of Malott, WA was blocked by debris at milepost 279.  Flash flooding clogged a culvert and washed out a portion of the roadway.  Railroad trestles were also taken out at this milepost.

A severe thunderstorm in the Blue Mountains over Columbia County in Washington produced a gust front that pushed through the Lewiston area.  Lewiston Orchards seemed to feel the brunt of this outflow boundary with wind gusts up to 45 mph recorded at the Lewiston-Nez Perce County Airport.  A few small trees were knocked over with trunks estimated at six to eight inches in diameter.  Some small branches were broken off as well.

The Road A wildfire started around 1300PST by a lightning strike three miles southwest of Mansfield.  The fire burned 2,455 acres of grass, sage, and standing wheat.  An abandoned grain silo was lost in this blaze.  A second, smaller wildfire, named as the McNeil Canyon fire, started about 45 minutes later due to another lightning strike.  This fire consumed only 53 acres with no reports of damages to any structures.  No injuries were reported by either wildfire.

The Foster Creek wildfire ignited late on July 12th along Highway 17 near milepost 132.  The fire was aided by thunderstorm outflow winds on July 15th that fanned flames across containment lines.  The fire ignited and toppled a power pole around 1830PST on July 13th, which cut off power to 400 customers in the area.  Power to these customers was restored around 0430PST the following day.  Bridgeport Hill Road was closed for a five hour period due to poor visibility from smoke.  Wet conditions helped to suppress fire activity with containment reported during the morning hours of July 19th, but not before the fire burned a total of 1,291 acres.  No structures were damaged, but some wheat fields were burned to an unknown extent.  Damages were estimated.

The Cashe Butte wildfire ignited in the remote Barker Canyon area.  Firefighters had to ferry across Banks Lake to reach the flames.  The fire burned 470 acres before it was contained on July 12th.  No structures were damaged and no injuries were reported.

High flows out of Libby Dam in northwest Montana resulted in widespread flooding along the Kootenai River in and around Bonners Ferry and downstream to the Canadian Border.  Flooding along the river began on June 25th and carried over through the beginning of July.  Damage occurred along the city dikes in Bonners Ferry.  Volunteers had to shore up 500 feet of levy behind the Kootenai River Inn to prevent water from spilling in.  Water filled sub-surface storage areas of the General Feed and Grain located near the river in Bonners Ferry.  Sloughing of dikes downstream of Bonners Ferry was observed as well.  This resulted in an extensive amount of water seepage into farm lands throughout the Kootenai River valley.  Over 5,000 acres of farm land was damaged resulting in four million dollars in crop damage.
Lightning struck and damaged the level sensor on the Tubbs Hill reservoir.
The hail report was received from Camp Grizzly.

Public reported quarter to half dollar size hail.  Storm total precipitation from 2100 to 0500 was 2.63 inches.  Extensive crop damage due to hail.  A small debris flow from the rainfall runoff covering the road and railroad track with 6 to 12 inches of debris.

Non-severe thunderstorms during the early morning of July 17th, produced frequent lightning strikes in and around the Post Falls area.  One bolt struck a man in his car while driving to work. The man did not receive any injuries from the strike however his car's sensors were damaged and he lost all power control while driving, including the brakes. He was able to safely pull the vehicle to the side of the road then noticed the car could not be turned off even without the key in the ignition. Two tires were also blown out from the strike.
Torrential rain and pea size hail was also observed with the storm.
The report was from Valley Gas in Lapwai.
Report from Nez Perce Tribal Police.
The hail caused major damage to a vehicle.
The hail caused numerous dents on vehicles.
Hail resulted in numerous dents to vehicles.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down several trees.  There was also roof damage to an outbuilding.
A roof was torn off an outbuilding.  Spotter also observed one inch hail.
Trees and power lines were blown down at Ogara and South Benewah Road.
Tree blown down on power line.
A large tree was blown down on highway 3 blocking the roadway near Interstate 90.
Measured at the Lake Pend Oreille Buoy.
Power lines were blown down.
Prichard Tavern reported a small utility trailer blown roughly 150 feet.  Several tree limbs down.  Pea size hail also observed.
A tree was blown down on a power line at Coeur D Alene River Road at mile post 27.
A tree was blown down onto a power line on School House Loop Road.
Nine trees were blown down at Tin Can Campground.
A tree fell on a moving vehicle killing the driver.
Priest Lake State Park reported numerous trees down.  RV and Cabins throughout the park received extensive damage.  A few cars were totaled by falling trees.
Park Ranger reported water out of ditches and over roads.  Road damage due to the water.
A washout occurred along Lower Crab Creek Road.
City Hall had to be sandbagged due to water flowing into the building.
Several dirt roads and driveways were washed out along D-Rez Loop Road.  State Route 155 was shut down for a short time at Milepost 59 due to undercutting of the roadway.
Hail broke one window and caused window trim from five other windows to break off.  The hail also damaged corn and alfalfa fields as well.
Measured at the Vantage Washington DOT sensor.
A large tree branch fell onto two cars near the intersection of Wall and Maxwell Streets.
Trees were blown down on West Ridge Drive.
Public reported a few trees completely blown down.  Numerous tree limbs were snapped off trees that remain standing.
Nespelem School reported a downed tree roughly 10 to 12 inches in diameter.   The tree fell on and damaged a dumpster.
One large tree and some smaller trees were blown down onto Highway 155.
Numerous trees were blown down in the town of Keller.  Several trees fell onto houses causing significant damage.
Law Enforcement reported trees down on Manilla Creek Road.
Hundreds of trees were blown down in the area.  Multiple trees landed on houses.
Trees were blown down on Silver Creek Road.
The Post Office building sustained roof damage.  Rain entered the office lobby and resulted in minor water damage.  Dime size hail was also reported with the storm.
Trees and power lines were down on Highway 21.
Trees and power lines were down on Cache Creek Road.
Numerous large trees and power lines were blown down in and around Republic between 4 PM and 430 PM.  Trees fell on a houses and blocked Highway 20 for a period of time.
A woman was killed by a falling tree while camping along Trout Creek.
Numerous trees were blown down on State Route 20 at Sherman Pass.  The highway was temporarily closed.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down trees and power lines temporarily blocking Highway 395.
Several trees were blown down from thunderstorm winds.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a 50 year old pine tree.  Two to four foot waves were observed on Lake Curlew.
A tree was blown down and landed on a house.  Several other trees were blown down at the adjacent campground.

At approximately 2000 PDT, torrential rains over the Nahahum Canyon triggered a large debris flow.  One resident, located at 8566 Nahahum Canyon Road, received significant damage with minor damage noted at two other residences.  Three to four feet of mud, logs, and rocks tore a hole in the side of a three-bay shop then blew out the three front doors and continued down the canyon.  The mud lifted a large pickup truck a foot and a half off the ground and carried it from one side of the shop to the other.  Three to four feet of mud surrounded the nearby house and filled the crawlspace.  Tools and other items from the shop along with landscaping rocks from the property were strewn a half mile down the canyon.
A debris flow occurred along Highway 20 at milepost 209.  The slide was large enough to temporarily close the highway.

A portion of Highway 95 was covered in mud and debris when a flash flood caused a section of the hillside to collapse down the hillside into the highway.  The water, mud, and debris flowed along the highway in a typically dry Lapwai Creek bed and eventually accumulating deep enough to flow back across the highway.  There was no damage to the highway however, it took several hours for the highway department to remove the mud and debris from the roadway.

A tree fell on a tent and trapped an unknown number of occupants.  Other downed trees were reported in the recreational vehicle park on the north side of the Conconully Reservoir.  Windows from some of the recreational vehicles located at the park were blown out as well.  Wind damage was localized to this one area in the town of Conconully.  No injuries were reported and damage was estimated.

A stationary thunderstorm anchored just southeast of Conconully, WA dumped well over an inch of rainfall.  This resulted in a large debris flow along Salmon Creek Road between milepost seven and nine.
Caller reported quarter size hail and very heavy rain which resulted in localized urban flooding.

Around 4,000 lightning strikes on September 8th through the 9th sparked around 100 wildfires north and west of Wenatchee.  The vast size of the complex of wildfires burning across this area combined with the very dry conditions, resulted in these fires continuing to burn into the month of October.  By the end of September, the wildfire complex was only about 50 percent contained and had consumed around 55,000 acres.  The wildfire burned in a multitude of fuel types from grasses to shrubs to timber.  One indirect fatality occurred as a firefighter grew ill as he battled the blaze.  He was taken to a local hospital where he died on arrival.  Around 180 evacuation orders were given for residential areas along the west side of Wenatchee soon after the fires were ignited, but no homes were reportedly lost; however, one shed was destroyed by the wildfires.  The damage for the shed was estimated.  Stable atmospheric conditions through much of the month of September resulted in poor ventilation of the wildfire complex and hazardous air quality for people living in and around the town of Leavenworth and Wenatchee.  No injuries or fatalities were reported due to the poor air quality.

The Okanogan wildfire complex composed of three fires that burned on the hillsides along the Methow Valley.  Dry conditions resulted in these fires burning into the month of October.  By the end of September, these fires had consumed a total acreage of 6,169 acres.  Road closures were included on Gold Creek Road (FS4340-100) and Forest Service Road 4330-100.

The Barker Canyon Complex was located along the western banks of Banks Lake. This complex was composed of two wildfires: the Barker Canyon Fire and Leahy Fire. Both wildfires grew rapidly during a windy period on September 10th through the 11th. The Barker Canyon Fire initially threatened the towns of Grand Coulee and Coulee Dam. Total acreage of both fires grew to 91,162 acres before they were contained on September 19th.  The fires destroyed three homes and nine outbuildings and burned through two power stations.  Total damage was estimated.
A downed tree was responsible for power outages four miles southeast of Dover, Idaho near the town of Sandpoint.  The power outage impacted 243 customers.
A downed pine tree damaged five power poles and associated lines along Highway 2 and Icicle Road.  Highway 2 was temporarily closed.  800 customers were temporarily without power.

Several areas across northeastern Washington experienced power outages due to downed trees or snapped limbs.  The following list indicates the city and amount of customers that lost power; Kettle Falls 569, Colville 152, Fruitland 27, Hunters 27, Chewelah 206, and Clayton 85.
Isolated power outages were observed north of Moscow, Idaho due to strong winds.
Several power outages were reported across the Spokane Area due to strong winds and downed trees.  One tree fell on 2100 West Broadway.
Power outages were reported in Stevens County due to strong winds.

Downed trees and broken tree limbs were responsible for multiple power outages across the Palouse.  Roughly 1400 customers were impacted by the outages.  The strongest wind gusts came with the passage of the cold front during the early morning hours.  A DOT sensor near Uniontown clocked a gust to 60 mph.
Multiple power outages were experienced across the Idaho Palouse due to strong winds and downed or snapped trees.

Multiple power outages were reported across the Lewiston Area due to strong winds and combination of downed trees and broken limbs on power lines.  A DOT sensor located on Shirrod Hill had an isolated gust of 57 mph.
Several power outages were experienced across the Coeur D Alene Area due to strong winds and combination of downed trees and broken limbs on power lines.
Several trained spotters and SNOTEL data reported three to seven inches of snow at elevations roughly 3000 feet and higher.  Lower elevations near the Canadian Border received upwards of two inches.

Several trained spotters and SNOTEL data reported three to seven inches of snow at elevations roughly 2500 feet and higher. Lower elevations near the immediate Canadian Border received upwards of two inches.
Ski resorts and SNOTEL data reported six to twelve inches of snow at elevations roughly 3000 feet and higher.  The one exception was at Bear Mountain SNOTEL which measured fifteen inches of snow.

The Okanogan wildfire complex composed of three fires that burned on the hillsides along the Methow Valley.  These fires began in September and burned into the month of October.  These fires consumed a total acreage of 6,169 acres.  Road closures were included on Gold Creek Road (FS4340-100) and Forest Service Road 4330-100.

Around 4,000 lightning strikes on September 8th through the 9th sparked around 100 wildfires north and west of Wenatchee.  These fires burned from the beginning of September through the end of October.  The complex of fires consumed 56,478 acres of grasses, shrubs, and timber.  One indirect fatality occurred as a firefighter grew ill as he battled the blaze.  He was taken to a local hospital where he died on arrival.  Around 180 evacuation orders were given for residential areas along the west side of Wenatchee soon after the fires were ignited, but no homes were reportedly lost; however, one shed was destroyed by the wildfires.  The damage for the shed was estimated.

Slick road conditions due to compact snow and ice resulted in a car accident involving two vehicles on Highway 41 at the intersection of Highway 54 in Spirit Lake.  One vehicle was traveling northbound along Highway 41 when the driver lost control of the vehicle and spun into an oncoming vehicle traveling southbound.  The driver of the northbound vehicle was killed (indirect) due to her injuries at the scene of the crash.  The driver and a passenger of the southbound vehicle were injured (indirect) in the accident.  Both were treated at a nearby hospital and later released.
A pair of funnel clouds was observed side by side near St. John.
A pair of funnel clouds was observed side by side near St. John.
A rock slide blocked the north bound lane on State Route 31 at milepost 8.  Short delays were reported as traffic in both directions alternated the use of the south bound lane.

A pickup truck and semi-truck collided head on along Highway 41 at Seasons Road. The driver of the semi-truck was not injured but the driver of the pickup truck was inflicted with serious non-life threatening injuries (indirect).

Moderate to heavy snow fell across the Spokane Area during the evening and early overnight time-frame from December 16th into December 17th.  Three to five inches of snow was observed at multiple observation platforms by midnight on the 17th.  Gusty winds and above freezing temperatures behind an accompanying warm front lead to rapid melting and very little impact on travel by the morning commute.

Three to six inches of snow had fallen by 0100 PST on the 17th mainly along and north of the Highway 2 corridor.  The snow quickly melted as gusty winds, rain, and warmer temperatures followed during the morning hours on the 17th.
Five to ten inches of snow fell across the Wenatchee Area.  The highest snow amounts were reported in northern sections of the zone with Entiat and Chelan reporting 9.5 and 8.0 inches respectively.
Five to nine inches of snow fell across the Waterville Plateau. The highest snow amount was reported at Chief Joseph Dam which received nine inches of snow.
Five to ten inches of snow fell across the Okanogan Valley.  Precipitation transitioned to freezing rain briefly before ending 0800 PST on the 17th.
Five to eight inches of snow fell across the Okanogan Highlands.

Six to ten inches of heavy wet snow was observed across most valleys within the East Slopes of the Washington Cascades.  Heavier amounts, generally ten to fourteen inches, were reported near the crest.

Five to ten inches of snow fell across northeastern Washington resulting in snowfall amounts ranging between five to ten inches.  Warmer air eventually found its way into the valleys during the afternoon on the 17th and snow accumulations during the afternoon hours on the 17th shifted mainly into the mountains.

Snowfall amounts across the Northern Idaho Panhandle ranged from five to ten inches in the valleys to near two feet in the mountains.  A backcountry snowmobiler reported numerous downed trees between Priest Lake and the Canadian Border however there was no damage reported.
Snowfall amounts ranged from 2 to 4 inches in the valleys to a foot in the mountains, generally above 4000 feet.

Moderate to heavy snow fell across the Coeur D Alene Area during the evening and early overnight time-frame from December 16th into December 17th. Three to five inches of snow was observed at multiple observation platforms by 0400 on the 17th. Gusty winds and above freezing temperatures behind an accompanying warm front lead to rapid melting and very little impact on travel by the morning commute.
The Bear Mountain SNOTEL observed twenty inches of snow.  Schweitzer Mountain Ski Resort reported fourteen inches.

Snowfall amounts ranged from six to thirteen inches across the Central Panhandle Mountains.  The most significant snow accumulations occurred above 4500 feet.|The Lost Lake SNOTEL recorded thirteen inches of snow.
Seven to fifteen inches of heavy wet snow fell across the area.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four to eight inches in the Wentatchee River and Methow Valleys to upwards of two feet near the Cascade Crest at locations including Stehekin and Holden Village.

Numerous valley locations received between three and seven inches of snow through noon on December 20th.  Warmer air infiltrated the area around midday shifting the main threat for additional snow to elevations above 2000 feet.
Snowfall amounts ranged between six and eleven inches with the highest snow of eleven inches reported ten miles northwest of Kettle Falls.

The Northeast Washington Mountains was one of the hardest hit areas with heavy snow receiving between seven to twenty inches.  An isolated report from Rice, Washington came in with twenty-three inches.
On average, snowfall amounts ranged between three to five inches across the Spokane Area.  A few locations on the northern reaches of the zone did report upwards of five to seven inches of new snow.
Widespread snowfall amounts of six to twelve inches were reported across the Northern Idaho Panhandle with local amounts to fourteen inches noted at Schweitzer Ski Resort.
Widespread snowfall amounts of four to six inches were reported across the Coeur D Alene with local amounts up to nine inches noted at a few of the higher elevations.

The heaviest snow fell under a narrower deformation band extending through the communities of Deary and Clarkia which reported seven and nine inches respectively.  Lower amounts of two to five inches were common outside of this band.
A deformation zone setup over much of the Idaho Palouse resulting in widespread snow amounts of four to seven inches.

A band of heavy snow across central and northern Whitman County resulted in five to seven inches of snow over the communities of Saint John, Rosalia, and Pullman.  Southern sections of the county received significantly lower amounts, generally in the one to three inch range.

Numerous power outages were observed across Northeastern Washington due to strong winds and tree limbs falling on power-lines.  Students from Columbia and Evergreen School Districts in Stevens County were released from school just after 0900 PST, due to the power outages.

Numerous power outages were observed across the Idaho Panhandle due to strong winds and tree limbs falling on power-lines. Students from Plummer-Worley School District and St. Maries School Districts were released from school just after 0900 PST on the 17th, due to the power outages.

Four reports of wind damage occurred across Spokane County. A 28 inch diameter tree was blown down and landed on two homes on the South Hill. The homes were located on the 1100th block of East 41st. Another large tree was snapped roughly five feet from the ground, landing in the street and onto power lines on Ninth Avenue between Perry Street and Altamont Street.  Utilizing references in a picture, this tree was estimated to be around 24 inches or larger in diameter.  A NWS employee located in the Deep Creek Area also relayed minor roof damage to a neighbor's pole barn. In Cheney, a metal roof was peeled from the top of a mobile home. The ASOS at Spokane International Airport and RSOIS at the NWS each measured sustained winds of 43 mph coupled with a gust of between 53 and 55 mph.

A trained spotter in Pullman measured sustained winds of 45 mph with gusts to 56 mph on a Davis weather station.  The sensor was located on the roof of the house.  Several houses in the neighborhood had shingles blown off.  In Pullman, a tree top snapped off and landed on a house on the 400th block of SE South St.  Utility companies reported that roughly 1200 power outages occurred across the Washington Palouse due to the strong winds.  Several other observation platforms measured gusts between 52 and 56 mph throughout the day.

A DOT site at Alpowa Summit, elevation 1775 feet, measured sustained winds of 52 mph with a peak gust of 69 mph between 0500 and 0700 PST.  The sensor continued to report sustained winds of 35 to 45 mph with gusts to 60 mph through 1400 PST.  Two additional CWOP sites in Pomeroy, WA also recorded wind gusts between 57 and 60 mph.  No damage was reported in the area.

Roads that were closed due to downed trees included: Cedar Brae, River Road, Shugart Flats, Chiwawa Loop, Baraburn, Cottonwood, and Highway 2 along a 35 mile stretch between Stevens Pass and Leavenworth.  The highway is one of two primary east-west routes through the mountains open during the winter.  About 7,000 to 10,000 drivers cross Stevens Pass during the Christmas holiday.  The 3800 power outages affected the following communities: Plain, Lake Wenatchee, Leavenworth, Mary Canyon, Little Chumstick, Coles's Corner, Kahler Glen, and Fish Lake.  The worst hit locations experienced outages in excess of five days.  Damage costs included 4.6 million dollars from Chelan County PUD, 218 thousand for Chelan County Public Works, and estimated costs for at least fifty houses or cabins damaged and four vehicles.  On December 19th, a tree struck a pickup truck traveling on Chiwawa Loop Road injuring the driver.  On December 21st, a tree struck a car on Highway two thirteen miles east of Stevens Pass killing two adults and injuring four passengers in the SUV.  Two of the four injuries were listed as serious and critical.  On the evening of December 22nd, a 2005 Audi slammed into a newly fallen tree while traveling on Highway 2 roughly 22 miles west of Leavenworth.  All five people inside the vehicle were injured, some seriously.
Storm total snowfall reports ranged between one and four inches.
Heavy snowfall reports from four to as much as six and a half inches were reported in the valleys.
Numerous reports between two and a half to five inches for the event; a report of eight inches of snow was reported in Worley.
Storm total snowfall reports ranged from one inch to up to five inches.

Numerous heavy snowfall reports of five to seven inches were observed around and south of the Colville area.  Snowfall reports were a bit lighter closer to the Canadian border in the range of two to three inches.

Storm total snowfall reports of five to six inches were common across the area.  Dozens of schools were closed for the morning of the 7th, and numerous slide offs and accidents were reported as the heavy snowfall resulted in a messy morning commute.  A major trouble spot was on Interstate 90 at the Argonne exit where a tanker truck driving west bound jacked-knifed.  Multiple vehicles, including a Spokane Transit Authority (STA) bus, collided into the semi-truck.  Traffic was restricted to only the right lane for at least an hour between 0530PST and 0630PST.
Storm total snowfall reports of four to over five inches were common across the area.
A total of 8.4 inches of snowfall was recorded from the evening hours of the 9th through 1900PST on the 10th, and another 5.1 inches was recorded from 1900PST on the 10th through 0415PST on the 11th.
Storm total snowfall reports ranged between three and six inches across the area.
Storm total snowfall reports ranged from 4.2 inches in Nez Perce to between 6 and 7 inches in Winchester.

Forty-nine Degrees North Ski Resort received nine inches of snow while Mount Spokane reported twelve inches from the storm.  Numerous valley locations including Clayton, Sacheen Lake, and Elk reported between one and three inches and mainly on grassy surfaces.  The exception was along roadways which climbed above elevations of 2300 feet.  Under a heavier snow shower, roughly half an inch of slushy snow accumulated along a small section of US 395 resulting in a brief period of slick driving conditions.  A driver heading northbound on US 395 lost control of his car and crossed the center line, striking a second vehicle resulting in one fatality.
Heaviest snowfall accumulations occurred in the mountains above 4,000 feet; Schweitzer Ski Resort reported seven inches of total snowfall with this storm system.

National Weather Service survey team reported straight line wind damage.  A total of 20 to 30 trees were blown over and another 30 to 40 trees were damaged in a swath of 150 yards wide and half a mile long.  One tree fell on a barn, another on a house, and a third fell on a trailer.  Some of the larger trees that fell over were up to three feet in diameter.  Trees were laying in a southwest to northeast direction.  Winds were estimated at between 70 to 80 miles per hour.  The home owner was in the basement at the time of the damage and was not injured.  A rough estimate was used for the total damage during the event.

A squall line moving across the Newman Lake area destroyed a barn before pushing into the Idaho Panhandle.  Wind speeds were estimated to up to between 55 and 60 miles per hour.  A rough damage estimate was used for the event.

Three to six inches of snow fell at elevations mainly of 3500 feet and higher.  Travel across Sherman Pass was hazardous at times due to the snow accumulations on the roadway.  This met local late season snow criteria.

CWOP in Pomeroy measured sustained winds of 43 miles per hour between 1500 and 1600 PDT.  The Alpowa Summit DOT sensor measured sustained winds between 45 and 49 miles per hour between the hours of 1500 and 1800 PDT.

Most observation platforms in the northeast mountains of Washington experience some degree of sheltering and more then likely do not measure the actual wind gusts that are occurring during a wind storms.  Numerous power outages were observed across the area due to downed trees or tree limbs.  The outages included: 132 outages in Northport, 1634 outages in Colville, and 122 customers in Springdale.

Most observation platforms in the Okanogan Highlands of Washington experience some degree of sheltering and more then likely do not measure the actual wind gusts that are occurring during wind storms.  128 customers in Boyd experienced power outages due to either a downed tree or tree limb falling onto power-lines.
Spokane ASOS measured sustained winds of 31 mph with gusts to 40 mph.  A tree was blown onto a power line three miles southwest of Chattaroy which resulted in power outages to 56 customers.

Strong winds resulted in power outages to 30 customers in the town of Hope, Idaho and 596 outages in Athol, Idaho.  The cause in Hope was unknown but a downed tree was to blame in Athol.  A NAVY Buoy on Lake Pend Oreille recorded a wind gust to 68 mph however no other observation platforms in the area observed winds greater then 45 mph.
Strong winds resulted in power outages to 110 customers in the community of Colfax.  The exact cause of the outages was not known but was thought to be tree or tree branches damaging power lines.
Strong winds resulted in power outages to 134 customers in the town of Calder.
Winds blew down trees onto power lines near Lake Wenatchee causing power outages in the area.  Dry Creek, the nearest observation platform recorded wind gusts to 51 mph during the event.
A National Weather Service employee surveyed the Okanogan River near Tonasket and found pasture fields, and, to a lesser extent, agricultural fields flooded during peak flow.

In the city of Wenatchee, Miller, Western, Springwater, and McKittrick roads experienced flooding.  Manhole covers were blown off along Miller Street between Millerdale Avenue and Springwater Avenue.  Sections of these roads were closed for roughly one hour as one to two feet of water filled some intersections.  Mud and water could be seen flowing across State Route 28 at the junction of US2 and US97 via a DOT camera on the northern sections of Wenatchee.  The water and mud was estimated to be less then a foot deep.  A CoCoRahs report from one mile west southwest of Wenatchee stated the lower level of their outbuilding was flooded however it is unknown if there was any damage.

High intensity rainfall on the 2012 Peavine burn scar caused a flash flood and debris flow in Tronsen Creek and across Upper Tronsen Road.  The culvert under Upper Tronsen Road was clogged with eight feet of debris and the creek now flows over the road.  Several large boulders were also deposited along the road.  On the eastern periphery of the Peavine burn scar, a large debris flow occurred in Devils Gulch.  A long segment of a USFS trail was wiped out.  Several hundred feet of the trail was covered in downed trees carried by the debris flow.

Lightning struck a transformer box in an alley behind a residential house, traveled through the lines and blew out a second transformer.  Several homes loss power that afternoon until utility companies were able to replace the transformers.  The transformers were located between Broadway and Boone Streets in west Spokane.  The exact time of the lightning strike was estimated.

Lightning struck a house on Spokane's South Hill starting a fire.  Firefighters were able to quickly extinguish the fire but the home did sustain heavy fire damage to a small portion of the attic and to the ceiling in one second floor bedroom.
The exact time of the lightning strike was estimated.

A CWOP mesonet site in Lewiston recorded 0.51 in twenty minutes.  The intense rainfall overwhelmed the city's infrastructure leading to urban flooding and closed streets.  Among the closures were G Street, Adams Lane, and Idaho Street.  Nearly a foot of water was observed on sections of the blue bridge.  The water receded within an hour and no injuries or damage was reported in this event.

Two low-centroid thunderstorms, each producing tropical like downpours, moved through Riverside between 1300 PDT and 1530 PDT.  The intense rainfall caused water, mud, and minor debris to briefly flood an intersection in town.  The nearest observation site, Omak ASOS, recorded 0.76 over a 134 minute period with the most intense rainfall occurring within the second cell.  This cell delivered 0.45 of the total rainfall in a span of 28 minutes.
Moderate to locally heavy rain of 0.25 to 0.50 inches resulted in cherry damage across portions of southern Grant County.
Moderate to locally heavy rain of 0.25 to 0.50 inches resulted in cherry damage across portions of Chelan County.
Moderate to locally heavy rain of 0.25 to 0.50 inches resulted in cherry damage in the GreenBluff area outside Spokane.

Heavy rain across the 2012 Peavine Canyon Burn Scar resulted in a large debris flow down Number One Canyon Road into southwestern portions of Wenatchee.  Upwards of eight inches of mud filled yards, basements, and garages of homes along the road.  Witnesses described a wall of water, mud, rocks, branches, and tree limbs coming down Number One Canyon Road with the sound of rocks scraping the road.  The debris flow reached the intersection of Lars Lane and Number One Canyon Road.  There were no injuries.
Most of the hail stones were the size of quarters and largest hail stone was the size of a ping pong ball.
A large tree was blown over onto Highway 95 at milepost 533.

Heavy rainfall led to a debris flow across Number Two Canyon Road roughly from mile post three to the end of the pavement around 0000 PST.  The slide left half to one foot of mud and debris, including rocks, over the roadway rendering the road impassible.  The Number One Canyon Near Wenatchee Rain Gauge (NOOW1) received 0.29 of rainfall over a span of 29 minutes.  Runoff incised ditches up to four feet in diameter exposing utilities.

A few basements and outbuildings were flooded from heavy rain.  Colockum Creek flowed out of its banks and across Colockum Road just upstream of the intersection with Kingsbury Road.  There was no damage to the road but a fence on the adjacent property did sustain some damage.

The fire was determined to be human caused and grew up to over 2,000 acres before it was contained. The fire burned in dry grass, brush and trees on steep slopes along the north shores of Lake Chelan near Manson. At one point, the communities of Emerson Acres and Greens Landing and the Antilon Campground were given a level one evacuation notice. No reports of any damaged structures as a result of the fire.

This was a fast moving brush fire that ignited along Highway 20 just west of Okanogan.  The fire was believed to be started by a lawn mower early on the sixteenth; the time of ignition was estimated.  The fire burned through 2,000 acres before being contained on the seventeenth.  Two outbuildings were destroyed.  The fire also burnt down a wooden 115 thousand volt transmission H structure on the Loup transmission line.  This resulted in the breaker opening at the Okanogan substation, which in turn resulted in a loss of power out of the substation into the Methow Valley.  Material damage to Public Utility District assets were estimated at fewer than 20 thousand dollars and the cost of the outage was estimated to be 60 to 70 thousand dollars.  The fire also destroyed one outbuilding (estimated at 10,000 dollars), one hay baler (estimated at 4,000 dollars), one hay swather (estimated at 12,000 dollars), five miles of orchard fence (estimated at 150,000 dollars) and two hundred fruit trees (estimate at 350,000 dollars).

A relatively small fire flared up along the north shore of Lake Wenatchee amongst a group of recreational cabins.  Three of these cabins were destroyed during the blaze, and another sustained major structural damage.  Damage costs were estimated.

The wildfire was human caused and started near the intersection of Colockum Road and Tarpiscan Road.  The fire spread south into neighboring Kittitas County and remained west of the Columbia River.  The fire continued to burn into the month of August.  Numerous homes, three major power lines, a natural gas line, two wind farms, timber, water quality, wildlife habitat and range resources were all threatened at one point or another.  Three primary residences and several outbuildings were burned.  Two fire fighters suffered minor injuries.

A brush wire burned twelve to thirteen acres on the West Plains of Spokane County.  The fire started near a mobile home park near Airway Heights and moved east.  The fire jumped across Spotted Road and stopped at Cheatham Road.  Three outbuildings and one abandoned car were burned.  The time of when the fire started and was put out and damage costs associated with the fire were estimated.

The Crescendo fire ignited in very rugged terrain approximately 22 miles south of Avery in the Crescendo Creek canyon.  The fire burned in rugged terrain, which made it difficult for firefighters to access the wildfire.  This fire did not pose a risk to any structures nor was there much of a threat to natural resources.  As such, this fire was monitored through the month and was allowed to continue to burn into August.
Hail fell along Highway 2 and St Andrews Road.  Some wheat crop damage was reported, but the extent of the damage was unknown.

This was a man-caused wildfire located twenty miles southeast of Keller. Fuels consisted of fallen dead trees, sage, grass and bitter brush. One home and one outbuilding were threatened, but escaped any damage from the fire.

Several trees and power lines were knocked down from strong thunderstorm winds across east and southeastern sections of Othello.  Reports from the utility company included:  power lines down from a fallen tree two miles southeast of Othello, a downed power pole six miles southeast of Othello, and another power pole downed six miles southeast of Warden.  A newspaper also reported at least eight large trees blown down in the town of Lind.  The downed trees resulted in damage to fences and power lines.

Roughly fifty customers in the Mae Valley subdivision of Moses Lake lost power when strong thunderstorm winds damaged five different power poles holding transmission lines.|As the gust front moved into northern sections of Grant County, law enforcement reported numerous trees and power poles downed in and around Grand Coulee.  Overall, 6500 customers loss power across Grant County during the storm.

A thunderstorm squall resulted in a dust storm across the Columbia Basin.  A trained spotter in Ritzville reported the dust storm and shared pictures which illustrated a wall of dust a couple hundred feet tall coupled with low visibility.

In the town of Harrington, two large trees were split.  One tree was located on the golf course and second on 5th and Sherlock.  No damage was noted to the property.  Widespread two to four inch branches were scattered on ground around town.  The Odessa Agrimet Sensor clocked a peak wind gust of 57 miles per hour.  Several trees were downed in Davenport but no property damage was reported.  One tree did land on a powerline leading to 29 power outages.  A large tree was blown down at the Sherman Cemetary.  A greenhouse was destroyed on a property located seven miles north of Reardan.  The Spring Canyon RAWS located three miles southeast of Coulee Dam clocked a wind gust of 65 miles per hour.  The storm also knocked down multiple trees at the Lakeview Terrace mobile home park.  Two mobile homes were damaged.

Numerous houses across sections of Omak east of Highway 97 between Omak River Road and Vista Vu Drive had shingles torn off the roof and large trees blown down.  One house near the intersection of Kruse Street and West Parkway Street had eight panels of cedar fencing blown down.  A few of the posts which were held down by concrete were snapped in half.  In addition to the wind, damage to the fence was likely due to the neighbors small metal shed which was tossed roughly 150 yards.  Metal roofing from a building at the Omak shooting range was peeled off.  Numerous other trees were blown down in Eastside Park and surrounding area.  Downed trees and damage to structures was also reported in the adjacent Colville Indian Reservation, specifically along Columbia River Road, Cold Springs Road, and North End Omak Lake Road including the Paschal Sherman Indian School.  The public relayed that Boy Scout Camp Bonaparte on Bonaparte Lake north of Wauconda also received significant damage to three buildings and the storm knocked down a swath of trees.  The Kramer RAWS clocked a wind gust to 62 mph before the storm entered city limits of Omak.  A Davis weather station located on private property in Okanogan measured a wind gust to 66 mph.

The Spokane NWS clocked a wind gust of 62 mph on the RSOIS.  Numerous trees, some large, were downed in Nine Mile Falls area, especially along West Charles Road.  Some trees were uprooted and other were snapped halfway up the trunk.  Trees fell on a combination of roofs, outbuildings, fences, and power lines resulting in multiple power outages.  A large tree was uprooted along Highway 2 in the Deep Creek community.  A large tree fell on a power line in Chattaroy leading to 178 power outages.
A weather spotter in Fernwood reported hail one inch in diameter.  Time was estimated based on radar.

A strong gust front associated with a thunderstorm squall resulted in numerous trees and power lines downed throughout the county.  Over 400 power outages were reported within the communities of Ford, Fruitland, Clayton, and Colville.  The Midnite Mine RAWS located six miles northwest of Wellpinit clocked a wind gust of 57 mph.  A DOT sensor located one mile west of Suncrest clocked a wind gust of 55 mph.  Both sensors experience some degree of sheltering.  One tree did fall on a house but the exact location is unknown.

Numerous trees and power lines were downed throughout the county resulting in power outages and some damage to structures.  Power outages were reported in Diamond Lake and Tiger but it was assumed many more power outages occurred in other communities.  There was one fatality and one injury when a 200 foot tall tree uprooted and fell on a tent at the Stagger Inn Campground in the Kaniksu National Forest.
A large tree was downed and fell across power lines in Republic resulting in numerous power outages.

Numerous trees and power lines were downed within and around Coulee City.  Downed trees blocked roads, damaged vehicles, boat trailers, street signs, and homes.  A large tree fell across State Route 155 closing the highway for over three hours.  The roof was partially torn off at the Coulee Dam Casino.  Several signs were also damaged at the casino.  Due to the roof damage, moderate rains trailing behind the wind resulted in water damage to portions of the casino and offices.  The Spring Canyon RAWS located three miles southeast of Coulee Dam clocked a wind gust of 65 miles per hour.

A large tree was knocked onto power lines resulting in 41 power outages in Oldtown, ID.  The storm also downed numerous trees across the Priest Lake Ranger District of western Bonner County.  An incident management team was put together to quickly assess and manage hazards discovered in developed campgrounds and recreation sites throughout the national forest given the approaching Labor Day holiday.  Based on the incident map, Navigation, Trapper, Geisinger, Plowboy, and Beaver Creek were among the sites that required hazardous tree removal.

Numerous trees and power lines were downed from thunderstorm winds across southern Douglas County.  Two large trees, estimated to be two feet in diameter, were downed at Desert Canyons Lodge.  In Orondo, three large trees, estimated to be two feet in diameter and 120 feet tall, were knocked into high voltage power lines starting a small fire.  At least 50 apple trees across multiple orchards were also damaged from the high winds.  In Waterville, two downed trees landed on houses along Poplar Street and numerous large limbs were on the ground throughout town.

High winds uprooted a 40 foot tree onto a car in southeastern sections of Quincy.  Power and phone outages were reported across southwestern sections of town.  Six inches of standing water was on sections of Highway 28 in town.

Highway 2 at Pine Canyon was closed due to mud and debris covering the roadway for a period of time.  The road was covered in six to eight inches of debris.  The water dug three to four foot trenches within the drainage.  The Douglas RAWS reported six tenths of rainfall in an one hour period.
Chelan County PUD reported numerous downed trees and power poles along the southern end of Lake Chelan.  Some apple trees in nearby orchards were also damaged.
Highway 971 was closed between mile markers nine and eleven due to a mudslide blocking the highway.

Heavy rain from a slow moving thunderstorm fell over the 2013 Colockum Tarps burn scar leading to flash flooding, a massive debris flow, and significant property damage.  One debris flow occurred down Robinson Canyon and across Colockum Road cutting through a home and barn along the way.  The home had water and debris flowing through it and out the front windows.  Residents escaped through the front windows and climbed a tree until water receded.  A large boulder went through the corner of the barn.  Asphalt was removed from Colockum Road between Colockum Creek and Kingsbury Road.  Kingsbury bridge over Colockum Creek also sustained minor damage.  Flash flooding was also observed down the Colockum Creek drainage to the intersection of Tapiscan and Colockum Roads.  Water washed out Colockum Road at mile post 12 making the road impassible.  A mobile home on Tarpiscan Road at the bottom of the drainage was washed off its foundation.  The residents in the mobile home were able to make it to higher ground before it washed away.  Flash flooding was also reported by the public down the Dry Gulch drainage located south of the Colockum Creek drainage.  Flood waters and debris led to the washout of the Dry Gulch Bridge on Colockum Road making the road impassible.
Highway 97 alternate was blocked temporarily at milepost 212 due to a small mudslide.

A collapsing thunderstorm and microburst was thought to be responsible for localized damaging winds near the city of Winthrop during the overnight hours of August 10th.  The NCSB RAWS station located four miles south southeast of Winthrop clocked a gust of 87 mph.  Several trees were damaged or blown down at the Bear Creek Golf Course but no other damage was reported with this storm.

Conconully was pounded by heavy rain for almost two hours leading to backed up culverts and mudslides.  One slide was two to three feet deep on Lake Street.  A second slide was two feet deep on Sinlahekin Road.  Three houses on Silver Street had some minor water damage.
A bolt of lightning started a home on fire on Good Hope Road in Althol, ID.  The homeowner got out safely but the fire, fueled by natural gas in the home, destroyed everything inside.
Visibility was reduced to 50 feet in Warden.
A large dust cloud engulfed the area reducing visibility to near zero.
Visibilities down to below one quarter of a mile in North Spokane due to blowing dust.  One indirect injury reported as a pedestrian was struck by a vehicle due to the poor visibility.

Numerous trees and power lines downed in Othello.  Trees toppled onto homes and fences.  An estimate of forty power poles snapped off.  Schools across the Othello area were closed the following day due to impacts from the storm.

Winds in Warden were sustained 30 to 35 miles per hour with gusts up to 58 miles per hour as the gust from moved through.  Numerous trees downed and widespread power outages across the Moses Lake area.  Some trees fell on houses and on vehicles.  An outbuilding was destroyed and a fence was damaged by flying debris.  At least six power poles were snapped off near Soap Lake.  Schools across the Moses Lake area were closed the following day due to impacts from the storm.
Large tree limb estimated at ten to twelve inches in diameter snapped off.  Numerous other three to four inch diameter limbs down across the area.  A metal roof was blown off of an enclosure.
Numerous trees and power lines downed in Ritzville.  Some trees fell on houses and on outdoor equipment.
A roof was blown off of a barn approximately eight miles southeast of Harrington.

Numerous reports of trees falling onto power lines resulting in over a thousand customers losing power.  Damage was reported in Cheney, to Spokane, to Mead and in Deer Park.  A large tree toppled over at 21st Street and High Drive in Spokane on South Hill.  Other trees reported down or snapped off resulting in damage to homes and/or vehicles.  Many tents at the Spokane County Interstate Fair were damaged or flipped over due to the strong winds from the gust front.
Strong winds from a thunderstorm destroyed a combine shed, uprooted 5 trees and blew off a roof of a barn.  Winds also knocked out power to 40 customers.
A tree fell into some power lines knocking out power to three customers.
Shop doors blown off and power poles downed across Wheeler Road.
Several power lines downed across the southwestern portion of Bonner County.
Tree fell onto some power lines and knocked out power to 115 customers.
Hail was mostly half an inch in diameter, but there were some hail stones up to 1.5 inches in diameter.  Time of the event was estimated by radar.

A 6 inch limb broke off and damaged a fence four miles south of La Crosse, and the power line to a residence was pulled out by the strong winds.  Tree limbs up to six inches in diameter were broken off five miles south-southeast of Winona.  Finally, at least ten trees were blown over in the town of Endicott.
A tree was knocked down across a roadway.  Time was estimated based off of radar.  Damage costs were also estimated.

Tree fell onto mobile home that briefly trapped the occupants.  Bedroom door was damaged and occupants had to crawl through an opening to the hallway to escape.  Minor injuries were sustained to an adult female and a child.

A flash flood down the Colockum Creek drainage washed out Tarpiscan Road at the Colockum Creek bridge.  Colockum Road, Kingsbury Road, and Agnew Road were closed due to the damage.  Multiple homes were damaged along the Colockum Creek Drainage as well by rocks, trees and other debris that traveled with the flood wave.  Damage costs were estimated.

Flash flooding from Number 2 Canyon blocked a portion of Number 2 Canyon Road above milepost 3.  Flood waters reached as far as western Wenatchee.  Flood waters also damaged homes and property to private residences in the Canyon.  Damage costs were estimated.
Heavy rain caused mud and debris to block a portion of Eagle Creek Road.  Damage costs were estimated.
A flash flood deposited mud and rocks approximately two feet deep over Jameson Lake Road at Sulphur Springs Road.  Damage costs were estimated.
Several flash floods and debris flows across a three mile stretch of Mission Creek Road from milepost 4 to milepost 7.  Damage costs were estimated.

Flash flooding and debris on Fourth of July Creek above Icicle Creek closed off National Park Road 76.  Many campers were stranded above where the flash flood occurred until the road was cleared of debris.  Damage costs were estimated.

Flash flooding and debris traveled down Imus Creek near Stehekin and covered approximately 350 linear feet of Stehekin Valley Road.  Mud and debris covered the road up to eight feet deep in spots.  Several vehicles and bicycles in a parking area were damaged and/or pushed into Stehekin Lake.  An office and residential building were surrounded by mud and debris, but only received minimal interior flood damage.  Damage costs were estimated.

X-NE Road was covered by water and mud for approximately 100 to 150 yards and appeared to be deep in sections.  It was likely that the road was impassable during the flash flood, but there were no reports of impacts during the event.  Timing of the flash flood was estimated by radar.
Highway 20 was closed across Chelan County due to flash flooding and debris flows.  Damage costs were estimated.
A flash flood washed out approximately 200 yards of a portion of the eastbound lane of Highway 20 at milepost 266.  One lane was kept open for traffic.  Damage cost were estimated.
A funnel cloud was spotted between the towns of Molson and Chesaw off of Fields Road.

A debris flow blocked the road to Harts Pass just below Deadhorse Point.  The slide continued down onto Lost River Road near the River Bend Campground.  Mud and debris accumulated to about five feet in depth across the road.  Damage costs were estimated.
Numerous trees either toppled over or tops snapped off at the Fort Spokane Campground.

Strong winds downed several trees along Highway Three at mile post 55 near the Clarkia Range Station.  No damage was reported but the highway was blocked until the debris could be removed.  Several power outages were observed across area from smaller limbs and branches falling on power lines.

Highway 57 was closed five miles north of Priest River due to downed trees on the highway.  Several power outages were observed across the North Idaho Panhandle from smaller limbs and branches falling on power lines.

Multiple trees were blown down blocking highway 206 near mile post 12.  Highway 206 was closed for over 24 hours until crews were able to remove the debris.  At 19th and Arthur on the South Hill, the top of a 50 year Ponderosa Pine was snapped off blocking the street and taking a tangle of cable and phone lines with it.  Numerous power outages were observed across the Spokane Area.

Strong winds uprooted trees that fell into the Pend Oreille PUD���s 115 kV transmission line near Box Canyon Dam. The outage affected approximately 3,000 customers between Dalkena and Ione.  Other smaller outages occurred throughout the county and kept line crews busy through the night.  A trained spotter reported an uprooted tree five miles west of Newport.  The size of the tree was unknown.

Heavy wet snow resulted in numerous power outages across northern Idaho due to downed power lines and trees onto power lines.  Kootenai Electric Cooperative reported more than 20 outages affecting more than 4,000 customers.
Downed power lines blocked Highway 2 just west of Coulee City at the intersection of Highway 17.  Damage costs were estimated.
Multiple power outages across the Spokane area due to wind and downed trees on power lines.  Damage costs were estimated.
Tree on power lines knocked out power to 23 customers.  Damage costs were estimated.
Tree fell onto power lines and knocked out power to 45 customers.  Damage costs were estimated.

Heavy wet snow fell across the Spokane area during the morning commute.  This resulted in slick driving conditions across the area with 80 vehicle collisions reported.  Numerous vehicles spun out descending out of the Spokane South Hill area; some of these roads were closed off due to the volume of accidents.  Multiple collisions reported on Highway 395 at milepost 175, four miles south of Deer Park; both lanes were blocked with long delays for motorists traveling that route.  Numerous vehicles were stuck traveling southbound on 395 on the Wandermere Hill. No serious injuries were reported.
Wet snow during the morning commute resulted in slick driving conditions along Highway 291 near Suncrest.  The Big Sandy hill in this area was closed for several hours due to vehicle spin outs.

A mixture of snow, freezing rain and sleet during the afternoon hours resulted in slick road conditions across the area.  Numerous vehicle collisions were reported: a two-car collision near Hatch Street, a two-car collision just north of Hawthorne Road, a one-car collision three miles south of Deer Park, and along Interstate 90 between mileposts 275 and 277.  Multiple slide-offs and two rollover collisions were also reported on Highway 195 between Hatch Street and Mullen Hill Road.

Freezing fog resulted in some icy conditions on Interstate 90 between Evergreen and Barker Road at around 0800PST.  The first accident was a pickup truck that had rolled over upside down.
