The driver of the vehicle had to be cut out.  Four other vehicles slid on the same patch of ice during the morning hours.  None of the accidents resulted in serious injuries.

Freezing fog resulted in icy conditions on an overpass along Interstate 90 in Medical Lake.  A pickup truck heading eastbound was driving too fast for the conditions and lost control.  The pickup truck proceeded to swerve into the opposite lane triggering a multiple vehicle collision.  One of the vehicles involved in the collision was a semi-truck that collided into two other vehicles; one of the vehicles struck by the semi-truck resulted in a fatality; eight other injuries were also reported with the accident.  The eastbound lanes of Interstate 90 were blocked just west of the Four Lakes exit for hours.
Moderate to heavy snow fell between 1400 and 1600 PST leading to multiple accidents during the evening commute across the Spokane Area.  Snowfall amounts were generally between two and four inches.

Moderate snow, slick conditions, and excessive speed was responsible for a ten car pile up along Interstate 90 seven miles east of Ritzville at 1246 PST.  Eleven people were involved in the crash, four which were injured and one which died on the scene.  Eight of the ten cars were totaled.  Snowfall totals at the time of the accident were generally around an inch.  Roughly an hour later, a car rolled over at mile post 77 along Highway 395, eighteen miles south of Ritzville.  The driver of the vehicle suffered serious injuries.
Snowfall amounts across the Washington Palouse ranged between four and seven inches.
Four to six inches of snow fell across the Central Panhandle Mountains including the Interstate 90 corridor.
Four to six inches of snow fell across the Idaho Palouse.
Snowfall amounts ranged from two to three inches across northern sections of Kootenai County increasing between four and five inches across southern sections.
Valley locations below 3000 feet across northern Stevens and Pend Oreille Counties received between three and five inches of snow.  Six to fourteen inches of snow fell above 3000 feet.

Snowfall amounts varied by elevation.  One to four inches of snow fell below in the valleys below 3000 feet; four to eight inches of snow was observed between 3000 and 4000 feet; eight to fifteen inches were observed in the mountains at elevations above 4000 feet.
Snowfall amounts ranged from one to three inches in the valleys to up to fifteen inches in the mountains.
Wind chills throughout the Purcell Trench fell between -18 and -22 degrees Fahrenheit.  Wind chills in the mountains dipped between -30 and -50 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wind chills across Kootenai County dipped between -15 and -20 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wind chills in the valleys dipped between -13 and -20 degrees Fahrenheit.  In the mountains, wind chills decreased between -20 and -30 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wind chills dipped between -15 and -20 degrees Fahrenheit at locations, especially those  exposed to north and northeast winds.
Wind chills values of -15 to -20 degrees Fahrenheit were observed.  Some mountain locations above 5000 feet observed wind chills as cold as -30 degrees Fahrenheit.

Widespread wind chills of -8 to -16 degrees Fahrenheit were observed across the Okanogan Valley but scattered observation platforms measured wind chills between -18 to -26 degrees Fahrenheit.  The coldest wind chill of -26 degrees Fahrenheit was observed nine miles west southwest of Wauconda.

Slushy snow accumulations and excessive speed were responsible for a two car accident along Highway 270, seven miles east of Pullman.  One driver was killed and the other was injured with the driver in the westbound lane loss control and crossed into the eastbound lane.  The time of the accident was 1605 PST.

A motorists traveling along State Route 211 was thought to be using excessive speed for the icy conditions when his car slid off the road, hit a ditch, and went airborne. The car eventually came to rest on its tires but the driver was killed in the accident.
Light slush and excessive speed along Highway 195 led to a three vehicle accident twenty miles north of Colfax.  Five people were injured but there were no fatalities.
Storm total snowfall accumulations ranged between two and six inches in the valleys with ten inches reported at Schweitzer Ski Resort.
Storm total snowfall of nine inches reported at Lookout Pass Ski Resort.
Storm total snowfall totals of nine and ten inches at 49 Degrees North Ski Resort and Mt. Spokane Ski Resort respectively.
Numerous snowfall reports of between three and seven inches and as much as ten inches reported in the valleys.
Storm total snowfall generally between four and seven in inches reported.
Heavy snowfall of up to 10 to 14 inches reported in places.
Widespread storm total snowfall amounts of two to five inches reported.
Storm total snowfall amounts generally between three to five inches.
Storm total snowfall totals of up to four inches.
Widespread storm total snowfall totals of between three and seven inches.
Sustained winds of 40 to 50 miles per hour with gusts between 70 to 90 miles per hour observed at the Lakeview sensor on Schweitzer Mountain.

Trees downed along Highway 3 at milepost 102.5 and partially blocked the road.  A blown tree  knocked out power to  2,000 Avista Utility customers in the Coeur d'Alene area.  Another tree fell over onto some power lines in Hayden, which knocked out the power to 2,000 customers in the area.
High winds knocked over a 26 inch diameter grand fir tree and the tree toppled over onto a residence.

Fleming Creek Road washed out in two locations and was closed off.  Little damage was reported along the side of the road and was reopened the next day.  Sandbags were placed around a house on Moon Shadow Road due to some basement flooding.  Damage to the home was estimated.

A portion of Highway 24 was closed due to an overabundance of wind-blown tumble weeds onto the highway.  Snow plows had to be called out to remove the tumble weeds before the highway could be reopened.

A ten inch diameter tree snapped off in the Five Mile Prairie area north of Spokane; some houses also lost shingles in the area.  There was also a report of an old growth tree that lost four large branches with a girth of eight inches in diameter north of Davenport.  One of these branches flew about ten feet away from the tree.

A 40 foot cell phone tower collapsed due to high winds at 49 Degrees North Ski Area.  The cell tower smashed through the rough of an adjacent building that contained some transmission equipment.  A tree also was knocked over into some power lines near the resort at 0948PST; power was later restored at 1135PST.
Winds snapped off the top of some trees.  Damage cost was estimated.

Minor urban flooding reported in and around Deer Park.  Residence living on 2nd Avenue indicated water over the roadway and some water seeping into a basement of a building.  Large puddles covering other roads around town, but all were passable without any closures reported.  Damage costs were estimated.
Heavy snow reported above 4,000 feet in elevation.  Storm total snowfall of nine inches at Schweitzer Ski Resort.
Heavy snowfall above 4,000 feet in elevation with a foot of snow reported at Lookout Pass Ski Resort.
Heavy snowfall above 3,000 feet in elevation with over a foot reported in the mountains, mainly near the Cascade crest.

A few homes in Athol were surrounded by standing water due to rain, snow melt and frozen soils.  Homes that were affected by flood waters were located along Sienna Loop, East Seasons Road and on North Clagstone Road.  Damage costs were estimated.
The Bonneville Power Administration reported issues of riming on their transmission lines running across the northern portions of the Columbia Basin.

The Bonneville Power Administration reported issues of riming on their transmission lines running from the Mead area (Bell substation) out onto the west plains.  Avista Utility also reported riming on their transmission lines with power outages reported across the Spokane area.  This included a broken conductor and broken poles between the Four Mounds area to the Idaho state border.
Avista Utility lost a transmission line, a broken conductor and broken poles located between Reardan to the Washington state border due to ice buildup.
Snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches leading to hazardous travel during the Friday morning commute.
Snowfall amounts ranged between two and four inches with local amounts to five inches which led to delays, accidents, and disruptions to travel during the Monday morning commute.
Snowfall amounts ranged between one and three inches.  This led to delays, accidents, and disruptions during the Monday morning commute.

Snowfall amounts ranged from two to four inches leading to delays and disruptions during the Monday morning commute.  Two children died Sunday, February 2nd after falling through ice covering a pond near Plummer.  The children were looking for their dog and it is unknown if the children were unaware of the pond which was blanketed with light snow.
Snowfall amounts ranged between four and six inches leading to disruptions to travel.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four to six inches across a majority of the zone with travel disruptions along Interstate 90 through the Silver Valley and Lookout Pass.
Snowfall amounts ranged between two and four inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between two and four inches.

Snowfall amounts ranged between one and three inches leading to slick travel across the Spokane area.  An accident related to slick road conditions led to temporarily closures of eastbound lanes of Interstate 90 near the Sprague exit.
Snowfall amounts were generally between two and four inches.  The heaviest snowfall was recorded in the city of Moscow where amounts were closer to four inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between four and seven inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between three to four inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between three and five inches at locations like Nez Perce and Winchester to seven inches at Waha.
Snowfall amounts across the zone ranged from two to three inches with 2.9 inches reported in the city of Lewiston.

One to three inches of snow fell across the Washington Palouse on the 8th, falling on top of two to four inches from the previous day.  Meanwhile, modified arctic air moving into the region brought gusty northeast winds resulting in blowing and drifting snow.  Large drifts resulted in a road closure on the 8th along a section of Highway 27 which stretches across southern Spokane and northern Whitman Counties.
Snowfall amounts ranged between three and four inches.
Four to six inches of snow fell during the evening of the 8th into the morning hours of the ninth.  Blowing and drifting snow led to closures of highway 27.
Snowfall amounts ranged between two and four inches.
Snowfall amounts generally ranged between one and three inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from two to four inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from three to four inches with locally up to five inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between three and four inches.
Two to three inches of snow fell across southern portions of zone 35, mainly in Adams County.  Northern sections of the zone only received around an inch of snow.
Snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches.

Snowfall amounts ranged from three to five inches.  The official snow observer from Lewiston reported five inches while a CoCoRaHs observer located 2.6 miles southeast of Lewiston reported four inches.

Snowfall amounts ranged from one to two inches across northern sections of Shoshone County to three to five over the south.  The highest amounts were received in Clarkia, ID which reported five inches.
Snowfall amounts were generally between four and five inches.  A CoCoRaHs observer located just northwest of Nezperce at an elevation of 3225 feet reported 5.8 inches of snow.
Snowfall amounts greatly ranged across the zone.  The northern half of the zone picked up between one and two inches while three to locally four fell across the southern half.
Snowfall amounts generally ranged from one to three inches.  An isolated report of four inches was received from the town of Wauconda.
The heaviest snow started around 0800 PST with storm total amounts in the three to four inch range across the Spokane Area.
Snowfall amounts of two to four inches were observed across Lincoln County leading to slick travel along the Highway 2 corridor.  Snowfall amounts were generally near an inch in Adams County.
Snowfall amounts range between one and three inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged between two and four inches.
A band of heavy snow brought a quick three to four inches along the Interstate 90 corridor with higher amounts in the higher terrain.  A COOP from Prichard received eight inches of snow.
A band of heavy snow brought quick accumulations of three to four inches across Bonner County while Boundary county only picked up around two inches.
A solid four to six inches of snow fell across northern Idaho.  The most snow fell in the community of Colburn which reported six inches.
Snowfall amounts ranged from four inches in the valleys to ten inches in the mountains.
Two to four inches of snow fell in the valleys before snow levels climbed near 3000 feet.  In the mountains, seven to fourteen inches of snow was observed.

Light to moderate snow fell across the East Slopes during the evening and overnight hours of the 11th resulting in four to six inches for most locations.  Post frontal convective snow showers slopping across the Cascade Crest brought an additional two to four inches of snow to locations near the Cascade Crest including Mazama, Holden Village, and Stevens Pass.  These locations received between seven and eleven inches of snow throughout the event leading to hazardous travel, especially across the mountain passes.

Light to moderate snow fell across the East Slopes during the early morning hours of the 14th resulting in four to six inches for most locations. Post frontal convective snow showers slopping across the Cascade Crest brought an additional one to three inches of snow to locations near the Cascade Crest including Mazama, Holden Village, and Stevens Pass. A COOP in Mazama reported ten inches from the event.  This led to hazardous travel across the mountain passes.

Light to moderate snow fell across the East Slopes during the morning hours of the 10th ahead of a strong cold front.  Behind the cold front, an unstable air mass and strong westerly flow resulted in numerous convective snow showers along and east of the Cascade Crest.  The morning snow brought between two and four inches then an additional four to eight inches fell at some locations with the post frontal showers.  Locations near the Cascade Crest including Mazama, Holden Village, and Stevens Pass received between nine and thirteen inches of snow from the event.  Further east away from the crest, snowfall amounts were generally in the six to nine inch range.

Steady light to moderate snow fell across the East Slopes through the evening hours of the 15th then snow transitioned toward convective post frontal showers with the heaviest activity focusing near the Cascade Crest.  Snowfall amounts generally ranged from six to eight inches with the highest amounts near the crest.
Snowfall amounts ranged between three and four inches with local amounts of five inches reported in Waterville.
Rising snow levels led to heavy snow in the mountains and little to no accumulations in the valleys.  Ski resorts in the area reported eight to twelve inches of snow.

Heavy snow fell above elevations of 2000 feet.  Snowfall amounts ranged from six inches near Leavenworth to sixteen inches in Holden Village.  Plain picked up between twelve and fourteen inches.  Six to ten inches fell in the upper reaches of the Methow Valley.

Heavy snow was confined to elevations of 3500 feet and higher.  Local ski resorts reported seven to nine inches of snow from the event.  In the valleys up to three inches of snow fell before switching over to rain.

Heavy snow fell at elevations of 2000 feet and higher with the exception of Stehekin, WA which is near the Cascade Crest.  Snowfall amounts at Plain, Leavenworth, and Stehekin were generally in the eight to fourteen inch range.  The most impressive twenty-four hour total was received from a COOP at Holden Village which reported seventeen inches.  This was the seventh snow storm to impact the East Slopes of the Washington Cascades since the 8th of February.  A family of six became stranded in a backcountry cabin located in the Sears Creek drainage.  The family had skied into the cabin on the 15th and were unable to ski out because two to three feet of new snow had fallen in the four day period.  Chelan County Search and Rescue successfully rescued the family utilizing a snow cat.
Schweitzer Mountain Ski Resort received eight inches of snow.  Snowfall amounts in the valleys ranged between one half and three inches.

A snowplow company on Schweitzer Mountain, located at an elevation of 5000 feet, reported fourteen inches during the early morning hours of the 17th.  Two to three inches of snow fell in lower elevations including Sandpoint and Hope.  Clark Fork reported six inches of snow.
Heavy snow was limited to elevations of 4000 feet and higher.  Local ski resorts in the zone received between eight and thirteen inches of snow.

The East Slopes of the Washington Cascades experienced nearly three days of light to moderate snow and occasionally periods of heavy snow from February 22nd through the morning hours of the 25th.  Snowfall totals over the three day period ranged from eight inches across the eastern reaches of Chelan County to forty inches along and near the Cascade Crest.  Mazama, located in the western reaches of the Methow Valley received seventeen inches of snow.

Snowfall amounts across the Spokane Area ranged between four and six inches from heavy snow on the 24th.  The previous day, the same area received between two and four inches resulting in two day totals of six to nine inches.
Snowfall amounts on the 23rd were in the two to four inch range.  A second round of snow on the 24th brought an additional two inches leading to two day totals in the four to seven inch range.

Valley snowfall amounts over the three day period ranged between seven and ten inches. Three to four inches of snow fell between the 22nd and morning of the 24th. An additional three to six inches fell on the 24th.

Snowfall amounts over the three day period ranged between seven and ten inches. Three to four inches of snow fell between the 22nd and morning of the 24th. An additional three to six inches fell on the 24th.

Snowfall amounts from the 22nd to the 23rd were near two inches in northern Lincoln County to half an inch in Adams County.  A second round of snow on the 24th brought an additional two to three inches across southern reaches of the zone to four inches across northern Lincoln County.

Two rounds of heavy snow impacting the Central Panhandle Mountains of Idaho.  Snowfall amounts in the valleys ranged from eight to fourteen inches over the two day period.  In the mountains, two day totals were around two feet.  The first round of snow which fell on the 23rd dumped around a foot in the mountains and two to six inches in the valleys.  A second round of snow on the 24th brought an additional three to six inches in the valleys and foot in the mountains.

Snowfall amounts over the two day period ranged between six and twelve inches. The first round of snow which fell on the 23rd brought three to six inches.  A second round of snow on the 24th brought an additional three to six inches.
Snowfall amounts on the 23rd were in the two to three inch range. A second round of snow on the 24th brought an additional two to three inches leading to two day totals in the four to six inch range.

Wind chill values dipped to minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit throughout the windier Purcell Trench and between minus 10 and minus 18 in the more sheltered valleys.  The coldest wind chill observed was at Sandpoint which dipped to minus 20 Fahrenheit.  Schools in the Sandpoint district closed due to the cold.

Wind chill values dipped down to minus 23 degrees Fahrenheit throughout the windier Purcell Trench and between minus 10 and minus 18 in the more sheltered valleys. The coldest wind chill observed was at Coeur D Alene Airport which dipped to minus 23 Fahrenheit.

Wind chill values greatly varied due to complex terrain and sheltering.  Windier locations experienced wind chills between minus 10 and minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit.  Wind chills in the sheltered valleys only dropped between minus 5 and minus 12 degrees Fahrenheit.  Mountain locations experienced wind chills near minus 30 degrees Fahrenheit.

Wind chill values varied due to complex terrain and sheltering. Windier locations experienced wind chills between minus 15 and minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit. Wind chills in the sheltered valleys only dropped between minus 5 and minus 12 degrees Fahrenheit.  The Deer Park ASOS observed a wind chill of minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit.

Wind chill values of minus 15 to minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit were observed across the West Plains and higher benches surrounding the city of Spokane.  More sheltered locations only observed winds chills between minus 10 and minus 15 degrees Fahrenheit.
The coldest wind chills 20 degrees Fahrenheit was observed at Priest Lake.  Most other locations experienced wind chills between minus 5 and minus 18 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wind chills of minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit were observed in the communities of Rathdrum and Spirit Lake.  Most other locations experienced wind chills between minus 5 and minus 15 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wind chills of minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit were observed in the communities of Prichard and Avery.  Most other locations experienced wind chills between minus 5 and minus 15 degrees Fahrenheit.
Very cold temperatures and winds near 10 mph resulted in wind chills of minus 10 to minus 21 across the zone.  The coldest reading of minus 21 was at the Teepee Seed Orchard RAWS.
Two passengers were killed and two others were injured when a car lost control on icy roads and ran head on into a semi-truck.  One passenger was ejected from the car.
Icy roadways across the Spokane Area led to multiple accident during the morning commute.  The largest accidents occurred along Highway 2 near Spotted Road and State  Route 195 near Mullen Hill Road.

Two men were found dead near a wrecked Jeep off a snowy Forest Service road in the Derby Canyon area.  Reports state the two men were going for a drive in an all-wheel-drive jeep along primitive roads that had snow two feet deep in places.  The vehicle was found on Thursday about 75 yards down a steep embankment off the primitive road.  It appeared the vehicle had lost traction while trying to drive up a slope on the road in deep wet snow.  The exact time of the accident was unknown.
Icy road conditions in the Ephrata area led to school closures on the 13th of February.
Snowfall amounts across southern Chelan County ranged from five to seven inches.  Further north near Lake Chelan and the Methow Valley, snowfall amounts were between two and three inches.

Numerous areas across Spokane County experienced flooding on the 12th of February.  Due to frozen grounds, the flood problems persisted through the 14th in some cases.  A small ice jam on Coulee Heights Creek caused the creek to become diverted and flow into a private residence.  Water was approximately five feet deep in the garage and surrounding home.  A NWS employee observed up to two inches of water with some mud and small  debris flowing down Rambo Road just north of the Forecast Office.  Water was over a foot deep along the shoulders.  The swift water washed out portions of the shoulder and foundation to the edges of the pavement.  A few blocks away from the Forecast Office, water flooded the West Prairie Village Mobile home park located on the corner of Craig and Haid Lane.  It was estimated that one to two feet of water filled sections of the park.  In southern sections of the county, many secondary roads were flooded in low crossings.  State route 27 just north of Latah near milepost 58 was impassible for a period of time due to water over the road.  Water was also over the roadway along SR 2 two miles west of Airway Heights.  Damage extended into the Spokane Valley with damage or flooding observed near the intersection of Sanson and MacDonald, Crown Street at Forker Draw, Ridgemont Estates on Shamrock Street, and Thorpe Road at Chester Creek.

Numerous areas across Lincoln County dealt with flooding between the 12th and 14th.  Some sections of highways that were flooded include SR 23 between mileposts 57 and 60 south of Harrington, SR 231 between mileposts 36 and 42 near Reardon, SR 231 between mileposts 18 and 19 near Edwall, SR 25 between Davenport and Lake Roosevelt, and SR 21 between mileposts 57 and 60 near Harrington.  A creek that runs through the middle of the Edwall flooded the Post Office and adjacent businesses with one to two feet of water.  Edwall-Reardon school district was forced to delay school openings because buses were struggling to navigate muddy dirt roads.  A tech company located on SR 231 reported 30 inches of water flooded its manufacturing facility.  Fortunately, the staff was able to get all valuable equipment off the floor before the flood waters entered.

Numerous areas of northern and central Whitman County experienced flooding between the 12th and 14th.  State route 23 was closed between Sprague and Saint John between mileposts 15 and 43 due to water over the roadway in several locations.    Colfax, WA experienced heavy flooding closing Mill Street from Canyon to Spring which also included mileposts 0 to 1 of SR 272.  Flood waters up to a foot were observed in portions of downtown Colfax.  Water undercut part of the roadway on SR27 five miles south of Oakesdale washing out part of the northbound lane.  Several homes in the community of Ewan were inundated with up to one foot of water.
Areas of flooding were observed across portions of northern and eastern Adams County.  State route 21 nine miles south of Odessa was flooded for a period of time.
A trained spotter located three miles northeast of Loon Lake reported two to three inches of standing water on property and around the area.  There were no known road closures from flooding.
Several low lying areas experienced minor flooding.  Sections of Lovell Valley Road near Plummer was covered in water in some sections.
Several low lying areas experienced minor flooding.  A few homes near Moscow, ID reported water seeping into their basements.

Heavy runoff led to several drive washouts for residents on hilly terrain across Kootenai County.  A swollen Latour creek washed away a small levee and parcel of land that supported a shed at a private residence on South Latour Creek Road.

A large tree branch snapped off a tree and landed in a Bengal tiger enclosure at Cat Tales in Mead, WA.  The 35 foot section of pine tree snapped a guide wire and crashed through two fences that hold the big cats.  No tigers or people were injured during the event.
Lookout Pass Ski Resort accumulated fourteen inches of snow over a 24-hour period.
A forty-foot tree fell on a house from winds behind the squall line.  Damage costs were estimated.
One tree of unknown size snapped off along Hatch Road on Spokane South Hill.  Another tree of unknown size was uprooted onto a trampoline.  Damage costs were estimated.
Two large trees snapped off middle of the way up the trunk.  One tree fell onto a corner of a structure with minor damage reported.  Damage costs were estimated.
Strong winds behind the squall line blew a road sign into a vehicle traveling on State Route 195.
Tree toppled over onto power lines and across two lanes along Highway 5 near St. Maries.  Damage costs estimated.
Half of a tree in Rathdrum City Park blew over from strong winds behind a squall line.
Power lines knocked down by toppled trees.  An estimated 5,000 customers lost power in the Spokane area.  Damage costs were estimated.
Strong winds blew off a tin roof in Grant County.  Damage costs were estimated.

Heavy rain and low elevation snow melt led to standing water in low lying areas, flooding along small streams and creeks, road washouts and isolated reports of some basement flooding.  Spangle Creek flowed out of its banks resulting in water surrounding homes with basement flooding along a three block stretch.  A vehicle became stuck on a flooded road and had to be saved by rescue personnel.  There were reports of flooding in fields in Cheney and in Elk.  State Route 231 between milepost 0 and 28 was closed due to water and mud over the roadway.  Flood waters over Jackson Road took out an eight foot culvert and a portion of the road above the culvert.  A small creek near Shady Slope and Little Spokane Drive came out of its banks resulting in minor flooding.  Damage costs for the event were estimated.

Numerous county roads damaged and culverts washed out.  State Route 231 was closed from Reardan to the Stevens County line due to flooding over the roadway.  State Route 223 was closed from milepost 44 to 66 due to water and mud over the road.  A four foot section of a driveway was washed out due to a culvert being overrun by flood waters.  Flood waters inundated a culvert resulting in damage to portions of Hawk Creek Ranch Road.  Pooling of water was reported in Edwall due to culverts being overwhelmed by flood waters.  Damage costs for the event were estimated.
Damage to numerous county roads due to flooding.  Flooding was also reported along Thorn Creek.
Prairie Avenue between Huetter Road and Atlas Road closed due to water over the roadway.

Large road washout ten feet across and eight feet deep on Rimrock Road due to a failed culvert.  Two cars drove into a ditch resulting in three injuries.  The washout also resulted in a loss of water to 150 residences in the area.  Damage costs were estimated.
Fleming Creek came out of its banks and flooded a single home.  Damage costs were estimated.
A rock slide blocked State Route 195 at milepost 68 between Rosalia and Plaza.  One vehicle was struck by some of the rocks.  Damage costs were estimated.
Standing water reported across the area.  A mobile home park in Ponderay was hardest hit with one trailer inundated with two feet of water inside the home.  Damage costs were estimated.
The southbound lane of State Route 31 at milepost 11 was blocked by a combination of mud and large rocks.  Time of the debris flow was estimated.

A long duration of heavy rain and snow melt resulted in high flows on the Coeur d'Alene River and surrounding small creeks and streams.  Water inundated numerous roads and low lying areas along the river from Cataldo to Harrison: Flood waters inundated CCC Road near the Mennonite Church, Latour Creek Road near a campground immediately south of Interstate 90, and along portions of Dudley Road west of Latour Creek.  High flows on Latour Creek resulted in soil erosion near the garage section of a residence on Latour Creek Road.  Damage costs were estimated.

Bus carrying school children slid of the road and flipped on its side in Springdale.  The accident occurred on Cementery Road near Highway 231.  There were twenty-seven children on board the bus and eight of the children were transported to the hospital with injuries.

A lot of field flooding and some road washouts in the area.  Deep Creek came up and washed out a culvert and the road above it.  Water also surrounded some homes along Deep Creek.  Damage costs were estimated.
A boulder temporarily blocked one lane of state Highway 155 near Disautel Pass during the morning hours according to an online article in the Omak-Okanogan County Chronicle.
Large rocks in roadway blocked SR20 Eastbound lane only near milepost 318 in Ferry county. Report received via e-mail from Washington State Patrol.
Public reported golf ball size hail.
Lewiston ASOS measured a peak gust of 62 mph.  Lewiston Tribune reported that the Lewiston Orchards experienced some minor flooding of roads and residential areas and some limbs were blown down.
A grass fire sometime after 2300 PDT Sunday evening burned a motor home and farm tractor on Wilmorth Road off Highway 97 east of Chelan, WA.

Several businesses along Howard Street near the intersection of 2nd Avenue were flooded when heavy rain overwhelmed the city's storm drains.  Water was spilling back into buildings through toilets and drain pipes.  Among the businesses were The Interplayers Theatre and Howard Street Boxing.

A gust front with winds estimated between 30 and 45 mph tore off a secondary metal rood from a one story apartment building located near the intersection of W Manilla and E Espanola Rd.  A section of roof blew into the powerlines resulting in power outages along the street.  No damage was observed to adjacent structures or vegetation.

Trained spotter estimated thunderstorm winds of 55 to 60 mph in Anatone near the intersection of Highway 129 and Pine Street.  Tree limbs branches were down across town.  Hail to the size of pennies was also observed.  Larger hail likely accompanied the storms prior to moving into Anatone.
Several trees including a seventy five foot healthy pine snapped.  Trees fell in the same direction to the west southwest.

Thunderstorm winds uprooted three to five large trees on the north end of town.  A lightning strike hit a power pole and knocked out power to portions of the town.  Heavy rain also overwhelmed storm drains resulting in some standing water over roadways.

A severe thunderstorm brought hail to the size of quarters along with very heavy rainfall.  Spotters in the area reported up to eight tenths of rainfall with this storm.  Winds of 40 to 55 mph also accompanied the storm.  The storm moved directly over the Carlton Complex fire camp in Winthrop.

Hail ranging from quarters to the size of golf balls fell across northern Garfield County impacting the communities of Pomeroy and Mayview.  The hail dented three cars and broke sky lights in a metal building at Dye Seed Ranch.  Hail also damaged some of the wheat crop.

Hail ranging from quarters to the size of golf balls fell across southwestern Whitman County impacting the communities of Pullman and Palouse.  Winds of 50 to 55 mph also accompanied the storm which blew a large water tank about 200 feet.  Whitman County Commissioner relayed a report that there was heavy crop damage in the Colton and Pullman areas, but the extent was unknown.

A spruce and locus tree were destroyed around a farm house.  Two roofs on farm buildings lost tin.  Tree limbs four inches in diameter were broken off into four foot chunks and flew 100 feet.  Fifty to sixty foot spruce trees with six inch diameter trunks had twenty feet of their tops taken off.

Hail ranging between quarters and hen eggs fell across eastern reaches of Kettle Falls, WA.  Seven vehicles were damaged at Pingston Creek Road and Highway 395.  The vehicles were dented in spots and some windows were cracked.  The hail also left dents on metal roofs of shop buildings with one resident stating that it was the worst storm he witnessed in 72 years.  A resident two miles south southeast of Kettle Falls stated the hail destroyed the vinyl siding on the south and western portions of his home.  The storm continued to produce severe hail as it tracked northeast toward the Canadian Border.  Hail to the size of half dollars was reported by the public four miles east southeast of Northport, WA.  Winds estimated around 50 mph also accompanied the storm leading to some tree damage eight miles southeast of Northport, WA.
Firefighters on the Carlton Complex reported a mud slide near the middle fork of Gold Creek.
Mills Canyon Fire personnel reported several small debris flows up the Entiat River Canyon near the Mills Canyon burn scar.
Fire personnel on the Chiwaukum Complex reported several small debris flows along Entiat River Road near the Duncan burn scar.
The Alpowa Summit observation platform located along Highway 12 at 1775 feet clocked sustained winds of 48 mph with gusts to 60 mph.
The Silcott Island observation platform located on an island in the Snake River clocked sustained winds near 35 mph with gusts between 59 and 72 mph.
Hail to the size of half dollars was reported four miles north of Colton.
Hail to the size of quarters covered the ground.

A wet microburst brought sustained winds of 35 to 50 mph with gusts 60 to 70 mph across Spokane County.  The winds descended near Cheney and peaked while passing through Airway Heights, Northwestern Spokane, and Deer Park.  Hundreds of Ponderosa Pines were snapped and downed from Northwestern Spokane to Deer Park.  Downed trees led to widespread structural damage, blocked roads, power outages, and injuries.  Significant damage was observed at the Riverside Village Mobile Home Park from trees falling on mobile homes prompting a search and rescue.  One woman was trapped but was not injured.  At least 40 mobile homes and cars in the park were severely damaged.  Forty eight trees were knocked down at a resort on Lake Eloika.  Trees fell on six RVs and the resort's oldest cabin forcing the owners to close their doors for a short period of time.  One person was injured when a tree landed on his vehicle while driving along Lakeside Dr near Reflection Lake in Elk, WA.  A tree branch flew through his windshield and drove him off the road severing his arm and impaling his hip.  He eventually lost his arm in the accident.  Three other people were injured near the Spokane Courthouse by falling tree branches.  Over 30,000 people lost power during the event.  Because of the extent of damage, some residents and businesses remained in the dark for up to four days.  Downed power poles and lightning strikes sparked several new wildfires which quickly grew due to the strong winds.  The winds completely damaged a airport hanger and caused between ten to twelve thousand dollars worth of damage to planes.

A splitting supercell thunderstorm tracked southwest to northeast through Benewah county.  The right mover produced hail ranging from a quarter to half dollar over southwestern reaches of the county.  This included the community of Santa.  The left moving cell produced nickel to quarter size hail across northwestern reaches of the county including Chatcolet Lake.

One inch hail was observed at Conkling Park on Lake Coeur D Alene.  As the storm tracked into northern sections of Kootenai County, strong outflow winds became the main threat resulting in a corridor of tree damage from Coeur D Alene to Althol.  The strongest winds surfaced near Althol and knocked down multiple trees in the RV park across the street from Silverwood Theme Park.  One person suffered a minor injury in the RV Park.  Trees damaged campers, flipped tents, and knocked over smaller campers.

A storm producing damaging winds and quarter size hail tracked through northern reaches of Shoshone County crossing Interstate 90 between Pinehurst and Kellogg.  Numerous cars at a car lot were dented from the large hail.  Trees and powerlines were knocked down in Cataldo and along Coeur D Alene Road.

Weak thunderstorms passing through the area in the wake of two supercell thunderstorms brought strong winds along the Snake River Valley and Lewiston, Clarkston Area.  Several small trees were blown down in Clarkston taking down power lines and damaging a residential fence.  The storm also brought down scattered trees and limbs across Lewiston causing power outages and minor damage.
Four cows and one calf were killed by a lightning strike in Hayden, ID.

Damaging winds led to widespread tree damage across central Bonner County.  A navy bouy located on the south end of Lake Pend Oreille clocked a wind gust of 75 mph.  Multiple trees were knocked down across the city of Sandpoint and smaller communities surrounding Lake Pend Oreille.  Many roads were closed until trees and power lines were removed including Highway 95 near the intersection of McArthur Street.  Power was out for the entire city of Sandpoint and majority of Bonner County directly following the storm.  Several trees fell on houses.  Southern exposed bays on Lake Pend Oreille experienced the worst damage.  Over thirty trees were knocked down between Gamlin Lake and Garfield Bay.  Two people were injured by a falling tree at Green Bay.  Further north on the lake, roughly twenty trees were downed in Shaw Bay.  On a ridge, known as Hawkins Point, over fifty trees were snapped four feet from the ground.  The winds created three to six foot waves in sections of the lake resulting in dock and boat damage.  Broadcast media also reported numerous trees downed at the Western Pleasure Guest Ranch located eleven miles northeast of Ponderay.

Thunderstorm winds ranging between 55 and 65 miles per hour knocked down numerous trees across central and eastern sections of Boundary County.  At least ten trees were knocked down in and around the city of Bonner Ferry.

A severe thunderstorm producing winds of 55 to 70 mph knocked down numerous trees across Pend Oreille County.  The storms also brought periods of very heavy rainfall and small hail.  The widespread tree damage led to power outages, blocked roads, and three injuries.  The worst of the damage occurred in southern areas of the county near Diamond and Sacheen Lakes.  There were two critical injuries at Diamond Lake.  A tree fell on a boat as a family was attempting to dock the boat.  The parents were critically injured but the two kids escaped without injury.

Numerous trees were knocked down across Stevens County with a majority of the damage occurring over southern portions of the county.  Several trees were downed near Addy, WA causing some structural damage to homes.  A CWOP located four miles northeast of Rice, WA clocked a wind gust of 61 mph.

Thunderstorm winds blew down trees across several areas of Ferry County.  Downed trees and power lines were reported in Keller, Inchelium, and Danville.  A media picture from the county shows damage to a car port but the exact location is unknown.
Media relayed report that a resident between Molson and Chesaw measured 74 mph wind gust.  Damage is unknown at this time.

Total cost to fight the fire was approximately 87 million dollars.  The fire spanned two different public zones and cost and acreage is highly uncertain per zone.

The Chiwaukum Complex erupted on July 15th at approximately 0600 PST and was started from a lightning strike on July 14th.  The complex of fires burned 50,540 acres. 543 homes were threatened over the 45 day period but none were lost. Four other structures were burned including one outbuilding and three seasonal cabins. The approximate cost for fighting the fire was 38 million dollars.  The Chiwaukum Creek Fire burned 13,895 acres; Alpine Fire burned 19 acres; Kelly Mountain Fire burned 124 acres; Shoofly Fire burned 163 acres; Mills Canyon Fire burned 22,571 acres; Hansel Creek Fire burned 1,073 acres; Duncan Fire burned 12,695 acres north of Entiat, WA.
Trees and power lines were blown down from thunderstorm winds across portions of Nespelem.

The Midnight Mine RAWS measured a wind gust of 68 mph.  Numerous boats were damaged on Lake Roosevelt due to the winds.  Boaters and videos indicated wind waves of four to six feet on the Lake.  At least ten boats were severely damaged, two boats capsized, and numerous other boats received minor damage.  Several docks were damaged.  No injuries were reported.  Numerous trees were downed across southern Stevens County.

Trained spotter three miles southwest of Miles estimated winds between fifty and sixty miles per hour.  A secondary thunderstorm cell that developed along the gust front produced hail to the size of quarters briefly three miles southwest of Miles.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down trees which blocked State Route 211.  Strong winds also led to numerous areas of tree damage between Newport and the Spokane County border along Highway 2.

Numerous trees were downed or snapped across Northern Spokane County including the communities of Deer Park, Chattaroy, Colbert, Mead, Nine Miles Falls, and Spokane north of Interstate 90 due to a west to east tracking outflow boundary.  A second cell developed along the boundary producing quarter size hail over Five Mile Prairie and sent an outflow boundary north to south across the South Hill and Spokane Valley roughly thirty minutes after the initial gust front went through.  A NWS employee stated winds associated with this boundary were less than 25 mph but witnessed a tree fall down.  Due to its isolated nature, it is assumed that this tree was damaged from a storm two weeks earlier.  Significant damage was observed from northwestern Spokane to Chattaroy to the Pend Oreille County border.  The Riverside Mobile Home Park was hit hard for a second time in as many weeks and forced to evacuate.  Numerous trees fell on homes.  One home on North Echo Road suffered major structural damage.  The nearby Eloika Lake Resort lost eight trees in the storm.  The trees damaged a home, RVs, and vehicle.  The resort which lost 48 trees in a storm ten days earlier was forced to shut down for the remainder of the summer.

Widespread wind damage was observed across the cities of Priest Lake, Sandpoint, Ponderay, Kootenai, Oden, and Lake Pend Oreille.  Hundreds of trees ranging from eight to twenty two inches in diameter were snapped or downed.  Some trees landed on homes, others took out miles of power lines and poles.  At one point after the storm, all of Sandpoint, Idaho was without power.  A spotter in Clark Fork stated fifteen foot trees were almost touching the ground while sixty foot trees were bending at 45 degree angles.  The most widespread damage was along the Highway 200 corridor between Hope and Sandpoint.  The Elk Golf Course in this corridor lost thirteen trees.  The Sandpoint AWOS, also in this area, measured sustained winds of 40 mph with gusts to 56 mph before the power outage.  A roof of a storage shed was blown off in downtown Sandpoint.  Numerous boats and docks on Lake Pend Oreille were damaged from waves that ranged between three to six feet.  Significant tree damage was observed on the south side of the lake in Bottle Bay between the 3800th and 5016th blocks.  All trees were leaning to the east southeast.  Residents interviewed during a storm survey mentioned the winds lasted roughly 40 minutes.
Numerous trees were downed along Coeur D Alene River Road between mile posts twenty and twenty-eight.  Eighteen trees downed on Miller Way in Prichard ranging in height between 75 and 105 feet.

A thunderstorm that passed over the Methow Valley produced wind gusts that knocked down power lines and toppled trees.  Several roads were temporarily closed from downed trees including Highway 20, Highway 153, and Twin Lakes Road.  Several residences in Twisp and Winthrop area were damaged when trees hit the homes or landed on roofs.  Lightning also sparked new wildfires within the Methow Valley, one which grew large and became known as the Little Bridge Creek Wildfire.

Coeur D Alene Press reported that thunderstorms brought high winds and downed trees across portions of Post Falls, Hayden, Spirit Lake, and northern Coeur D'Alene.  The Stateline Speedway and several other businesses on Pleasant View Road lost power and were forced to cancel the Idaho 200 race.  The storm and strong winds also sparked a quick grass fire causing Love's Travel Center to evacuate.  The storm was also blamed for a house fire on Cimmaron Street in Post Falls and another one at Fir and 13th Street caused by downed power lines.
The operator of the Keller Ferry reported winds clocked at 84 mph.
A large tree was blown down at a golf course in Ritzville.

Near zero visibility due to a haboob or dust storm contributed to a six vehicle accident along Interstate 90 twenty-two miles west of Ritzville.  Five people were injured in the accident.  A second accident was contributed to the dust involving two cars on Highway 395 twenty-six miles south of Ritzville.

Outflow winds sustained 30 to 45 mph with gusts to 56 mph passed through Grant County.  Visibility at the Moses Lake Airport dropped near one mile due to blowing dust from the wind.  No damage was reported around the county but the anticipated winds and dust lead to the closure and evacuation of 8000 people at the Grant County Fair hours before the winds arrived.

A line of winds sustained 30 to 45 mph with gusts ranging between 50 and 65 mph blew through Whitman County ahead of a line of thunderstorms.  Visibility across western sections of the county lowered below a quarter mile due to blowing dust.  Numerous tree limbs were down across the town of Palouse ranging between four and six inches in diameter.

Sustained winds of 30 to 45 mph with gusts to 60 mph knocked down trees in Harrington and produced a wall of dust across Lincoln County.  Visibility was reduced below a mile along sections of Highway 2 as the storm moved through.  A sensor at the Sevens Bay Marina clocked a wind gust of 59 mph.
Wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph crossed into southern Stevens County resulting in isolated downed trees and power outages.  The storm weakened while crossing into central sections of the county.

Numerous power lines were knocked down between Spokane and Chattaroy due to winds sustained between 25 and 35 mph with gusts 45 to 55 mph.  A brush fire destroyed three outbuildings and damaged a house near Mt Spokane Park Drive and Peone Road.
A wall of dust from thunderstorm winds resulted in near zero visibility across areas of Whitman County.  Two semi trucks crashed on State Route 26 in the town of Dusty.

Thunderstorm winds of 50 to 60 mph carried a wall of dust into southern Ferry County.  Isolated power line and tree damage was noted across far southern sections of the county.  Power lines were downed on the Colville Reservation along Highway 21 between Keller and mile post nine.

IMET stationed in Nespelem Fire Camp received winds between 50 and 60 mph along with blowing dust.  The winds knocked trees down, tossed boxes, tents, tarps, and signs around fire camp.  Several porta potties were knocked down as well.  The storm weakened as it reached Brewster, Okanogan, and Omak.  These areas received wind gusts near 35 mph which blew down small branches causing some isolated power outages in the community of Twisp.
A large tree and several power lines were blown down in Moscow resulting in 5000 power outages.

A section of a wall and roof was blown off a tribal maintenance shop in Tensed.  Several large branches were blown down near a wastewater plant one mile south of Tensed.  In northern sections of the county, numerous branches three to four inches in diameter were blown down at the Saint Joe Landing Campground.
A large tree was blown down in Coeur D Alene.  Numerous limbs were down across the county.
A tree was blown down on a power line in Sandpoint, ID.

Route 153 was closed at Cow Creek due to a mudslide approximately one foot deep covering eighty feet of the roadway.  The slide crossed the road and went into the Twisp River.  Mud and rocks washed on to Route 20 near Loup Loup Pass from Frazer Creek.  A second hand report stated that a motorcyclist accident occurred at the location of the flow due to the motorcyclists attempting to drive through the mud.  It is unclear if the motorcyclist saw the mud or not.  It is unclear if the motorcyclist was injured.  French Creek at Burma Road flooded sending water and some debris onto private property and up to four homes.  At least two homes got some mud and water into home.
Debris flow down the Chiwaukum Creek caused a two foot flood wave near Highway 2 and mouth of the creek.

IMET informed us that Pope Creek blew out and changed the channel.  The new channel was threatening USFS cabins and resources in the area were forced to sandbag to protect the cabins.  Time was estimated.  A second hand report stated that Pope Creek sent two feet of mud over Entiat River Road on the east end of Duncan Fire and deposited mud around homes at bottom.
Second hand report passed on by the USFS of a debris flow near the Hansel Creek Wildfire burn scar.  No additional information was received.

Heavy rain caused a mudslide at Thimbleberry Creek at the 7.5 mile marker on Stehekin Valley Road.  Three large culverts and creek channels are filled with debris.  The water became rerouted around the debris and along the road to a culvert 1000 feet down valley.  A second smaller slide was at the No Named Creek.  A third slide is at mile 9.2 where debris slid to a barn and corral at a ranch.

Debris flowed onto Highway 153 out of small drainages between Black Canyon Road and Squaw Creek Road.  Squaw Creek Road washed out approximately five miles west of Highway 153.    The entire area was part of the Carlton Complex burn scar.
Numerous spots on Highway 150 between Chelan and Manson experienced flooding from heavy rainfall.  Water got into some homes.  Rainfall amounts ranged between one inch and one and a half inches.
A small debris flow was observed over Rocklyn Road six miles southwest of Davenport, WA.  Rainfall amounts were near one inch.

At approximately 1745 PST, a debris flow blocked Benson Creek Road six miles south of Twisp.  Benson Creek eventually flowed across Highway 153 blocking the road at milepost 24.  An hour later, at 1845 PST, a three to four foot flood wave came down Benson Creek Road trapping several vehicles.  One vehicle which was transporting a convoy of resources from the Carlton Complex was carried down the road by the torrent of water approximately 1000 feet until it got caught in a log jam.  No passengers were injured.  Some people had to be rescued from their vehicles.  Debris flows from earlier rains plugged spillways along five man made lakes known as the Wenner Lakes.  Due to the plugged spillways, three of the five natural dams holding back the Wenner Lakes breached sending a floodwave down Benson Creek Road.  No injuries were reported.  Five to ten vehicles were cut off by the mud and slides and were temporarily unable to get off Highway 153 in the Methow Valley.  The Chiliwist Area was under mandatory evacuations due to the flooding and deteriorating road conditions.  Highway 20 closed due to multiple debris flows between B-O Road and intersection of Highway 153 between mile posts 204 and 229.  The DOT reported that the road was partially washed away in places and unsafe for travel.  The Incident Command Post in Winthrop had significant flood damage to some yurts and some fire personnel had to be relocated.
A debris flow from a thunderstorm closed Highway 97 north of Orondo.
Water was flowing over the roadway half a mile east of Creston on Miles Creston Road.
One inch hail reported by trained spotter in Davenport, WA.
A tree was blown down on MCatty Road.  Heavy rain accompanied the storm causing small rocks and mud to flow onto Thunder Hill Road.

A series of rain storms and low elevation snow melt caused saturated soil conditions through out Spokane County through the second half of March. These conditions lead to numerous small stream and field flooding issues through out the county. Homes and buildings along the shore of Williams Lake and Newman Lake experienced flooding from high lake levels. In Mead a hillside began slowly sliding in a residential area necessitating the evacuation of two homes. Spokane County was included in a State of Emergency declaration issued by the state Governor. ||Twenty two roads in the county were washed out or at least temporarily closed due to flooding.

Lincoln County experienced flooding issues from periodic heavy rain and low elevation snow melt through much of March. The county was included in a State of Emergency declaration due to this flooding. The town of Sprague experienced widespread flooding when Negro Creek overflowed it's banks with most homes and structures in the town experiencing basement, yard and minor first floor flooding. The road into town was cut off by flooding. The National Guard was mobilized to help sandbag. ||The town of Creston also experienced extensive field, basement, road and parking lot flooding. In Edwall a grain elevator collapsed due to saturated soil conditions.

Periods of heavy rain and snow melt produces numerous road closures due to flooding and debris flows in Stevens County through the second half of March. Extensive flooding of fields near the Colville River occurred. The fire station at Hunters was closed due to flooding. Near Northport a lane of flooded road collapsed under a driver, who escaped unharmed. The most notable road closure was Highway 395 near Colville which is a major route through the county. This road remained closed through the end of the month with extensive repairs needed which could not be started until soil conditions dried out.||Stevens county was included in a Washington State State of Emergency declaration as a result of the damage caused by this episode.

Numerous roads in Ferry County were closed due to flooding and debris flows through the second half of March due to spring snow melt and periodic heavy rain. Ferry County was included in a Washington State State of Emergency declaration due to widespread flooding issues.

Flooding and debris flows resulted in numerous road closures across the county due to spring snow melt and periodic heavy rains. Homes were threatened with flooding on Davis Lake as the lake level rose due to run off. Pend Oreille county was included in a Washington State State of Emergency declaration because of this widespread flooding episode.

The Palouse River Gage at Potlach, ID recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 15.0 feet at 10:00 PM PST March 14th, cresting at 17.5 feet at 10:30 AM March 16th. The river dropped below Flood Stage during the evening of the 17th but then rose again above Flood Stage during the afternoon of the 19th cresting 15.6 feet before receding below Flood Stage for the end of the event during the evening of March 19th.

The Spokane River at Spokane River Gage recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 27.0 feet at 10:00 AM PST on March 18th. The river crested at 28.7 feet at 8:30 PM on the 23rd. The river slowly receded but remained above Flood Stage through the end of March and into April. Extensive flooding of fields and park land along the river occurred as well as basement flooding of some homes and businesses.

The Little Spokane River Gage at Dartford recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 6.5 feet at 2:45 PM PST March 15th. The river fluctuated slightly above and below Flood Stage before rising again and cresting 6.8 feet at 11:15 AM on March 19th. The river then slowly receded, dropping below Flood Stage at 2:15 AM March 20th.
A debris flow consisting of rocks and mud 30 feet deep cut State Route 971 near Manson.

Periodic heavy rain and spring snow melt during the second half of March promoted numerous debris flows and landslides through out Boundary County. On March 15th  vibrations from a train caused a saturated ground landslide which undermined the tracks and caused 12 rail cars full of grain to derail and slide into a ravine near Moyie Springs. Debris flows cut numerous roads in the county during the next two weeks. Boundary County was included in a Presidential Disaster Declaration as a result of damage created by this episode.

Periodic heavy rain and spring time snow melt created saturated soil conditions which promoted numerous debris flows and widespread areal flooding through out Bonner County from the middle to the end of March.  A train carrying 50 to 60 empty coal cars derailed near Kootenai after flooding undermined the tracks. A landslide knocked a home off it's foundation and carried it down a hillside near Sagle, with six more homes threatened. Numerous roads were closed due to flooding or cut by debris flows. Bonner County was included in a Presidential Disaster Declaration  issued as a result of the damage caused by this episode.

Snow melt and periodic heavy rain during the month of March caused numerous debris flows and areal flooding issues through out the county. Many road washouts and closures affected travel and cut off residents of some communities until emergency repairs could be made days later. Shoshone County was included in a Presidential Disaster Declaration as a result of the damage sustained during this episode.

Snow melt and periodic heavy rain during the month of March produced numerous debris flows and areal flooding issues across Benewah County. Numerous roads were damaged by flooding. Most notably debris flows and rock slides closed the road between  Plummer and St. Maries, and flooding severely damaged State Highway 5 near Round Lake. Benewah County was included in an Idaho State State of Emergency Declaration as a result of this episode.

Periodic heavy rain and spring snow melt produced debris flows and widespread areal flooding across Latah County during the second half of March. Numerous roads were closed and the county was included in a Presidential Disaster Declaration as a result of the disruption and damage caused by this episode. Paradise Creek near Moscow flooded multiple times leading to damage on roads and parks as well as basement flooding of homes along and near the creek.

The Palouse River Gage at Potlach, ID recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 15.0 feet at 10:00 PM PST March 14th, cresting at 17.5 feet at 10:30 AM March 16th. The river dropped below Flood Stage during the evening of the 17th but then rose again above Flood Stage during the afternoon of the 19th cresting 15.6 feet before receding below Flood Stage for the end of the event during the evening of March 19th.

The Coeur D'Alene River Gage at Cataldo reported a rise above the Flood Stage of 43.0 feet at 7:30 AM PST on March 15th. The river crested at 46.1 feet at 3:15 PM March 15th and then dropped below flood stage. The river then rose to Flood Stage again on March 18th, cresting at 44.7 feet at 3:00 PM on March 19th. The river dropped below Flood Stage at 4:30 PM March 20th, ending the flooding episode.

The Coeur D'Alene River Gage at Cataldo reported a rise above the Flood Stage of 43.0 feet at 7:30 AM PST on March 15th. The river crested at 46.1 feet at 3:15 PM March 15th and then dropped below flood stage. The river then rose to Flood Stage again on March 18th, cresting at 44.7 feet at 3:00 PM on March 19th. The river dropped below Flood Stage at 4:30 PM March 20th, ending the flooding episode.

The St. Joe River Gage at St. Maries recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 32.5 feet at 6:15 AM PST on March 15th. The river continued to rise through the Moderate Flood Stage by March 16th and passed through the Major Flood Stage of 38.0 feet at 9:15 AM March 19th. The river crested at 10:45 PM on March 19th at 39.2 feet. The river receded to below Major Flood Stage at 11:30 PM March 24th and dropped through the Moderate Flood Stage by the morning of March 25th. The river remained in Minor Flood through the end of March and into April.

The St. Joe River Gage at Calder recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 13.0 feet at 5:15 AM PST on March 16th and crested at 13.1 feet later that morning. The river then dropped below Flood Stage during the afternoon. A second and higher rise above Flood Stage occurred at 11:00 PM on March 18th. The river crested at 13.5 feet at 6:30 AM on March 19th and then receded to below the Flood Stage by 6:00 PM March 19th.

Snow melt and periodic heavy rain during the month of March caused numerous debris flows and areal flooding issues through out the county. A debris flow near Harrison forced the evacuation of a residential neighborhood with the land continuing to move through the beginning of April. Over 20 roads through out the county were washed out or cut by debris flows and numerous homes experienced basement and first floor flooding. Kootenai County was included in a Presidential Disaster Declaration as a result of the damage inflicted by this episode.

Flooding along the St. Joe River at Calder, ID flooded and severely damaged a 1200 foot stretch of road leading into the town. In the town of Calder high water threatened homes and flooded basements. Roads along the river bottom were flooded and impassable.

The Lake Coeur D'Alene Lake Height Gage at Coeur D'Alene recorded a rise above the lake Flood Stage of 2133.0 feet at 3:30 PM PST on March 18th. The lake crested at 2134.9 feet at 8:00 PM on March 21st. The lake then slowly fell through the next week, passing back below the Flood Stage at 1:00 PM on March 21st.
Okanogan County Dept. of Public Works closed Peter Dan Road between mile 0.0 and 2.4 due to a landslide.
A debris flow cut Highway 95, which is a primary route through Boundary County, near the town of Naples.
A second debris flow cut Highway 95, which is a primary route through Boundary County, between Naples and Bonners Ferry.
The Bonner County Sheriff reported a debris flow across East River Road, temporarily cutting travel along the eastern shore of Priest River.

The USGS St. Joe River Gage at St. Maries recorded a Minor Flood on the St. Joe River during the first week of April. The river receded to below the Flood Stage of 32.5 feet at 6:15 AM PST on April 5th and continued to fall through the rest of the month.

The Latah County Emergency Manager reported broken tree branches and downed power lines  in Latah County. The Moscow area was impacted with several large trees down, at least one tree falling on a house, and at least two cars damaged by falling trees.

The Wheatland Fire Station near Lewiston measured a wind gust of 66 mph with estimated 50 mph sustained winds for a brief period. Scattered power outages were noted around Nez Perce County by the Emergency Manager.
Wind gusts from a thunderstorm resulted in roof and antenna damage to a business in St. Maries.

Periodic heavy rain and spring time snow melt continued to cause travel problems in Pend Oreille County through the first half of April. Numerous secondary roads were damaged or cut by small stream and field flooding and debris flows. Most notably, Flowery Trail Road which crosses a mountain range and connects the towns of Usk and Chewelah was closed due to dangerous and unstable conditions caused by a 300 yard section of hillside slowly flowing onto the road bed.

Saturated soil conditions caused by periodic heavy rain and snow melt during the month of March and the first half of April produced extensive field flooding along the Colville River and debris flows through out the county. Flooding also damage area roads with the most notable event being the closure of Highway 395 near Colville due to persistent flooding. The road was cut by a flood in March, and opened back up in the first week of April. Thirteen other secondary roads in the county were closed due to flooding and debris flows.

On April 2nd a hillside along the Porcupine Bay Road near the Porcupine Bay recreation area gave way and cut the road, cutting off access to the campground. Three days later the hillside was still moving. Extensive debris was washed into Lake Roosevelt during this slide. The road remained closed into the month of May and may be closed indefinitely with repair work not able to commence until soil conditions stabilize and careful analysis of further landslide hazard is complete.

Saturated soil conditions brought about by spring snow melt in March and periodic heavy rain in March and early April resulted in areas of small stream, field and basement flooding over parts of Spokane County. Numerous secondary roads were closed due to flooding on the roads and damage to the road beds.
A Flash Flood closed Highway 129 near where Rattlesnake Creek meets the Grande Ronde River. The road was closed for three hours and then opened up to one lane of traffic.

The USGS Spokane River Gage at Spokane recorded the Spokane River continuing to achieve Minor Flood level through the first few days of April. The river receded to below the Flood Stage of 27.0 feet at 5:15 PM PST on April 3rd.
The Shirrod Hill Mesonet station reported a wind gust of 62 mph as a thunderstorm gust front passed through the area. The ASOS station at the Lewiston Airport reported a wind gust of 56 mph.

The USGS River Gage near Jack Creek recorded a rapid rise  beginning on April 8th with a peak on the 9th near 8.5 feet. A second rise occurred on April 14th. While no official Flood Stage exists for this gage, this period of high flow corresponded with extensive flooding of bottom lands, roads, bridges and parks along the river. One residence on the river bank  was undermined and eventually toppled into the river.  ||A second river gage at Keller, also with no official Flood Stage was observed to achieve 9.7 feet on April 8th which may have set a record flow for this gage.

A residence located along the Sanpoil River just north of Keller was undermined by the flooding river and eventually toppled into the river. The resident was able to remove most of the valuables and furniture from the house before it went into the river.

Ferry County was affected by numerous road washouts due to areal flooding and debris flows during much of the month of April. Travel was disrupted through out the county with at least 20 roads closed or reduced to one lane due to damage. ||The most notable road closures include Highway 395 near Boyds, which suffered a 100 foot section of the road washed away into a 20 foot deep chasm on April 13th, and Highway 21 where a temporary one lane bridge was constructed to cross a 100 foot total washout of the road 15 miles south of Republic, and the Inchelium Highway near Inchelium where a debris flow cut the road on April 15th. All of these roads are major north-south highways through the county. ||The Sanpoil River flooded during this period causing one house to wash away into the river and threatened another home as the flood undermined the bluff it was located on.

Areal Flooding, mudslides and debris flows in rough terrain plagued Okanogan County during the month of April as a result of saturated soil conditions brought on by periodic heavy rain and spring snow melt. ||At least 24 roads through out the county were closed or damaged by washouts and debris flows during the month. ||Most notably, State Route 20, a main east to west route between Twisp and Okanogan was cut by a washout on April 7th near mile post 221 and then suffered a second washout on April 15th near mile post 211. Both washouts cut deep chasms through the road bed and closed a 10 mile section of the highway through the rest of the month and into May. Five residences between these washouts were isolated while the road was repaired.||A second major route through the county, State Route 153, was cut by a debris flow on April 7th causing a temporary closure of a three mile stretch near Pateros.||Salmon Creek near Conconully flooded and damaged summer homes and properties along it's banks.

A debris flow on Myrtle Creek Road exposed two cases of vintage dynamite apparently buried and abandoned after road work in the 1970s. The dynamite was rendered safe and removed but the road remained closed due to unstable surface conditions through April 13th.

Periodic heavy rain during the month of April and spring time snow melt created small stream flooding and road closures due to debris flows through out Okanogan County during April and extending into the month of May. State Highway 20 remained closed between Twisp and Okanogan due to a pair of extensive debris flows which cut the road in April. The north fork of Salmon Creek overflowed due to snow melt and flooded streets in and near the town of Conconully periodically through the middle of May. Most notably a surge of water 7 to 8 feet deep covered a bridge in Conconully due to a log jam break-up on the creek on the evening of May 5th. A bridge in Oroville was also flooded on May 5th when Nine Mile Creek overflowed it's banks. On May 29th a landslide in the Chiliwist Creek Valley destroyed a driveway and debris from the slide plugged a culvert creating a flood from the backup, which blocked another driveway and flooded Chiliwist Road.

Periodic heavy rain during the month of April along with spring-time snow melt created saturated soil conditions during April and continuing through the first week of May. Numerous small stream floods and debris flows plagued the county. In the Curlew area on May 5th and 6th several reports of flooding were reported, including Curlew Creek near Curlew flooding basements and roads and Toroda Creek overflowing and affecting several bridges. Cottonwood Creek northwest of Curlew washed out a driveway to a residence. Highway 395 was washed out near Boyds in April and remained closed and under extensive repairs during the month of May.
A thunderstorm wind gust lofted a glass table top and shattered it near East Wenatchee.
The remote weather observing station at Entiat recorded a thunderstorm wind gust of 62 mph.
A thunderstorm wind gust toppled a tree onto power lines near Twisp. A power outage resulted from this damage.
A thunderstorm briefly produced 1 inch diameter hail in the town of Nespelem.
The Alder Ridge remote weather observing station reported a thunderstorm wind gust of 66 mph.
A funnel cloud was reported appending from a weak thunderstorm just west of Sprague.
A funnel cloud was observed for approximately 10 minutes over the mountains west of Moyie Springs.
Washington State Patrol reported a debris flow partially blocking Highway 25 twelve miles south of Kettle Falls.
The Forest Service reported a debris flow cutting Prospector Creek Road near Calder which necessitated a temporary road closure.
A debris flow blocked Highway 3 near Kendrick.
A member of the public photographed a brief funnel cloud near Plaza.
The Spromberg Canyon Wildfire burned 42 acres and a sawmill over three days near Leavenworth before being contained by firefighters.

The Stehekin River Gage at Stehekin recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 24.0 feet at 5:00 PM PST May 23rd, crested at 24.8 feet at 12:30 AM May 24th and then dropped below Flood Stage at 10:15 AM May 24th. The river then rose again above Flood Stage at 8:30 PM PST on May 28th, crested near 25.8 feet at 2:15 AM on May 31st, and remained above Flood Stage through early June.

The Kettle River Gage near Ferry recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 18.5 feet at 6:45 PM PST on May 5th, passed through the Major Flood Stage of 20.5 feet and crested at 20.7 feet at 10:15 PM on May 6th. The river dropped back below Flood Stage at 11:15 PM on May 7th. The river rose above flood stage again later in the month.
The Kettle River flooded with water over Highway 21 near Little Goosmus Creek.
The Kettle River flooded with water washing out portions of Customs Road near the Canadian Border.

The Kettle River Gage at Ferry recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 18.5 feet at 12:15 PM PST on May 23rd. The river rose above Moderate Flood Stage and crested at at 19.6 feet at 8:00 PM May 24th then dropped back below Flood Stage at 8:15 AM on May 25th.

The Okanogan River Gage at Tonasket recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 15.0 feet at 7:30 AM PST on May 23rd. The river crested multiple times in Minor Flood around 16.5 feet and continued to flood into the month of June.

The Methow River Gage at Pateros recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 10.0 feet at 8:30 AM PST on May 31st. The river crested in Minor Flood at 10.3 feet at 4:00 PM May 31st and then dropped below the Flood Stage at 10:30 PM May 31st.

The Okanogan River Gage at Tonasket recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 15.0 feet at 7:30 AM PST on May 23rd. The river continued to flood into the first week of June, achieving and cresting at the Moderate Flood Stage of 17.0 feet from 7:30 PM to 10:15 PM on June 1st. The Diamond Creek wildfire was first reported on July 23rd, and the cause remains unknown. The fire spread aggressively through the month of August eventually consuming 128,272 acres of forest land in the Pasayten Wilderness of northern Okanogan County. The fire crossed the international border into Canada on August 29th. The fire originated and spread through a remote region of wilderness and no structures were lost or injuries reported. The fire continued to burn through the month of September.

The lightning caused Bridge Creek fire burned 3,711 acres of timber on the Colville tribal reservation during the month of August. Some road closures were imposed due to firefighting activity, but no structures were lost and no injuries were reported.
