The USGS Lake Level Gage at Osoyoos Lake near Oroville recorded a  steady rise in the lake level beginning on May 5th. There is no official Flood Stage for this lake. The Lake level peaked at 916.5 feet on May 12th, and remained slightly above 916 feet through May 20th before steadily falling through the end of the month.

The USGS River Gage on the Moyie River at Eastport recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 9.0 feet at 9:00 PM PST on May 7th. The river crested at 9.5 feet at 9:30 PM PST on May 8th. The river receded below Flood Stage at 5:45 PM on May 11th.  The river rose again on May 16th and crested at 9.1 feet at 9:15 PM before receding below Flood Stage on May 17th at 7:30 AM.

The USGS Lake Level Gage on Lake Pend Oreille near Hope recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 2063.5 feet on May 18th. The lake level crested at 2063.8 on May 23rd. The lake level remained at or slightly above Flood Stage through the remainder of the month.

The USGS River Gage on the St. Joe River at St. Maries recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 32.5 feet at 2:15 PM PST on May 7th. The river crested at the Minor Flood level of 33.9 feet at 6:00 PM PST May 10th and remained at that level until beginning to recede on May 11th. The river receded below Flood Stage at 10:45 AM PST on May 19th.

The USGS River Flow Gage at Abeni Falls Dam which controls the flow of the Pend Oreille River surpassed the Flood Flow of 95,000 Cubic Feet per Second (CFS) at 2:30 PM PST on May 11th. The flow increased and passed through the Moderate Flood Flow of 115,000 CFS at 12:15 PM on May 18th. The flow continued to increase and peaked at the  Moderate Flood reading of 121,000 CFS at at 5:00 AM on May 27th. The flow continued to fluctuate between 118,000 CFS and 121,000 CFS through the end of May. The flow receded to below the Flood Flow on June 6th.

The USGS River Flow Gage at Abeni Falls Dam which controls the flow of the Pend Oreille River below the dam surpassed the Flood Flow of 95,000 Cubic Feet per Second (CFS) at 2:30 PM PST on May 11th. The flow increased and passed through the Moderate Flood Flow of 115,000 CFS at 12:15 PM on May 18th. The flow continued to increase and peaked at the Moderate Flood reading of 121,000 CFS at at 5:00 AM on May 27th. The flow continued to fluctuate between 118,000 CFS and 121,000 CFS through the end of May. The flow receded to below the Flood Flow on June 6th.||Above Albeni Falls Dam the river is a slow moving extension of Lake Pend Oreille. The USGS Lake Level Gage on Lake Pend Oreille near Hope recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 2063.5 feet on May 18th. The lake level crested at 2063.8 on May 23rd. The lake level remained at or slightly above Flood Stage through the remainder of the month.

The USGS River Gage on the Kettle River near Ferry recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 18.5 feet at 6:00 AM PST on May 5th. The river continued to rise and passed through the Moderate Flood Stage of 19.5 feet at 11:30 AM on May 7th, and through the Major Flood Stage of 20.5 feet at 6:00 PM PST on May 9th. The river crested at a new record flood level of 22.5 feet at 6:15 PM on May 10th. This level broke the previous record level of 21.2 feet set in 1948. The river then receded, passing down through the Major Flood Stage on May 11th, and below the Moderate Flood Stage on May 19th. The river finally receded below the Flood Stage at 1:30 AM PST on May 20th.

The USGS River Gage on the St. Joe River at Calder recorded a sharp rise to the Flood Stage of 13.0 feet at 10:45 AM PST on May 7th. The river crested right at the Flood Stage for about 4 hours before slowly receding after 3:00 PM.

The USGS River Gage on the Similkameen River at Nighthawk recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 14.0 feet at 8:00 PM PST on May 8th. The river continued to rise and passed through the Moderate Flood Stage of 15.0 Feet at 3:45 AM on May 10th. The river crested at 15.5 feet at 12:15 AM on May 11th before receding below the Flood Stage at 6:15 PM on May 12th. The river rose again and passed through Flood Stage at 9:00 PM PST on May 14th, with this second crest reaching the minor flood level of 14.8 feet at 2:00 AM on May 17th. The river then receded back below the Flood Stage at 5:00 AM on May 19th.

The USGS River Gage on the Okanogan River at Tonasket recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 15.0 feet at 4:45 AM PST on May 5th. The river continued to rise, passing through the Moderate Flood Stage of 17.0 Feet at 11:45 PM on May 7th and through the Major Flood Stage of 18.0 feet at 9:15 AM on May 9th. The river crested twice, the first and highest crest of 19.7 feet at 4:30 PM PST on May 11th and the second crest of 19.3 feet at 10:30 AM on May 18th. The river then receded, passing below Major Flood Stage at 9:30 PM on May 20th and below the Moderate Flood Stage at noon PST on May 22nd. The river continued to slowly recede finally passing below the Flood Stage at 2:30 AM on May 27th.

The USGS River Gage on the Methow River at Pateros recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 10.0 feet at 1:00 PM PSt on May 9th. The river crested at 10.7 feet at 7:15 AM on May 10th then receded below the Flood Stage at 7:30 PM on May 10th. The river rose again on May 16th and briefly touched the Flood Stage at 10.0 feet at 11:45 AM on May 16th before receding again.

The USGS River Gage on the Stehekin River at Stehekin recorded a rise above the Flood Stage of 24 feet at 5:15 PM PST on May 15th. The river fluctuated slightly above and below the Flood Stage due to the diurnal snow melt and run off cycle through May 17th, with a maximum crest of 24.4 feet at 11:00 PM on May 15th. The river dropped below the Flood Stage and continued to recede at 3:30 AM on May 17th.

Heavy rainfall from a slow moving thunderstorm during the evening of May 20th caused Flash Flooding across Ladlow Butte Road near Garfield. A car was swept off the road and into a ditch. The car's occupants were rescued without injury by bystanders. Photos taken as the flood was abating showed mud and debris over a quarter mile stretch of roadway.
Highway 3 between Juliaetta and Kendrick was cut by a debris flow caused by a slow moving thunderstorm.  The debris was cleared by highway crews and the road was re-opened about an hour later.
Five main and 4 secondary roads in Latah County were washed out or otherwise damaged by heavy rains.

Heavy rain in and around Lewiston created numerous urban flooding problems during the morning of July 18th. A retention pond overflowed and caused a hillside washout with another hillside also suffering erosion damage. A number of roads and parking lots were flooded in the city and a block of apartments in low laying poor drainage areas suffered  first floor and yard flooding.

Flooding from heavy rain producing thunderstorms occurred in Ephrata during the late evening of May 17th. Basin Street, the main road through the downtown business district  was flooded with 4 to 8 inches of water with first floor damage to multiple businesses in the downtown area. A portion of the ceiling in the Department of Corrections building collapsed due to standing water on the roof.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms during the evening of May 17th resulted in a debris flow of rocks and mud onto the Malaga-Alcoa Highway betrween mileposts 10 and 12.

The rise on Osoyoos Lake, which has no official Flood Stage, began to flood properties and seep into homes around the lake shore beginning on May 9th.  By the morning of the 10th  flood waters had submerged Deep Bay Park and were flooding the basements and threatening the first floors of homes along Blackler Road and the boat launch along Veranda Drive.  As the lake crested and the level stabilized between May 11th and May 19th extensive flooding of low lands along the lake was noted with Veterans Memorial Park completely inundated. Numerous lake shore homes suffered first floor flooding during this crest period.

On May 8th Conconully Lake reached the spillway level on the Conconully Dam due to heavy Spring runoff from the upper reaches of the Salmon River. The increased flow caused flooding along the river below the dam and resulted in the flooding and subsequent closure of Salmon Creek Road between Spring Coulee Road and Danker Cutoff Road.

The City of Conconully reported that the North Fork of Salmon Creek had a rapid rise on May 6th, causing water to flow over the Broadway Street Bridge. Over a span of the next  two weeks, the North Fork rose and fell daily with the diurnal snow melt cycle, causing the water to occasionally flow over the bridge.

The flooding form the Similkameen River backed up into Palmer Lake during the high water period. This resulted in flooding along the Loomis Oroville Road along the lake shore and the inundation of Chopaka Road which crosses Palmer Creek which drains Palmer Lake into the Similkameen River.
A small debris flow deposited rock onto the southbound lane of Highway 395 near Orient. Traffic was delayed as the rock was removed.

Spring time snow melt caused the Chewuch River near Winthrop to rise and cause minor flooding during the second and third weeks of May. Roads and fields along the river were inundated and a few homes suffered yard inundation and first floor minor flooding.
Highway 21 along the Kettle River near the intersection of Big Goosmus Road was closed due to flooding.

Flood water flow undermined the western abutment of the Rockcut Road Bridge across the Kettle River near Orient. This erosion is considered critical by an inspecting engineering firm. The bridge remains open but with weight and speed restrictions.

One home and two outbuildings were destroyed in the Upriver Beacon Fire near Spokane.
The Angel Springs Wildfire destroyed 6 structures, at least two of them homes, and 7 outbuildings.
The Chelan Hills Wildfire damaged 4 homes in the Orondo area as well as destroying several outbuildings and damaging orchards and crops in the fire area.
A firefighter was injured when he was trapped by flames while fighting the Grass Valley Wildfire.

The Washington Dept. of Natural Resources reported two homes and several additional structures destroyed in the Boyds Wildfire. The cost of fire fighting resources involved in containing this fire was calculated at 12.6 million dollars.

The Crescent Mountain Wildfire 20 miles southwest of Twisp was caused by lightning and first detected on July 29th. The fire grew through the month of August eventually consuming 52,609 acres of timber in the upper reaches of the Twisp River Valley before being contained in mid September.  The fire burned in unpopulated wilderness and no structures were lost. The cost of the resources to fight the fire was estimated at 39.4 million dollars.

The Cougar Creek Wildfire 12 miles northwest of Ardenvoir was started by lightning in late July. During the month of August the fire grew and consumed 42,712 acres of timber and brush. While the fire burned in unpopulated forest land, the margins of the fire did threaten nearby homes at times, however no structures were lost. The firefighting resources necessary to bring the fire under control were estimated at 42.3 million dollars.

The McCleod Wildfire 10 miles north of Mazama was started by lightning and first reported on August 11th. The fire grew to 24,411 acres, consuming mostly timber in unpopulated  mountainous terrain before being largely contained by mid September. No structures were lost but some back country roads were closed. The cost of fighting the fire was calculated at 13.1 million dollars.

The Cougar Wildfire near Hope Idaho is believed to have been started by lightning on July 28th. The fire grew and eventually burned 7,866 acres of timber. No structures of homes were lost or threatened. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 5.1 million dollars.

The Surprise Creek Wildfire in a remote portion of Shoshone County is believed to have been caused by lightning on July 27th. It grew and eventually burned 3300 acres of timber in a wilderness area. No structures were threatened or lost. The cost of firefighting resources to contain the blaze was calculated at 1.3 million dollars.

The Rampike Wildfire is believed to have been caused by lightning on July 31st. The fire burned 3100 acres in a remote wilderness area of Shoshone County. No structures were lost or threatened. The cost of the resources necessary to contain the fire was calculated at  1.0 million dollars.

The Smith Creek Wildfire is believed to have been caused by lightning on July 27th. The fire consumed 1113 acres of timber in the mountains 7 miles NE of Priest Lake. No structures were lost or threatened. The cost of the resources needed to contain the fire was calculated at 299 thousand dollars.

An air quality sensor at Twisp recorded Unhealthy air quality from August 3rd through August 27th with occasional spikes into the Hazardous category. A cold front passage on August 27th brought breezy westerly winds which ventilated the area.

An air quality sensor in Wenatchee recorded a period of Unhealthy to Hazardous air quality during the third week of August. On August 21st and 22nd smoke concentration peaked in the city with air quality spiking into the Hazardous range.

An air quality sensor in Nespelem recorded periods of Unhealthy air quality due to smoke from area wildfires through much of August. Air quality deteriorated into the Hazardous range for much of August 19th, and fluctuated between Unhealthy and Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups until a frontal passage brought breezy conditions and some rain on August 27th.

An air quality sensor in Inchelium recorded periods of Unhealthy air quality due to smoke from area wildfires through much of August. Air quality deteriorated into the Very Unhealthy and Hazardous range from August 19th through August 20th before marginally improving until a cold front passage on August 27th.

An air quality sensor at Winthrop recorded Unhealthy air quality from August 3rd through August 27th with occasional spikes into the Very Unhealthy category. This sustained period of Unhealthy air quality was the result of large nearby wildfires and was only alleviated with a breezy cold front passage on August 27th.

The air quality sensor at Omak recorded Unhealthy air quality through most of the month of August. On August 19th and 20th air quality deteriorated into the Hazardous range before moderating back to Unhealthy until a cold front passage cleared out the smoke on August 27th.

An air quality sensor in Republic recorded almost continuous Unhealthy air quality due to smoke from area wildfires through much of August. Air quality deteriorated into the Very Unhealthy and Hazardous range from August 19th through August 20th. Air Quality fluctuated between Unhealthy and Very Unhealthy until a cold front passage on August 27th ventilated the region.
An air quality sensor in Colville recorded occasional periods of Unhealthy air quality with a few spikes into the Very Unhealthy range due to smoke from area wildfires through much of August.

An air quality sensor in Quincy recorded generally Unhealthy air quality with occasional spikes into the Very Unhealthy and Hazardous range from August 19th through the 21st as smoke from regional wildfires blew into the region.

An air quality sensor in Moses Lake recorded generally Unhealthy air quality with a brief peak into the Very Unhealthy range from August 20th through the 21st as smoke from regional wildfires blew into the region.
The air quality sensor in Lewiston recorded a period of Unhealthy to Very Unhealthy air quality on August 21st due to smoke from regional wildfires.

Air quality Sensors at Sandpoint and near Bonners Ferry measured periods of Unhealthy air quality during the third week of August due to smoke from nearby wildfires. Air quality deteriorated into the Hazardous range at both locations on August 19th and 20th, and remained occasionally Unhealthy until a cold front passage with significant rain passed through the region on August 27th.

An air quality sensor near Hayden recorded periods of Unhealthy air quality during the third week of August as smoke from regional wildfires drifted into the area. Air quality  deteriorated into the Very Unhealthy range for much of August 20th and into the 21st.

The air quality sensors in the Spokane area recorded generally Unhealthy air quality with a period of Hazardous air quality during the second and third weeks of August as smoke from regional wildfires infiltrated the region. Air quality deteriorated into the Hazardous range for much of August 20th and 21st and remained generally Unhealthy until a cold front passage ventilated the area on August 27th.

The USGS River Gage on the Palouse River near Potlatch recorded a rise to the Flood Stage of 15.0 feet at 8:30 PM PDT on April 9th. The river continued to rise and pass through the Moderate Flood Stage of 16.0 feet at 10:45 pm on the 9th. The river crested just under the Major Flood Stage of 17.0 feet at 5:00 am on the 10th and then began receding. The river passed down through the Moderate Flood Stage at 3:00 PM on the 10th and then receded below the Flood Stage at 9:15 PM PDT on April 10th.

The USGS River Gage on Paradise Creek in Moscow recorded a sharp rise to above the Flood Stage of 9.2 feet at 2:45 PM PDT on April 9th. The creek continued to rise passing through the Moderate Flood Stage of 10.0 feet at 7:00 PM. The creek continued to rise and crested at 11.4 feet at 7:15 PM which is a record high crest beating the previous record crest of 11.3 feet set in 1996. The creek then quickly receded passing below the moderate Flood Stage at 8:00 PM and then below Flood Stage at 9:15 PM PDT.

The USGS River Gage on the South Fork of the Palouse River at Pullman recorded a rise to the the Flood Stage of 7.0 feet at 10:30 PM PDT on April 9th. The river level stabilized and fluctuated just at or slightly below Flood Stage until 4:00 AM April 10th and then receded.||This was a minor and short lived flood event which mainly impacted bottom lands and pedestrian walkways through park land along the river.

Several mud slides were reported over Highway 12 just west of Kamiah on the morning of April 9th. One of the slides completely covered the road and caused the temporary closure of this primary road through the region while crews cleared the debris.

High water in the Clearwater River augmented by a levee break along Lawyer Creek  produced extensive flooding near the confluence of these two streams on the eastern edge of the city of Kamiah. The flood waters were reported to be waist deep in the Kamiah Riverfront Park. Flood waters also partially inundated a lumber yard, undermined a railroad grade and trestle crossing Lawyer Creek and high water prohibited access to the city's water plant. The levee was temporarily repaired by the public works department as the creek receded.

Lapwai Creek flooded bottom lands and flowed over Highway 95 in places between Lapwai and Culdesac causing the temporary closure of this primary route through the region. A few homes were threatened by the flood waters but no damage to any structures was reported.

Heavy rain during the afternoon and evening of April 9th caused Paradise Creek running through Moscow to rapidly rise and inundate lower elevation portions of the city along the creek.  In addition heavy rain in the hills north of Moscow caused flash flooding in the northeastern areas of the city as runoff drained through valleys and ravines along North Polk Street and into the East D street neighborhood, then through downtown before  draining into Paradise Creek.  In some areas flood waters were reported to be 3 feet deep with numerous roads, intersections and underpasses impassable. Most of the reported damage involved basement and first floor flooding of buildings.

Missouri Flat Creek experienced a Flash Flood which resulted in the North Grand Avenue business district being inundated with up to 4 feet of water in places. Numerous businesses were damaged and parked cars were floated and carried away. Pullman police and fire crews made numerous water rescues of stranded customers and employees of at least 4 businesses including the rescue of 16 people from one business.  There were no known injuries and by the next morning the creek had receded back into it's banks.
Local media photographed and broadcast on social media a large tree pushed over onto a house in central Spokane.

Three large trees were uprooted at the southern end of Priest lake by locally strong winds during the morning of May 26th. The trees crushed an SUV and damaged a pickup truck as well as heavily damaging a shed with minor roof damage to the adjacent house. This was a very localized event and probably the result of terrain channeling between nearby mountains.
A spotter submitted photos of a Flash Flood flowing down a driveway and washing out a culvert creating a breach in the driveway 3 to 4 feet deep with a similar width.

The Benewah County Sheriff reported two trees blown down by thunderstorm winds near St. Maries. Trees were blocking a road.

Firefighters on the Williams Flats Wildfire reported numerous roads washed out due to heavy rain from a series of thunderstorms passing over the burn area. An estimated 2 inches of rain from persistent thunderstorms impacted the active fire site. Sixty four firefighters were stranded overnight when their access road was washed out by a flash flood during the evening of the 10th. They were successfully extracted the next morning using an alternate route.
Mud and debris from thunderstorm heavy rain blocked State Route 3 miles east of Douglas.
Water was reported over State Route 2 and flooding into an adjacent house east of Waterville due to thunderstorm heavy rain.

Numerous streets in the southern portion of Wenatchee were reported as flooded and residents were advised to avoid travel in the area. Mud and debris flows in the Squilchuck, Pritcher and Halverson Canyons flowed down these canyons and into the city. In addition heavy rain in the city of Wenatchee backed up storm drains and sewers and contributed to the flooding.

The Williams Flats Fire started on August 2, 2019 after a band of early morning thunderstorms with lightning moved across the eastern portion of the Colville Indian Reservation. The Spring Coulee Fire began from an unknown cause during the afternoon of September 1st two miles west of the town of Okanogan. The fire was quickly contained after burning 142 acres of range land and damaging some vehicles. One firefighter was severely burned while fighting the fire and eventually died of his injuries on October 2nd.

A hillside along route 231 near Valley began slowly sliding and compromising the road bed. Temporary traffic lights were installed to restrict traffic to one lane while highway crews stabilized the road bed.

The Road 11 brush fire consumed approximately 10,000 acres of grassland and wheat. Several outbuildings were lost and there was damage to one home. The cost of firefighting resources to contain the blaze was calculated at 980,000 dollars.
A local utility company reported a tree blown into powerlines due to strong winds caused a small power outage.
The Pullman Radio reported that the Chief Timothy Wildfire started when a motorhome traveling along the Snake River caught fire. There were no injuries.

The Colockum Road Wildfire grew and eventually burned 2,967 acres of brush and grassland. No structures were lost, but the fire threatened over 100 homes and several crops and orchards. The cost of firefighting resources to contain the blaze was calculated at 2.4 million dollars.
The Bartholomew Fire destroyed four structures: one residence and three outbuildings.
The cost of firefighting resources to contain the blaze was calculated at 2.6 million dollars.
The Nespelem Transfer Station and the Colville Tribal Recycling Center were severely damaged.

The Green Fire, 12 miles northeast of Riverside, started on July 27th by human causes and burned a total 1,480 acres of grass and brush before contained on August 1. There were Level 1 evacuation notices, but no structures or homes were damaged or lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 250,000 dollars.

The Anglin Fire, 8 miles east of Tonasket, started on July 27th by human causes and burned a total 1,992 acres of timber before contained on August 1. Three structures were destroyed: one human residence and two out buildings. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 1.8 million dollars.

The Coulee Meadows Fire, 18 miles east of Ephrata, started on July 30th and burned a total 794 acres of dry sage and brush before contained on August 5. There were Level 1 evacuation notices, but no structures or homes were damaged or lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 250,000 dollars.

The Badger Lake Fire, 10 miles southwest of Cheney, started on August 18 by unknown causes and burned a total 244 acres of timber before contained on August 21. There were Level 3 evacuation notices and approximately 30 structures threatened, but none were damaged or lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 1.3 million dollars.
A Mesonet station 2 miles west of Athol measured a wind gust of 60 mph. There were an estimated 115,000 people in Kootenai County who lost power due to downed trees and powerlines from the winds.

The Idaho Department of Lands closed State Highway 41 for 2 miles after Hunter Fire 2 grew to 100 acres and jumped the highway. People were evacuated on both sides of the highway in Blanchard. Four homes were destroyed by the wildfire.
The cost of firefighting resources to contain the blaze was calculated at 937,528 dollars.

The Palmer Wildfire grew and burned a total 17,988 acres of timber and brush.  The cost of firefighting resources to contain the blaze was calculated at nine million dollars. No structures were lost, but the fire threatened many in the towns of Loomis and Nighthawk.

The Customs Road Wildfire, 1 mile west of Curlew, was started by human causes on September 7th. There were 11 structures lost. The wildfire grew to 2,208 acres, driven by wind and topography, before largely contained by mid-September. The cost of fighting the fire was calculated at 850,000 dollars.
The Washington Department of Transportation reported State Route 26 closed for 21 miles from US 395 to Washtucna due to poor visibility from blowing dust.
The Washington Department of Transportation reported State Route 23 closed between St. John and Sprague due to blowing dust and wildfire smoke.

The Cold Springs Wildfire, 3 miles south of Omak, was ignited due to unknow causes late September 6th. It was fueled by a high wind event and grew rapidly. The wildfire became known as the Pearl Hill Wildfire when it crossed the Columbia River. Two adults were severely injured and one infant passed away. After numerous road closures and a total 55 structures lost, the total acres damaged grew to 413,653 with 8.4 million dollars cost fighting the fire. The wildfires were fully contained by mid-September.

The Inchelium Complex Wildfires, 1 mile north of Inchelium, was ignited by human causes on September 7th. The Inchelium Complex was comprised by three fires on the Colville Indian Reservation: Inchelium Highway, Fry, and Kewa Field. The wildfires grew to 19,399 acres of timber and brush. They were driven largely by strong winds and dry conditions before contained by the end of September. The cost of fighting the fires was calculated at 8.1 million dollars.

The Whitney Wildfire, 6 miles northwest of Davenport, was ignited by a downed powerline on September 7th. Fueled by dry conditions and strong wind gusts, the extreme fire behavior and rapid growth lead to a total 127,430 acres, which included buildings, livestock, and grass lost. The cost of fighting the fire was calculated at 2.5 million dollars and contained by mid-September.

The Manning Road Wildfire, 13 miles northwest of Colfax, was ignited by unknown sources on September 7th. It was fueled by a high wind event and dry conditions. A total five structures were lost and acres damaged rose to 2,885 before containment a week later. The cost of fighting the fire was calculated at 250,000 dollars.

The Malden Wildfire was ignited by a tree on a powerline and fueled by high winds and dry conditions on September 7th. Eighty percent of the small community of Malden, and nearby town of Pine City, were destroyed by the fire. This included 121 homes, eight businesses, 94 other buildings, and more than 15,000 acres. The cost of fighting the fire was calculated at 800,000 dollars and fully contained by September 14th.

The Grant County Sheriff reported Road W-NE, north of Waterville, was closed due to blowing dust and near zero visibility.
National Weather Service employees received numerous reports of visibility near 1/2 mile due to blowing dust on Highway 2 between Grand Coulee and Waterville.

A Grant County official reported road closures 5 miles northeast of Moses Lake. Blowing dust created near zero visibility due to strong winds. There was one fatality in a vehicle stopped on the side of the road to wait out the poor visibility. The car was subsequently rear ended by a semi-truck.

Local broadcast media reported many trees down on cars and power lines, as well as road closures, across the greater Spokane area. Avista Utilities and Inland Power reported a total of over 8000 customers without power due to strong winds in the greater Spokane area.

The Idaho State Police reported that State Highway 41 at Spirit Lake Cutoff Road was shut down due to many crashes during heavy snowfall.

A NWS employee, via webcam at a snow board, estimated Mt. Spokane received 7.0 inches of new snow accumulation. The remainder of the northeastern Washington region only received a few inches of snow from this winter system. The heavier snowfall kept to the Spokane Metropolitan area.

The Spokane Metropolitan area received 3 to 5 inches of new snow accumulation. Local broadcast media reported that Spokane police responded to an approximate 33 crashes in Spokane starting December 25th evening into December 26th morning. The roads became slick with the snow coverage leading to numerous collisions.
The heaviest snowfall in the Idaho Panhandle was observed in the far northern counties. Numerous CoCoRaHS observers and spotters submitted reports of 4 to 6 inches of new snow accumulation.

Most of the central Idaho Panhandle received 1 to 2 inches of snow, if any, especially in locations such as the Coeur d'Alene area. There was a public report of 4.0 inches of snow accumulation in Dalton Gardens.
A member of the public, in east Wenatchee, reported an estimate 4.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
The Idaho Palouse received between 4 to 6 inches of new snow accumulation. This led to poor road conditions and numerous spin offs and crashes across the entire Idaho Panhandle.

The northern Idaho Panhandle received a significant amount of snowfall during from the late morning hours into the early afternoon on December 30th. Local spotters and observers reported 6 to 12 inches of new snow accumulations across Bonner and Boundary Counties.

In the Upper Columbia Basin, from Ritzville to Odessa, there were reports of 4 to 6 inches of new snow accumulation. Vehicles driving too fast for poor road conditions led to many collisions and slide offs along Interstate 90 and other state highways.
A member of the public, in Newport, reported 5.0 inches of new snow accumulation.

Heavy snow accumulation was not as widespread in the Washington Palouse, compared to locations to its north, but there were spotter and CoCoRaHS reports from 4 to 8.5 inches of new snow.
A trained spotter, in Marshall, recorded 11.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
A trained spotter, 2 miles east of Five Mile, recorded 10.1 inches of new snow accumulation.

The National Weather Service office in Spokane recorded 8.7 inches of new snow accumulation.
Spokane International Airport recorded 8.1 inches of new snow accumulation. This broke the previous snow fall record for this date of 5.4 inches set in 1990.

The Washington Department of Transportation recorded 20 inches of new snow accumulation at Stevens Pass. This occurred within a 48 hour time period and led to difficult driving conditions from snow covered roadways.
The Mount Spokane Ski Resort recorded 20 inches total snow accumulation.
A CoCoRaHS observer, 2 miles southwest of Clayton, recorded 11.7 inches of new snow accumulation.

Across the varied elevation in northeastern Washington, there were reports 4 to 20 inches of new snow accumulation. Two mountain resorts, 49 Degrees North Ski and Mountain Spokane, reported 12 - 20 inches at the summits. Other locations, from Clayton to Northport, received 5 to 12 inches.
A trained spotter, in Metaline Falls, recorded 10.5 inches of new snow accumulation.

Heavy, freezing fog created slick roadways which led to rolling cars, collisions, and blocked roadways. Many occurred on US Highway 2 and Interstate 90. Washington State Highway troopers responded to 63 crashes overnight December 25th and the 26th. There are no reports of injuries or fatalities.

Local broadcast media, KREM 2, reported that Spokane police responded to an approximate 33 crashes in Spokane between December 25th evening and December 26th morning. The roads became slick with the snow coverage leading to numerous collisions.

There were sustained winds 20 - 30 mph with gusty winds to 55 mph in the eastern slopes of the Cascades. Local utility companies reported 1,200 people in Chelan County without power due to large trees falling on power lines.

Gusty winds were measured to 55 mph at the Pullman/Moscow Airport. Pullman city law enforcement reported large trees down and two power poles broken with lines hanging. This left approximately 2,300 people without power and numerous road closures in Pullman.
The RAWS site at Alder Ridge measured wind gusts to 61 mph.

Numerous locations across the Methow Valley, in Okanogan County, received heavy snowfall in this winter storm. There were reports of 24 hour accumulations of 7 to 9 inches, as well as 48 hour reports of 12 to 14 inches.
A member of the public, in Mazama, reported 9.0 inches of new snow accumulation.

A member of the public, in Twisp, reported 7.0 of new snow accumulation.

Most of the northern Panhandle received 24 hour rainfall totals up to 0.25 - 0.80. The near to freezing temperatures and wet surfaces created isolated black ice and slick surfaces. The Bonners Ferry Herald reported one fatality and one person injured after hitting black ice on Highway 95 outside of Eastport. Their car hydroplaned and overturned into a creek.

Idaho State Police reported several spun out semi-trucks on US-95 on Mica Grade leaving lanes blocked during the afternoon. There are no known injuries or fatalities. 13 miles to the north, Coeur D'Alene Airport had been reporting snow, ice fog, and mist throughout the day.

Idaho State Police reported a crash on Interstate 90 near Rose Lake leaving lanes blocked. There are no known injuries or fatalities. Local observation stations and sensors had been reporting snow, ice fog, and mist throughout the day.

Across Spokane County, there were reports of total snowfall from 5 to 11 inches. Spokane International Airport recorded 8.1 inches of new snow accumulation. This broke the previous snow fall record for this date of 5.4 inches set in 1990. By late afternoon, Washington State Patrol reported that there were more than 100 crashes, with of them 65 in Spokane County. On Interstate 90 in the Spokane metropolitan area, the snowy morning commute created collisions, spin-offs, and travel delays. No reports of fatalities and the total amount of injuries are unknown.

In addition to wet conditions, the evening of the 21st into the early morning hours of the 22nd were windy. The winds were sustained 20 - 30 mph and gusts up to 35 - 55 mph throughout the entire region. There were scattered power outages due to downed trees on power lines. An amateur radio operator in Athol recorded winds reaching gusts to 53 mph.
A RAWS site in Corral Creek recorded winds reaching gusts to 58 mph.

A heavy, wet snow fell overnight into the early morning hours of January 4th. The significant snow accumulations fell in the Methow Valley and eastern Cascades, which received 4 to 6 inches over approximately 12 hours.
A trained spotter, 7 miles northwest of Malott, recorded 4.5 inches of new snow accumulation. It was still snowing at time of report.
A trained spotter near Twisp recorded 5.5 inches of new snow accumulation. It was still snowing at time of report.

A CoCoRaHS observer, 12 miles north of Leavenworth, recorded 7.5 inches of new snow accumulation.
The Washington Department of Transportation site at Stevens Pass recorded 17.5 inches of new snow accumulation.

A heavy snow fell overnight into the early morning hours of January 12th. Numerous locations across the Okanogan Highlands, especially in northern Ferry County, recorded 4 to 6 inches of new snow accumulations in the early morning hours of January 12th.
A CoCoRaHS observer, 12 miles northwest of Entiat, recorded 7.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
