A member of the public, 7 miles north of Molson, reported 5.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
The Mission Ridge Ski Resort reported 8.0 inches of new snow accumulation.

Two mid-level waves brought an impressive two day snow accumulation. Enhanced lift brought a boundary of heavy snow on January 27th. Light snow fell on the following day, but there was a two-day total snow of 9 to 11 inches in the Wenatchee area along the Columbia River.
A CoCoRaHS observer, 12 miles northwest of Entiat, recorded 10.3 inches of new snow accumulation.

Two mid-level waves brought an impressive two-day snow accumulation. Enhanced lift brought a boundary of heavy snow on January 27th. Light snow fell on the following day, but there was a two-day total of 7 to 12 inches across the Methow Valley.
A CO-OP observer, 8 miles west of Lucerne, recorded 11.9 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CO-OP observer in Stehekin recorded 7.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CoCoRaHS observer, 10 miles northwest of Kettle Falls, recorded 8.5 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CO-OP observer in Wilbur recorded 4 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CoCoRaHS observer, 9 miles north of Davenport, recorded 5.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
A trained spotter near Carlton recorded 7.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
A boundary of heavy snow moved through eastern Washington late January 26th into the 27th. It brought a 24 hour total snow accumulation of 4 to 6 inches of snow in the southern Okanogan Valley.
A CO-OP observer near Mazama recorded 7.9 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CoCoRaHS observer near Twisp recorded 9.5 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CO-OP observer, 9 miles north of Metaline Falls, recorded 5.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
A trained spotter in Springdale recorded 7.5 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CoCoRaHS observer near Clayton recorded 5.7 inches of new snow accumulation.
A CoCoRaHS observer near Evans recorded 7.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
A member of the public, near Northport, reported 4.0 inches of new snow accumulation.
Broadcast media reported approximately 40 miners trapped after the Galena Mine Complex lost power due to strong winds. Power was restored 24 hours later and all miners made it out safely.
Broadcast media reported numerous large pine trees blown down at Comstock Park in South Spokane. There are approximately 20 to 30 trees down in pictures taken from aerial view.
Broadcast media reported one fatality when a large tree fell on a car and trapped the driver.

Broadcast media reported that a motorist drove off the side of an embankment after the tree struck his truck on Highway 97, near Lake Coeur d'Alene. The motorist succumbed to his injuries at the scene.

There were numerous reports of downed trees and power lines, roadways blocked, and house damage due to the high winds early January 13th. A motorist drove off the side of an embankment after the tree struck his truck on Highway 97, near Lake Coeur d'Alene. The motorist succumbed to his injuries at the scene. Due to wind damage, an estimated 30,000 customers were without power in Kootenai County, most in the Coeur d'Alene and Hayden Lake area.
Broadcast media reported numerous blockages on US 95, north of Tensed, due to a crash from downed power lines.
A utility company reported approximately 10,000 customers without power in Bonner County due to damage to power lines from wind damage.

A hillside along State Route 2 began slowly sliding, striking the Department of Transportation guardrail, and partially blocked the eastbound lane. The mudslide was triggered by already saturated soil and wet snow.
Numerous reports and pictures from the public of trees and power lines down leading to many closed roads in the Five Mile area.
The broadcast media reported that a tree fell on a home and trapped an occupant in bed. They were extricated and hospitalized for a crush injury to the shoulder.
The Washington Department of Transportation reported US 395 was closed in both directions due to power pole and lines across the roadway near Clayton.
A member of the public in Rosalia reported that a vinyl fence was destroyed by the wind and created a large debris field about two blocks away.

A grain truck was blown over in a field, just north of Odessa. No one was driving at the time. The truck was empty and estimated to weigh 20,000 pounds. The wind gust speed is estimated based on the truck weight.

A wind storm, with 60 to 70 mph observed winds, impacted the Spokane and Coeur d���Alene region on the morning of January 13th. The Spokane International Airport tied its second strongest all time wind speed record of 71 mph. This led to extensive damage in the Spokane area and the neighborhoods south of Interstate 90 were the hardest hit. The total home damage is unknown and damage totals is estimated, much due to downed pine trees and power poles. There were numerous reports of downed power lines and poles on Interstate 90, which blocked interstate lanes and on ramps. One fatality occurred when a large tree fell on a car and trapped the driver. Additionally, a tree fell on a home and trapped an occupant in bed. They were extricated and hospitalized for a crush injury.

The Washington Department of Transportation and local broadcast media reported numerous events of downed power lines and poles on Interstate 90. It blocked interstate lanes and on ramps. These closures occurred during the morning hours, with some impacting the morning commute.

Local news reported that the iconic 50 feet tall butterfly in Downtown Spokane fell over in the wind gusts. The butterfly structure is covered in fabric that extends to approximately 60 feet. Previously, city leaders said that it could withstand winds to up to 110 mph.

The heaviest snow fell in the northern Cascades and eastern Cascade valleys overnight Monday, January 11th, into early Tuesday afternoon. The Cascade valleys received 6 to 10 inches of new snow accumulation. The mountains and passes received 12 to 15 inches. With saturated soils and snow covered branches, the heavy snow caused isolated power outages and fallen trees. The Chelan County Public Utility District reported widespread outages in the county with most restored by the afternoon of January 12th.
The Washington Department of Transportation reported State Route 20 south bound lanes blocked due to trees down near Usk.
Avista Utilities reported approximately 2,200 customers without power in the Lewis Clark Valley and Camas Prairie due to high winds.
A measured wind gust of 62 mph was recorded at the Wenatchee Airport. Local utilities reported power outages in parts of the Wenatchee area due to wind damage.
A trained spotter reported a 20 foot by 60 foot metal roof blew off a building in Dishman near Spokane Valley.
A brief tornado touched down six miles southwest of Kettle Falls.

Lookout Pass and Silver Mountain ski resorts reported 9 to 12 inches of new snow accumulation. The heavy, new snow loading and winds led to high avalanche danger. The Idaho Panhandle Avalanche Center advised against backcountry travel in the St. Regis and Silver Valley. Severe driving conditions across Lookout Pass on Interstate 90 made for difficult travel on the 6th and overnight.

The Washington Department of Transportation reported that Stevens Pass received 18 inches of new snow accumulation in 24 hours. Heavy snow led to limited visibility and poor road conditions. US Highway 2 was closed due to spinouts, dangerous travel, and to perform avalanche control.

Heavy snow and winds created dangerous driving conditions across the Idaho Palouse. There were reports of new snow accumulations measuring 6 to 10 inches in locations near Highway 95, such as Viola, Harvard, and Potlatch. Winds with gusts to 30 mph created blowing snow and drifts with heights up to 12 inches.

The Silver Mountain Ski Resort reported 6 inches of new snow accumulation. There were numerous other reports of 4 to 5 inches of snow in the Silver Valley. New snow pack and weak layers led to moderate avalanche danger in the mountainous terrain.

Heavy snow resulted in 4 to 7 inches of new snow accumulations across the Lewiston-Clarkston Valley, especially in Lewiston. Most snow fell in less than 12 hours overnight into the early morning hours of February 15th. Snow covered roads and blowing snow made travel dangerous, especially for the morning commute. Light snow continued through the day and on the 16th. The Lewiston-Nez Perce County Airport set a new record February 15 snowfall with 3.7 inches, which was previously 0.6 inches in 2019. The airport received another 1.6 inches on the 16th.

The Spokane area received 4 to 6 inches of heavy snow. Most snow fell overnight, but lingering snow continued during the day. Snow accumulation and poor visibility on Interstate 90 and local roadways had a significant impact on the morning commute. The Washington State Patrol reported eight crashes on I-90 in just 45 minutes. Poor driving conditions continued into the evening commute, but not as severe as in the morning.

Post Falls and Coeur d'Alene area received 3 to 6 inches of heavy snow. Most snow fell overnight, but lingering snow continued during the day. Snow accumulation and poor visibility on Interstate 90 and local roadways had a significant impact on the morning commute. There was near zero visibility from Liberty Lake to Coeur d'Alene on I-90. The Washington State Patrol and Department of Transportation reported numerous collisions on the I-90 corridor between Spokane and Coeur d'Alene. Poor driving conditions continued into the evening commute, but not as severe as in the morning.
Heavy snow fell in the Pomeroy area overnight February 14th into the early morning hours on the 15th. Several CoCoRaHS and trained spotters reported 5 to 7 inches of new snow accumulation by 8AM PST.

Heavy snow and breezy winds created blowing snow and dangerous road conditions across the Washington Palouse. Widespread snow fell - from 4 inches in Oakesdale, 8 inches in Pullman, and 12 inches in Dusty. Winds, with gusts to 35 mph, created blowing snow, which limited visibility and contributed to poor driving conditions.

Heavy snowfall, over 72 hours, brought severe and dangerous conditions across the Cascades, especially on US-2 and Stevens Pass. From 6AM February 14th through 6AM February 17th, 40 of snow fell at the pass. This contributed to numerous closures of on U-2 at Stevens Pass due to vehicle spinouts, avalanche control, and clean up. Breezy winds in the Cascades contributed to blowing snow and poor visibility.

Several bands of heavy snow closed Stevens Pass at 6PM February 22nd through 8AM on February 23rd. The Washington Department of Transportation reported 11 inches of new snow accumulation at Stevens Pass. Heavy snow continued falling through the day adding to already dangerous driving conditions. The Northwest Avalanche Center reported very dangerous avalanche conditions and urged people to avoid backcountry travel due to strong winds and the ongoing snow. There are no reports of injuries due to avalanches.

There was heavy snowfall and ice coverage in the eastern Cascades, which led to pass closures, dangerous road conditions, and snow slides. US-2 Highway at Stevens Pass was closed on February 25th night due to the slide which covered the roadway. There were 27 inches of new snow accumulation at the pass on February 25th and 26th. The Washington Department of Transportation reported ice covered power lines were hanging less than 12 feet from the roads and led to further closures.

The Washington Department of Highways reported a large rock slide on US-2 in Pine Canyon. The debris covered approximately 300 yards, which included many large rocks. The highway was closed from MP140 near Orondo to MP148 near Waterville. There was no known time of reopening the road at time of report.
A culvert failed leading to mud, water, and debris over State Route 23, at MP33 south of Lamont. The road was closed for clean up. No other reports of damage.

Strong winds and dry conditions resulted in blowing dust and near zero visibility in southeastern Douglas County. A state trooper reported that an eight vehicle pile-up, with minor injuries, occurred along State Route 26, near Othello. Blowing dust led to hazardous driving conditions.

The Department of Transportation closed an approximate 30 mile stretch of Interstate 90 in Adams County due to dangerous, life threatening travel conditions. There was near zero visibility from blowing dust across the interstate. Wind gusts reached 45 to 55 mph at nearby RAWS and COOP stations.

Sustained southwest winds reached 40 mph for several hours across northern Idaho Panhandle behind a powerful cold front. Gusts of 60 mph or higher were recorded in Athol. Numerous trees were blown down and created road hazards.
The Corral Creek RAWS site recorded a peak gust of 66 mph. Numerous other sites in Lewis and southern New Perce counties reached gusts of 50 to 60 mph.

Sustained west-southwest winds reached 40 mph for several hours across the southern Idaho Panhandle behind a powerful cold front. Gusts of 60 mph or higher were recorded at the Shirrod Hill Idaho Department of Transportation site.

Multiple large trees were down due to strong winds and created road hazards in Hayden, Coeur d'Alene, and Post Falls. A power outage was reported due to power lines down. A tree fell on a home in Coeur d'Alene. No reports of injuries.

The National Weather Service in Spokane recorded a wind gust of 58 mph. There were many other local sites in Spokane County with 45-50 mph gusts. The strong winds downed many large trees across the county causing power lines down, power outages, and hazardous roadways to due blockages. There was extensive damage in northern Spokane, including two homes were damaged from downed trees.
A CoCoRaHS observer in Thorton measured a 59 mph maximum wind gust on March 28th. The time is an estimate based on other peak winds in the area.

Across the upper Columbia Basin many observation sites measured wind gusts from 40-50 mph. The peak winds occurred in northern Lincoln County at the Keller Ferry site. The ferry on State Route 21 was closed due to gusts of 60 mph and higher at the final crossing. There were no reports of damage or injuries.

Strong winds from a passing cold front created dangerous driving conditions in the dry Columbia Basin. The peak wind gusts reached 40-50 mph across the area, which included Moses Lake, Ephrata, and Othello. A significant portion of Interstate 90 and State Route 26 were closed due to blowing dust. The reduced visibility on SR-26, southeast of Othello, caused an eight car pile up. There were two, non-life threatening injuries.

The Department of Transportation measured 14 inches of snow at Stevens Pass on March 28th. At the Cascade Crest on Highway 2, there were reports of light-to-heavy snow and blowing snow due to gusty winds. This led to hazardous road conditions and avalanche control planned for the next day. There are no reports of accidents or injuries.

A trained spotter in Blachard reported large trees down from strong winds. Wind gusts up to 50 mph were recorded at numerous observation sites across Bonner and Boundary Counties. There were over 15,000 Northern Lights Power Company customers in the northern Panhandle without power due to wind damage.

The Northern Lakes Fire District responded to multiple fires from downed power lines and smoldering slash piles that rekindled with the wind in the Hayden, Rathdrum, and Garwood area. Hundreds of trees were blown down in the Chilco area leading to numerous damaged buildings. There were recorded wind gusts 40-50 mph at numerous nearby RAWS and Mesonet sites.

Hundreds of trees were blown down in the Chilco area in Kootenai County. A shop and a few outbuildings were damaged. There were recorded wind gusts 40-50 mph at numerous nearby RAWS and Mesonet sites.

Strong winds and blowing dust made for a difficult task fighting a small brush fire off Palouse Highway in southern Spokane. There were many power lines and trees down across the roads with blowing dust resulting in near zero visibility. There were no fatalities or injuries. No lost property or evacuations needed.
A CWOP site in Washtucna measured a 69 mph maximum wind gust.

Motorists driving from Lake Roosevelt to Spokane encountered several areas of 1/16 mile visibility or less due to blowing dust. This occurred on both U.S. Highway 2 between Davenport and Deep Creek and Washington State Route 25 north of Davenport. There were no reports of accidents due to the near zero visibility.
A Mesonet station in Beverly observed wind gusts 30-40 mph. There were reports of several broken power poles and power lines covering streets.

High winds led to moderate blowing dust, widespread trees down, and property damage in Green Acres. The peak wind gust of 60 mph is estimated based on damage reports. Across southern Spokane, the winds downed many large trees causing power lines down, power outages, and hazardous roadways to due blockages.

Strong winds and dry conditions resulted in blowing dust and near zero visibility in southern Adams County. A National Weather Service employee reported blowing dust on US-395 south of Ritzville. There were numerous walls of dust across State Route 26, from Hatton Coulee to Othello, with zero visibility. No known accidents or injuries.

A National Weather Service employee reported blowing dust south of Othello, on State Route 24, with near zero visibility. There were reports from Washington State Patrol of blowing dust across I-90 near Warden and Moses Lake. There were no reports of accidents or injuries.

Strong winds, with gusts from 40 to 55 mph, led to blowing dust and near zero visibility in Odessa. There were no reports of accidents in the area. Avista Utilities reported power outages in the Odessa area around the time of peak winds.

Strong winds, with gusts up to 50 mph, and dry conditions led to numerous dust storms throughout the afternoon in the Columbia Basin. The Department of Highways reported significant blowing dust with near zero visibility across roadways. Decreasing visibility contributed to multiple collisions on Interstate 90 around Moses Lake. This led to road closures for several hours. Avista Utilities reported power outages in the Othello area around the time of peak winds.
Gusty winds, measured up to 50 mph, occurred through the Eastern Cascade slopes into the upper Columbia Basin. There were public reports and photos of roof damage and broken tree limbs in Chelan.

Snow started in Sandpoint and Bonners Ferry shortly after midnight on the morning of the 13th, ending just before sunset.  The snow did change to rain during the afternoon according to the Sandpoint airport sensor, but remained as snow in most locations.  Snowfall observations generally ranged 4 to 8 inches, with 12 inches reported east of Colburn and southeast of Elmira.  A spotter in Spirit Lake reported a storm total of 8 inches, four of which fell in a span of 5 hours.

Snow moved into the area on the evening of November 9th through the morning of the 10th. There were numerous reports of 3 to 6 inches total snow in less than 24 hours. Trained spotters and CoCoRaHS observers, in northern Pend Oreille and Stevens counties, reported the most snow accumulation.
Snowfall reports along the Highway 95 corridor ranged from 2 to 6 inches.  Some of the higher amounts included 6.6 inches on the western bank of Lake Pend Oreille and 6 inches in Dover.

Several snowfall reports from the Coeur d'Alene and Post Falls metro area indicated snowfall amounts ranging from 3 to 4 inches.  Temperatures warmed above freezing around 8am on the 10th making additional accumulations light.
Snow accumulations from the Silver Valley ranged from 2 to 4 inches.  There was a CoCoRaHS report from Avery in the St. Joe River Valley of 4.9 inches of snow.

Heavy snow fell in the Cascades with 10 inches reported by the DOT at Blewett Pass and 25 inches at Stevens Pass. 10.8 inches fell near Mazama, 18.8 inches west of Lucerne, and 12.8 inches at Holden Village.  There were reports of 7 inches in the Wenatchee River Valley.
Snowfall reports included 12 inches in Inchelium,  7 inches north of Republic, 4.6 inches east of Tonasket and 8 inches southwest of Chesaw.

Widespread heavy snowfall reports included 12 inches at Cusick and Orin, 10.7 inches near Diamond Lake, 9.4 inches at Clayton, 8 inches northeast of Deer Park, 7 inches at Metaline Falls and Newport.  The heaviest snowfall report was 15 inches at Carrs Corner.  Local utility companies reported 8,586 customers without power, mainly in Colville, due to snow laden trees and branches falling on power lines.

Light snow fell overnight with temperatures above freezing.  Reports in the Spokane area ranged from 1 to 3 inches on grassy surfaces.  There was a report of 7.3 inches of snow fall in the northwest corner of Spokane county.  At the U.S. Highway 2 interchange, Interstate 90 was closed briefly for a snow laden power line that fell across the road.

Light snow fell overnight, but temperatures remained above freezing and limited accumulations. The Highway 97 corridor saw 1 to 2 inches of snow.  A few outlying locations east of Tonasket picked up 3 to 5 inches of snow. An observer outside of Malott received 7 inches of snow.

The Coeur d'Alene area received 5 to 8 inches of new snow accumulation from this passing winter storm. Idaho State Police reported several spun out semi-trucks on US-95 on Mica Grade leaving lanes blocked during the afternoon. There are no known injuries or fatalities. Coeur D'Alene Airport had been reporting snow, ice fog, and mist throughout the day. Numerous power outages were reported by Avista Utilities on December 30th.

An extended period of excessive heat occurred across the Wenatchee area from June 26th to July 2nd. Afternoon high temperatures ranged from 102 to 114 degrees most afternoons. Overnight lows only fell into the mid-to-upper 70 degrees. There were two all time records set in the Wenatchee area. On the 28th, a new record high maximum temperature was set at Chelan with a high of 111 degrees. On the 30th, Wenatchee's overnight low only dropped to 79 degrees setting a new record high minimum temperature. Numerous cooling centers opened for those without air conditioning during the extreme heat. There are no known heat related deaths.

Republic reached an all time record high temperature of 109 degrees on the afternoon of June 28th. On June 30th, there was a report, from the Washington State Department of Transportation, that there was damage to road surfaces at Sherman Pass due to the heat. Local libraries were arranged to act as cooling centers across the area. There are no known heat related deaths.

Two locations reached an all time record high temperature on the afternoon of June 28th: Plain at 109 degrees and Mazama at 112 degrees. Local broadcast news reported that, near Inspiration Lake, a hiker was rescued after suffering from heat exposure. Local libraries were arranged to act as cooling centers across the area. There are no known heat related deaths.

From June 26th through 30th, peak temperatures across the Okanogan Valley reached 100 to 117 degrees. Overnight low temperatures cooled to a warm 67 to 73 degrees. Omak reached an all time record high temperature of 117 degrees on the afternoon of June 29th. Local libraries were arranged to act as cooling centers for those with out air conditioning across the area. A report from the Washington Department of Health stated that there were four heat-related deaths in Okanogan County. Further specifics were statewide and not given by counties.

From June 26th through July 2nd, the town of Mansfield recorded six consecutive days with a high temperature at 100 degrees or above. Local cooling centers were set up by emergency management for those without air conditioning across the area. A report from the Washington Department of Health stated that there were two heat-related deaths in Douglas County. Further specifics were statewide and not given by counties.

Two new all time records were set across the Palouse. The town of Rosalia set a new all-time maximum temperature of 111 degrees on June 28th and Pullman reached 106 degrees on June 29th. There was a report, from the Washington State Department of Transportation, that there was pavement buckling on Highway 195 due to the heat. Due to the extreme high temperatures, Pullman cooling center was established for those without air conditioning across the area. There are no known heat related deaths.

The town of Northport set a new all-time maximum temperature of 113 degrees on June 28th. Over a five day range, Deer Park Airport afternoon highs reached 100 to 111 degrees and one overnight low only cooled to 74 degrees. There was a report, from the Washington State Department of Transportation, that there was roadway peeling on State Route 20, west of Tiger. There are no known heat related deaths.

From June 26 to 30th, Moses Lake and Ephrata had high temperatures reach between 103 to 116 degrees, which is abnormally warm for end of June. Ephrata broke their all time high maximum temperature when the airport reached 116 degrees on June 29th. Local libraries were arranged to act as cooling centers for residents without air conditioning. There are no know heat-related deaths.

Two new all time record high maximum temperatures were set across the upper Columbia Basin on June 28th: Wilbur reached 110 degrees and Odessa 115 degrees. Due to the extreme high temperatures, local libraries for those without air conditioning across the area. There are no known heat related deaths.

A period of excessive heat left numerous heat-related impacts and new all time record high maximum temperatures in the Spokane Metropolitan area. Spokane International Airport broke their record when they observed an afternoon high of 109 degrees on June 28th. The record warmest low temperature followed on June 30th when only cooling to 78 degrees. Avista Utilities performed two blackouts due to the heat which impacted approximately 8300 customers. There are eight known heat-related deaths in Spokane County. There are no other known specifics about the fatalities.

Temperature observations taken at Lewiston Airport were unseasonably warm from June 26th through July 2nd. No records were broken in the Lewiston Area; however, high temperatures ranged from 103 to 115 degrees with lows only cooling to 67 to 78 degrees. On the 29th, Avista Utilities performed blackouts in Lewiston to help cope with the exceptionally hot temperatures. There are no known heat-related deaths.

Temperature observations taken in Wallace and St. Maries, Idaho were unseasonably warm from June 28th through June 30th. The high temperatures were at, or above, 100 degrees all three days. St. Maries set a new maximum June temperature when reaching 108 degrees on the 30th. There are no known heat-related deaths.

The excessive heat on June 26 through 30th brought record breaking high temperatures across the Idaho Palouse. Three towns have new June high temperatures when afternoon highs reached Moscow at 105 degrees, Plummer at 107 degrees, and Potlatch at 107 degrees. There are no known heat-related deaths.

During the late June heatwave, the Coeur d'Alene Airport had four consecutive days with afternoon highs at 100 degrees or above. Two of those days were 108 degrees. On June 28th through 30th, Post Falls high temperatures were 105 to 108 degrees. The Coeur d'Alene Ironman was held on the 27th and extra precautions were taken to prevent heat exhaustion due to the extreme temperatures. There is no known count of heat-related injuries at the event.

Three locations reached an all time record high temperature on the afternoon of June 28th: Priest River at 108 degrees, Sandpoint at 106 degrees, and Bonners Ferry at 108 degrees. Priest River and Blanchard set up cooling centers to help those without air conditioning. There are no known heat related deaths.
Hail, up to 1 inches, fell in Moscow and Viola as a strong thunderstorm cell moved through early morning June 15th.
Numerous reports of hail, from 1 to 1.25 inches, fell in Pomeroy as two strong thunderstorm cells moved across northern Garfield.

There were numerous reports of hail, from 1 to 1.5 inches, associated with two strong thunderstorm cells that moved across western Whitman County. The reports were from Endicott, Peyton, St. John, and La Crosse.

The Whitehall Road Fire, near Coulee Meadows, started on July 8th and burned a total 800 acres before it was contained on July 10th. The fire was ignited by lightning with a passing evening thunderstorm. Local news reported that gusty winds created blackout conditions from blowing dust and fire spread in many directions. There are no known injuries or property loss. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 300,000 dollars.

The Red Apple Fire started on July 13th and burned a total 12,288 acres before it was contained on July 25th. It began at the US-97 and US Highway 2 corridor, on the outskirts of Monitor. The cause of ignition has not been confirmed and under investigation by authorities. There were 400 structures threatened and numerous evacuations. There was one firefighter with a minor injury and five outbuildings lost in the fire. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 4.7 million dollars.

The Batterman Road Fire, in eastern Wenatchee, started on July 4th and burned a total 14,100 acres of brush before it was contained on July 13th. The cause of ignition is unknown and under investigation by authorities. There were no injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 6.6 million dollars.

The Steptoe Canyon Fire started on July 21st and burned a total 2,605 acres before it was contained on July 27th. The cause of ignition was due to lightning from thunderstorms that passed through the area that evening. There were homes, rangeland, and crops threatened. There are no known homes lost or injuries from the fire. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 550,000 dollars.

There was damage from wind at the Art on the Green Festival in Downtown Coeur d'Alene. The winds toppled tents, knocked over tables, and damaged vendor items. Wind speed is approximate based off damage report. There is no known total loss from wind damage and no reports of injuries.
There were reports of a power pole and lines down due to strong winds. Blowing dust reduced visibility across Highway 28 in Soap Lake.
A rock slide blocked both lanes of State Route 20 near mile post 166, two miles west of Cutthroat Creek Road. Heavy rain in the area lead to the slide and water over the roadway.

The US Forest Service reported a debris flow that blocked the NF-4440 Road, one mile east of the Gilbert Trailhead. The flow was approximately four feet deep and stranded two cars overnight. Time is estimated based on radar.

There were widespread gusts up to 60 mph, which led to power outages, across Shoshone County. Approximately 40 miners trapped after the Galena Mine Complex lost power due to strong winds. Power was restored 24 hours later and all miners made it out safely.

Gusty winds occurred across the Idaho Palouse early January 13th. Downed power lines on US Highway 95 led to a vehicle crash and numerous blockages until the road was safely cleared. The estimated wind gust of 50 knots is based on wind damage.

Strong winds led to US Highway 395 closure in both directions due to power pole and lines across the roadway near Clayton. Wind gusts are estimated based on wind damage and surrounding wind speed observations.

The Leland Complex was composed of four wildfires ignited by lightning on July 7th: Bonami, Johnson Creek, Pine Creek, and Sand Mountain. The fires burned a total 3,514 acres in Clearwater and Latah Counties before all fully contained by August 14th. There were no injuries or structures lost. Numerous campgrounds, forest areas, and hiking trails were closed. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fires was calculated at $10,305,160.

Lightning ignited several wildfires across Garfield and Asotin counties on July 7th: Dry Gulch, Lick Creek, and Silcott. The Silcott Fire was contained in four days after burning 8,633 acres. By the 8th, Dry Gulch and Lick Creek fires merged and were fought as Lick Creek Fire until containment on August 26th. Steep slopes with insect infestation and dead material from past fires hindered access to fight the fire. The hot and dry conditions added to the vast acreage burned. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the 80,638 acre wildfire was calculated at $24,379,000.

Lightning ignited the Chuweah Creek Wildfire on the Colville Indian Reservation, just outside of Nespelem, on July 12th. This was signficantly driven by strong winds and very dry conditions. There are no known injuries or fatalities. Damages include 7 buildings/homes, 7 outbuildings, and numerous cars. The quick spreading fire did not give all farmers time to evacuate livestock which lead to many horse and cattle injuries and fatalities. The Chuweah Creek Fire burned a total 36,752 acres before it was contained on August 30th. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $8,915,000.

Heavy rainfall, with reports of 0.40 - 0.50 in one hour, occurred in the early evening hours of August 20th outside the town of Conconully. The brief heavy rainfall lead to 4 to 6 inches of debris flow on the roadway. Some local observation sites reported a total 0.75 - 1.25 of rainfall after a long, evening of showers. Additionally due to the heavy rain, a roadway in Twisp was covered in mud and gravel. There were CoCoRaHS and spotter reports of over 2.0 of rain in Twisp that evening.
There was a rock slide, partially blocking a road near a golf course in Orondo, due to brief, heavy rain.

The Snake River Complex was composed of three wildfires ignited by lightning on July 7th: Captain John Creek, Hoover Ridge, and Shovel Creek. Located in steep terrain in the southern Idaho Panhandle, the fires merged and burned a total of 109,444 acres before fully contained on August 19th. There are no known injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $9,498,972.

The Trestle Creek Complex was originally composed of seven fires ignited by lightning July 9th. After two mergers, there were five fires: Trestle 1, Trestle 2, Trestle 3, Trestle 5, & Trestle 6.  There was significant wind driven fire growth starting spot fires up to �� of a mile ahead of the fire. The Trestle Creek Complex fires burned a total of 6,631 acres before fully contained on September 11th. There were five injuries and no known structures lost. There were numerous areas, near Hope, Idaho, that were closed by the Forest Service. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $14,175,000.

The Character Complex was composed of two wildfires ignited by lightning north of Kellogg, Idaho on July 10th: Deceitful and Prichard fires. The fires burned a total of 12,367 acres before fully contained on September 30th. There were 14 firefighter injuries and 3 structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $29,123,714.

The Larkins Fire Complex was composed of 12 wildfires ignited by lightning on the St. Joe River Ranger District of the Idaho Panhandle National Forests on July 16th. The fires burned a total of 4,638 acres before fully contained on September 30th. There are no known injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $150,000.

The Upper Lime Creek Fire was ignited by lightning on August 4th and jointly managed with Summit Trail Fire. Steep, rough, and often hard to access terrain challenged containment. Additionally, many red flag conditions, with wind ignited spot fires, fueled fire spread. The fire burned a total of 376 acres on Colville Reservation before fully contained on September 15th. There are no known injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $643,051.

The Chickadee Creek Fire was ignited by an unknown source on August 4th and jointly managed with Walker Fire. Fire fighting crews faced many set backs such as red flag conditions, spot fires, and inclement weather preventing infrared aircraft flights. The fire burned a total of 5,855 acres of timber before fully contained on September 17th. There are no known injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $5,800,000.

Lightning ignited the Muckamuck Wildfire, which spread in and around the town of Conconully, on August 4th. The fire was on lands managed by Colville National Forest that had not burned in several years. There are no known injuries or fatalities. There were seven structures lost: four primary and three secondary. The fire burned a total of 13,297 acres before fully contained on September 16th. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $14,009,000.

The Ford Corkscrew Wildfire was ignited, near the town of Ford, due to an unknown cause on August 15th. The fire spread to the east, further threatening the towns and communities of Tum Tum, Springdale, Clayton, and Loon Lake, which led to numerous evacuations. Ford Corkscrew Fire destroyed at least 18 residences and eight outhouses or barns. There are no reports of injuries or fatalities. The fire burned a total of 15,777 acres before fully contained on September 17th. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $8,000,000.

The Summit Trail Fire was ignited during a lightning storm on July 12th and jointly managed with Upper Lime Creek Fire. Steep, rugged, and often hard to access terrain challenged containment. Additionally, many red flag conditions, with wind ignited spot fires, fueled fire spread. The fire burned a total of 51,328 acres on Colville Reservation before fully contained on September 30th. There are no reports of injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $58,000,000.

Bulldog Mountain and Mack Mountain fires were jointly managed after ignited approximately five miles apart on August 5th. The cause of the wildfires was lightning after thunderstorms passed through northeastern Washington. Steep, rugged terrain, with limited access, and heavy fuels led to difficulty with containment. There are no reports of injuries or fatalities. The pair of wildfires burned a total 6,723 acres on the Colville National Forest before fully contained on September 30th. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fires was calculated at $5,800,600.

The Stateline Fire Complex was detected on July 16th and composed of 12 individual fires: Berge Peak, Broadax, Deception,  Dolly Creek, Fly, Fly Creek, Simmons-Leg, Simmons Ridge, Simmons Ridge, Swimming Bear, Tumbledown, and Wampus Creek. |Ignited by lightning, there were numerous closures of roadways and recreation areas of St. Joe National Forest in southern Shoshone County. The Stateline Fire Complex burned a total of 13,199 acres before fully contained on October 8th. There were three firefighters injured with no structures threatened or damaged/lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $23,000,000.

Lightning ignited the Nason Fire, seven miles west of Lake Wenatchee, on August 4th. The fire was located in steep, rocky terrain that made it difficult for firefighters to safely access. The fire was slow with limited growth due to the shaded and moist, sub-alpine environment. The fire burned a total of 1,269 acres of the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forecast before fully contained on October 19th. There are no known injuries or structures lost. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $300,000.

Ignited due to an undetermined source on August 3rd, the Walker Creek Fire surrounded Bonaparte Lake and Wacounda in the Colville National Forest. On August 14th, it merged with the Spur Fire and from then on, they were managed as the Walker Creek Fire. Due to the proximity of communities, there were numerous level 3 evacuations for the first month. Three single residences and 14 minor structures were damaged or destroyed. Shorter burn windows, with cool and showery weather, led to the slow containment of the Walker Creek Fire. It burned a total of 23,733 acres before fully contained on October 15th. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fires was calculated at $26,171,346.

The Twentyfive Mile Fire, west of Lake Chelan, was ignited on August 15th with the cause of the fire remains under investigation. Cooler and wetter weather, in mid-September, helped slow fire behavior, but return to drier and warmer weather fueled fire activity. The proximity to Lake Chelan were useful for frequent water drops in rugged terrain. The fire burned a total of 22,117 acres of the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forecast and Twentyfive Mile Creek State Park before fully contained on October 19th. There were two homes destroyed with no known injuries or fatalities. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $31,887,321.

On the night of August 3rd, passing thunderstorms resulted in several new fire starts on the Colville Indian Reservation, which included the Hamilton and Whitmore Fires, northwest of Nespelem. Gusty, erratic winds effected fire behavior and lead to numerous evacuations of residences and animals. All evacuations were lifted by August 18th, but due to the dry fuels and red flag conditions, the smoldering continued into September. There are no reports of injuries or fatalities. The pair of wildfires burned a total 57,860 acres before fully contained by September 30th. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fires was calculated at $9,320,000.

The Cedar Creek, Delancy, and Varden wildfires were ignited by lightning during passing widespread thunderstorms, from July 8 to 11th, near Mazama. There was minimal activity by the Delancy Fire, which grew to 225 acres. Varden Fire grew 700 acres before merging with, and from then on referred to as, Cedar Creek Fire. This pair of fires burned a total 56,572 acres of the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest with containment by the end of September. There was very steep and rocky terrain, which made fire fighting efforts difficult. There are no known injuries/fatalities or structures damaged. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the three fires was calculated at a total of $41,562,323.

The Cub Creek 2 Wildfire was human caused, due to a spark from illegal activity, on July 16th. The fire was ignited five miles north of Mazama and grew to a total 70,186 acres before contained by the end of September. Several areas within the Cub Creek 2 Wildfire remained closed, after containment, due to public safety concerns such as tree hazards or increased probability of debris flows. There are no known injuries/fatalities or structures destroyed. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at $27,788,529.

There was a minor flood on the Okanogan River with a majority of the flood impacts found north of Tonasket. In this area, the flood plain is wide and flood water is able to spread. This includes a lot of pasture land or swampy areas near the river. In Ellisforde, there was a farm that had flooding on the property, which included pasture lands and outbuildings. The Okanogan River gage near Tonasket, at minor flood stage, crested at 15.48' at 12:00 PST on November 17th.

The Similkameen River, near Nighthawk and Oroville, reached minor flood stage on November 16th. There were post-flood surveys completed that found several properties damaged due to flooding. The flood impacted pasture land, structures, and crops both upstream and downstream of the Similkameen River gage at Nighthawk. The property and crop damage is an estimate due to no official reports of private and public land damage cost. The Similkameen River gage, near Nighthawk, crested at 14.41' on November 16th at 15:00 PST.

The Washington State Department of Transportation measured 11 of new snow at Stevens Pass on November 9th. The new snow accumulation grew to a total of 37. With heavy snow, there were gusty winds up to 30-40 mph in morning. These winds created blowing snow and poor visibility at the mountain pass on U.S. Highway 2.

Strong, gusty winds created widespread damage across Spokane County. With winds ranging from 50-62 mph, the peak gusts 62 mph were reached at the Spokane International Airport in the late afternoon. There was a portion of the metal roof ripped off the Fed-Ex building at the airport. There were numerous reports of obstructing trees and power lines down to leading widespread outages. The winds led to damage to buildings' siding and large signs across Spokane.

Widespread gusts of 50-63 mph were recorded across Whitman County. The Pullman-Moscow Airport ASOS site reached a peak wind gust of 63 mph in the late afternoon. There were trained spotter reports of downed trees across the Palouse and Pullman areas. The high winds lead to damage to the Pullman City Hall roof.
A Mesonet station in Pomeroy measured a wind gust of 62 mph in the late afternoon. Nearby Mesonet and CWOP stations in Peola and Pomeroy measured gusts from 50-60 mph.

Sherman Pass, on State Route 20, was closed due to 4-5 large trees down from the winds. They blocked the road in both directions for over an hour before cleared. There were several reports throughout Ferry County, in the Okanogan Highlands, of large downed trees, including ponderosa pines.

Southwest winds gusting to an estimated 40 to 60 mph led to widespread damage across the Coeur d'Alene area. There were many downed large trees and damaged power lines. Power outages across Coeur d'Alene, Post Falls, and Harrison left some customers without power for nearly 24 hours.
The RAWS site at Magee Peak (4720 ft) measured a wind gust at 82 mph. Surrounding, lower elevations measured peak wind gusts of 45 - 55 mph.
The Mesonet site at Athol measured a wind gust at 72 mph. There were law enforcement reports of downed power lines and power outages in Athol, Sagle, and Spirit Lake due to the gusty winds.

A winter storm moved across the Cascades late December 10th through the 11th. There were 10 to 14 inches of snow accumulating over 24 hours in locations such as Lucerne and Stehekin. Stevens Pass reported a two day total of 30.5 inches of snow. There were gusty winds with gusts up to 40 mph reported across the Cascade ridge tops. Travel became very difficult on US Highway 2, especially across Stevens Pass, due to heavy, blowing snow. These poor travel conditions lead to numerous slide-offs and accidents.

A winter storm moved through eastern Washington late December 10th into the 11th. It brought heavy snow, with 6 to 8 inches of snow accumulating, in the eastern Cascade valleys, including the towns of Plain and Leavenworth.

A winter storm passing through the northern Idaho Panhandle brought heavy snow and gusty winds on December 11th. Local ski resorts reported total snow accumulations up to 5 to 7 inches. The strong winds, with gusts up to 30 mph, led to blowing snow and poor travel conditions. The Idaho State Police reported numerous crashes, slide-offs, and spun-out semis on Interstate 90, mostly at Lookout Pass, that blocked lanes of traffic.

A winter storm passing through the northern Idaho Panhandle brought heavy snow and gusty winds on December 11th. There were total snow accumulations up to 4 to 6 inches across Bonner and northern Kootenai counties. The strong winds, with gusts up to 45 mph in Athol, led to blowing snow and poor travel conditions.

A winter storm moved through eastern Washington late December 10th into the 11th. It brought heavy snow, with 4 to 8 inches of snow accumulating, in the northeastern Cascade valleys, including the towns of Mazama and Winthrop.

Heavy snow with strong gusty winds led to poor visibility and dangerous driving conditions in the Cascades. The Washington Department of Transportation reported that Highway 2, at Stevens Pass, was closed due to multiple collisions and spin outs on December 23rd. Stevens Pass measured a three day total snow accumulation of 32 inches. Due to the short term, heavy snowfall, avalanche control was performed following the winter storm's passage.
Snow began to accumulate at 0700PST December 8th and tapered off mid-day December 9th. A total of 20 inches of snow fell in 24 hours on US Highway 2 at Stevens Pass.

Heavy, blowing snow led to white out conditions throughout Spokane Valley. The sudden snow squall and hazardous driving conditions led to stranded cars and multiple accidents, especially along Interstate 90.

Washington Department of Health reported that there was 1 cold-related death on December 27th in Spokane County. The exact time of death is unknown. Minimum wind chills were in the single digits across the county including 4 degrees at Spokane International Airport and 7 degrees at Felts Field.

Snow began to accumulate at 1000 PST, and tapered off by 1700 PST. A total of 6 to 7 inches of snow fell across the Lewiston Valley. A new record was set, for total snow on December 30th, of 7.2 at the Lewiston Airport.
Snow began to accumulate at 0100 PST, and tapered off to flurries by 1600 PST. A total of 5 to 7 inches of snow fell from Moscow to Potlatch.

Snow began to accumulate around 0000 PST and tapered off by 1600 PST. A total of 4 to 6 inches of snow fell from across the Washington Palouse, including Pullman and Colfax. There were reports of drifting snow and poor driving conditions across U.S. Highway 195 and State Route 26.
There were numerous reports of snow accumulations reaching totals of 9 inches by the late afternoon in Clarkston. The event time fame is approximate and Lewiston Airport was used for reference.

Accumulating snow overnight led to on-ramps and off-ramps at the exits packed with snow and ice in the early morning commute. Around 0830 PST, eastbound Interstate 90 in Spokane was fully blocked and closed due to a jackknifed semi-truck. There was a car wedged under the trailer leading to non-life threatening injuries for the driver. There were numerous accidents in the Spokane area due to hazardous driving conditions.
Snow began to accumulate around 0500 PST and slowly tapered off by 2100 PST. A total of 6 to 9 inches of snow fell across northern Idaho Panhandle, from Athol up to Bonners Ferry.
Scattered snow showers began around 0600 PST on December 18th with off and on snowfall throughout the following 24 hours. A total of 4.9 inches of snow accumulated in Moscow.

Scattered snow showers began around 0400 PST on December 18th with off and on snowfall throughout the following 24 hours. A total of 12 to 15 inches of snow accumulated at local ski resorts in Lookout and Kellogg.

Scattered snow began around 0300 PST on December 18th and slowly tapered off by 2100 PST. A total of 4 to 6 inches of snow accumulated across parts of northern Spokane and Pend Oreille Counties, including the towns of Elk and Tiger.

Snow and ice accumulated to the roadways which created hazardous driving conditions on U.S. Highway 2 near the Cascade ridgetops. Over a 24 hour time period, Stevens Pass and Stehekin recorded 13 to 18 inches of snow accumulation.

Early morning light snow across Spokane County led to hazardous driving conditions throughout the day. The Spokane Police Department received reports of over 100 collisions due to slick roadways. Overnight, roads iced over and led to multiple collisions and rollovers the following morning.

Slippery driving conditions, created by refreezing precipitation, led to numerous accidents during the evening commute in Spokane metropolitan area. The icy roads caused multiple vehicle pile ups, slide-offs, and road blockages. The Spokane Police Department issued an emergency alert requesting residents limit their driving due to the hazardous driving conditions.

Multi-day snow showers moved across northern Idaho Panhandle from December 24th into early 26th. It brought heavy snow, with 4 to 8 inches of snow accumulating in a 24 hour period. Another 1 to 3 inches of snow accumulated on the 25th with a two-day total snowfall of 7 to 11 inches in locations such as Spirit Lake, Priest River, and Twin Lakes.

A multi-day winter storm moved through northeastern Washington from December 24th into early 26th. Over a 24 hour time period, it brought heavy snow with 5 to 10 inches of snow accumulating across areas such as Metaline Falls, Deer Park, and Newport. Early on the 25th, the 49 Degrees North Ski Resort reported 15 to 20 inches inches of snow in the past 24 hours.
